title: Audio Shifting Adjustable
rawBody:
Audio shifting designed to create a perception of motion can be paused or turned off.


:::applies-when
- content includes audio shifting.
:::

:::except-when
- operating system or user agent triggers audio shifting.
:::

appliesWhen: • content includes audio shifting.
exceptWhen: • operating system or user agent triggers audio shifting.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For audio shifting caused by the digital content (in contrast to the operating system or user agent):

  1. Check that there is a setting to pause or turn off the audio shifting.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.
derived.methods: • Add a setting to pause audio shifting or turn it off.

plainEnglish.summary: Audio that pans or shifts between channels to simulate movement must be something a user can pause or switch off. It does not apply when the shifting comes from the operating system or the browser rather than from the content.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Simulated motion in sound can provoke nausea, disorientation or vestibular symptoms, and it makes speech harder to follow for people who process audio with one ear or with a hearing aid.

title: Haptic Stimulation Adjustable
rawBody:
Haptic feedback can be reduced or turned off.


:::applies-when
- content triggers haptic feedback.
:::

:::except-when
- the operating system or user agent converts non-haptic feedback to haptics at user request.
:::

appliesWhen: • content triggers haptic feedback.
exceptWhen: • the operating system or user agent converts non-haptic feedback to haptics at user request.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For haptic feedback caused by the digital content (in contrast to the operating system or user agent).

  1. Check if there is a setting that allows for reducing or turning off the haptic feedback.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.
derived.methods: • Add a setting to reduce haptic feedback or turn it off.

plainEnglish.summary: Vibration and other haptic feedback the content triggers must be reducible or switchable off. Haptics the operating system generates on the user's own request are out of scope.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Vibration can cause pain for people with chronic pain conditions or tremor, and it can be startling or disorienting for people with sensory processing differences.

title: No flashing over threshold (no exceptions)
rawBody:
Flashes are below the general flash and red flash thresholds without a minimum size.

:::applies-when
- Content includes flashes.
:::

:::note
Avoiding flashing entirely is the safest option because some people who may not know they are susceptible to photosensitive seizures, and some people may have a much larger view of content than the default (zoomed in or with the display close to the eye).
:::

appliesWhen: • Content includes flashes.
notes: Avoiding flashing entirely is the safest option because some people who may not know they are susceptible to photosensitive seizures, and some people may have a much larger view of content than the default (zoomed in or with the display close to the eye).
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each instance of flashing:

  1. Check that the flashing is below the size threshold defined by the general flash and red flash thresholds.
  2. Check that the flashing is below the frequency defined by the general flash and red flash thresholds.

Expected results

  • #1 or #2 is true.
derived.methods: • Design content without using flashing.

plainEnglish.summary: The same flash thresholds as the foundational requirement, but with no minimum-size allowance: a flashing area under the size threshold is no longer exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: The size exemption assumes a small flashing area is safe, which does not hold for everyone or for every viewing distance. Removing it closes that gap for people with photosensitive epilepsy.

title: No Flashing Over Threshold
rawBody:
Flashes are below the general flash and red flash thresholds.

:::applies-when
- Content includes flashes.
:::

:::except-when
- The flashing is essential.
:::

:::note
If there is an accessibility supported method of setting a user-preference to prevent flashing, the content can be considered to avoid flashing if that preference is respected.
:::

:::ednote
There is research into the size and frequency metrics underway. The exact values are likely to change before WCAG3 is published.
:::

appliesWhen: • Content includes flashes.
exceptWhen: • The flashing is essential.
notes: If there is an accessibility supported method of setting a user-preference to prevent flashing, the content can be considered to avoid flashing if that preference is respected.
editorNotes: There is research into the size and frequency metrics underway. The exact values are likely to change before WCAG3 is published.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each instance of flashing:

  1. Check if the flashing is essential.
  2. Check that the flashing is below the thresholds defined by the general flash and red flash thresholds.

Expected results

  • #1 or #2 is true.
derived.methods:
• Consider if flashing is essential and, if it is not, remove it.
  • Ensure that an accessibility supported user setting to avoid animation and flashing is respected.
  • Ensure that any flashing is below [X] size in the users’ view.
derived.intent:
Some people with seizure disorders can have a seizure triggered by flashing visual content. Most people are unaware that they have this disorder until it strikes. In 1997, a cartoon on television in Japan sent over 700 children to the hospital, including about 500 who had seizures. Warnings do not work well because they are often missed, especially by children who may not be able to read them.

The objective of this requirement is to ensure that content avoids the types of flash that are most likely to cause seizures when viewed even for a second.

plainEnglish.summary: Anything that flashes has to stay under the general flash and red flash thresholds, unless the flashing is essential to what the content is.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Flashing above these thresholds can trigger seizures in people with photosensitive epilepsy. This is one of the few accessibility failures that can cause immediate physical harm.

title: No visual motion (no exceptions)
rawBody: Content does not include pseudo-motion or visual motion lasting longer than 5 seconds.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each page/view:

  1. Check if content includes visual motion or pseudo-motion.

Expected results

  • #1 is false.
derived.methods: • Design content without using visual motion or pseudo-motion.

plainEnglish.summary: The same five-second limit on visual motion and pseudo-motion, with the 'essential' exception removed.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Where the exception applies, a user who cannot tolerate motion has no route through the content at all. This version leaves none.

title: No Visual Motion
rawBody:
Content does not include pseudo-motion or visual motion lasting longer than 5 seconds.

:::except-when
- The motion or pseudo-motion is essential.
:::

exceptWhen: • The motion or pseudo-motion is essential.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each page/view:

  1. Check if content includes visual motion or pseudo-motion.
  2. For each instance, check that the visual motion or pseudo-motion is essential.

Expected results

  • #1 is false, or
  • #2 is true.
derived.methods: • Consider if motion or pseudo-motion is essential, and if it is not, refrain from including it.

plainEnglish.summary: Visual motion and pseudo-motion - things like parallax scrolling and moving backgrounds - must not run longer than five seconds, unless the motion is essential.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Sustained motion can cause nausea, dizziness and migraine in people with vestibular disorders, and it pulls attention away from the content for people with attention-related disabilities.

title: Safe Content Review
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:  

* We have reviewed content for violent, explicit, or troubling content and provided appropriate warnings before accessing the content. 

::assertion-required

- title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
- date of when the review was conducted
- date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

:::note
Troubling content will vary based on culture or individual situations, and reviews should take target audiences into consideration.
:::

notes: Troubling content will vary based on culture or individual situations, and reviews should take target audiences into consideration.

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion, not a technical check: the organisation states that it has reviewed its content for violent, explicit or distressing material and warned people before they reach it. The assertion has to name who made it and when the review happened.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Encountering distressing content without warning can trigger trauma responses, and people who need to prepare for or avoid such material cannot do so if nothing signals it is coming.

title: Single Flash
rawBody:
Content does not include a change of contrast (over 4.5:1) going from light to dark (or dark to light) of more than 30% of the visible content area (viewport).

:::except-when
- A new page/view is loaded.
- The flash is essential.
:::


:::ednote
This is a new provision for a big, intense, single on/off flash. This is reported as a trigger by group members, but we need data on this, and a definition that includes size/intensity to avoid including non-triggers such as menus.
:::

:::ednote 
This provision relies on the color contrast algorithm in WCAG 2. When the algorithm is updated for WCAG 3, the contrast metric will also be updated.
:::

exceptWhen:
• A new page/view is loaded.
  • The flash is essential.
editorNotes: This is a new provision for a big, intense, single on/off flash. This is reported as a trigger by group members, but we need data on this, and a definition that includes size/intensity to avoid including non-triggers such as menus.
This provision relies on the color contrast algorithm in WCAG 2. When the algorithm is updated for WCAG 3, the contrast metric will also be updated.
derived.tests:
For each change of contrast:

  1. Check if the change of contrast is triggered by a loading a new page/view.
  2. Check that the change of contrast is less than 4.5:1.
  3. Check that the area of the change of contrast is less than 30% of the viewport.

Expected results

#1, #2, or #3 is true.
derived.methods: • Design content without large changes of contrast. For example, when a menu with a light background is opened, it opens over a light background. Videos do not go from a dark to light background in less than a second.

plainEnglish.summary: A single large change of contrast counts too: content must not swing from light to dark, or dark to light, by more than 4.5:1 across more than 30% of the viewport. Loading a new page and essential flashes are excluded.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A single full-screen flash can trigger seizures and can cause pain or after-images for people with light sensitivity, migraine or eye conditions - the harm does not require a repeating flash.

title: Trigger Warning Available
rawBody:
A warning is provided before users encounter triggers and a mechanism is available to access the same information without the triggering content.

:::applies-when
- triggers are present.
:::

:::note
Triggers are flashing, motion lasting more than 5 seconds, and pseudo-motion.
:::

appliesWhen: • triggers are present.
notes: Triggers are flashing, motion lasting more than 5 seconds, and pseudo-motion.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each trigger:

  1. Check if a warning is provided before the user encounters the trigger.
  2. Check that the same information is available without triggers.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.
derived.methods: • Provide a warning for triggers and provide an option without the triggers.

plainEnglish.summary: Where content contains triggers, a warning comes before the user reaches them, and there is a way to get the same information without the triggering content.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A warning alone still forces a choice between the content and the trigger. Providing an alternative route means people with PTSD, anxiety disorders or phobias can get the information without the exposure.

title: Visual Stimulation
rawBody: Visual stimulation from combinations of density, color, movement, etc. can be reduced or turned off.

plainEnglish.summary: An exploratory requirement: visual intensity built out of density, colour, movement and similar factors can be reduced or turned off.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Visually busy interfaces can overwhelm people with sensory processing differences, autism, migraine or cognitive disabilities, to the point where the content cannot be used at all.

title: Consistent Navigation Labels
rawBody:
The labeling of navigation items within blocks of navigation that are repeated on multiple pages/views in the conformance scope or process is consistent.

:::except-when
* Labels for navigation items that are marked as 'current' within the conformance scope or process.
:::

:::ednote
This relates to consistency and terminology within blocks of navigation. The consistent ordering of blocks of navigation within a page/view is covered by 'Consistent relative order'.
:::

exceptWhen: • Labels for navigation items that are marked as ‘current’ within the conformance scope or process.
editorNotes: This relates to consistency and terminology within blocks of navigation. The consistent ordering of blocks of navigation within a page/view is covered by ‘Consistent relative order’.
derived.tests:
Consistent main navigation labels

Procedure

For each repeated block of navigation across multiple pages/views of the conformance scope or process:

  1. The navigation items within each block of navigation have the same names across all pages/views of the conformance scope or process.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.
derived.intent:
The intent of this success criterion is to ensure consistent identification of functional components that appear repeatedly within a set of web pages. A strategy that people who use screen readers use when operating a website is to rely heavily on their familiarity with functions that may appear on different web pages. If identical functions have different labels (or, more generally, a different accessible name) on different web pages, the site will be considerably more difficult to use. It may also be confusing and increase the cognitive load for people with cognitive limitations. Therefore, consistent labeling will help.

This consistency extends to the text alternatives. If icons or other non-text items have the same functionality, then their text alternatives should be consistent as well.

If there are two components on a web page that both have the same functionality as a component on another page in a set of web pages, then all 3 must be consistent. Hence the two on the same page will be consistent.

While it is desirable and recommended practice always to be consistent within a single web page, 3.2.4 Consistent Identification only addresses consistency within a set of web pages where something is repeated on more than one page in the set.

plainEnglish.summary: Navigation blocks that repeat across pages must label the same item the same way each time. Items marked as the current page are exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: People who navigate by searching for a remembered label - screen reader users, voice control users, and anyone with a memory or reading disability - lose their way when the same destination is called something different on the next page.

title: Consistent Navigation Order
rawBody:
The relative order of navigation items is consistent within blocks of navigation that are repeated on multiple pages/views of the conformance scope or process.

:::applies-when
- In a set of pages/views.
:::

:::ednote
This relates to consistency and terminology within blocks of navigation. The consistent ordering of blocks of navigation within a page/view is covered by 'Consistent relative order'.
:::

appliesWhen: • In a set of pages/views.
editorNotes: This relates to consistency and terminology within blocks of navigation. The consistent ordering of blocks of navigation within a page/view is covered by ‘Consistent relative order’.
derived.tests:
Consistent main navigation relative order

Procedure

For each repeated blocks of navigation across multiple pages/views of the conformance scope or process:

  1. The navigation items within each block of navigation have the same relative order across all pages/views of the conformance scope or process.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.
derived.intent:
The intent of this success criterion is to encourage the use of consistent visual layout and source order for users who interact with repeated content within a set of web pages and need to locate specific information or functionality more than once.

Individuals with low vision who use screen magnification to display a small portion of the screen at a time often use visual cues and page boundaries to quickly locate repeated content. Presenting repeated content in the same order is also important for visual users who use spatial memory or visual cues within the design to locate repeated content.

Likewise, users who are blind and navigate through content on pages sequentially benefit from having navigational mechanisms occur in a consistent order relative to the overall source order and structure of the page.

It is important to note that the use of the phrase “same order” in this section is not meant to imply that sub-navigation menus cannot be used or that blocks of secondary navigation or page structure cannot be used. Instead, this success criterion is intended to assist users who interact with repeated content across web pages to be able to predict the location of the content they are looking for and find it more quickly when they encounter it again.

Users may initiate a change in the order by using adaptive user agents or by setting preferences so that the information is presented in a way that is most useful to them.

plainEnglish.summary: Where a block of navigation repeats across a set of pages, the items keep the same relative order on each page.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Once someone has learned that a link is the fourth item, changing the order makes every page a fresh problem. That cost falls hardest on screen reader, switch and voice users, for whom re-scanning is slow.

title: Consistent Structural Order
rawBody:
The relative order of structural components remains consistent throughout each variation of pages/views in the conformance scope.

:::applies-when
- In a set of pages/views.
:::

:::note
Relative order means that content can be added or removed, but repeated items are in the same order relative to each other.
:::

appliesWhen: • In a set of pages/views.
notes: Relative order means that content can be added or removed, but repeated items are in the same order relative to each other.
derived.tests:
Consistent relative order for website

Procedure

For each variation of pages/views in the conformance scope:

  1. Identify common structural components across multiple pages/views.
  2. Check that components are presented in the same order within each page/view.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: The main structural parts of a page keep the same relative order across the variations of pages in scope.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A predictable structure is what lets people move quickly to the part they want. Reordering it between pages forces everyone to re-orient, and forces assistive technology users to re-explore.

title: Error Messages Collocated
rawBody:
Error messages are visually collocated with the error source or the focus is moved to the error message and a mechanism is available to move to the input that is in error. 

:::applies-when
- Error messages relate to user input.
:::

appliesWhen: • Error messages relate to user input.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each page/view:

  1. Zoom in 400%.
  2. Trigger errors.
  3. Check that the error is visible next to the trigger or that the focus moves to the error.

Expected results

  • #3 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: An error message about user input either appears next to the input it concerns, or focus moves to the message and there is a way to get from the message back to the field in error.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: An error announced far from the field it belongs to can be missed entirely by someone using magnification, and leaves screen reader users to hunt for which field is wrong.

title: Error Messages Persistent
rawBody: Error messages persist at least until the error is resolved or the user dismisses them.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each error message:

  1. Check that the error message persists until the user fixes the error or dismisses the message.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.
derived.methods:
• Keep track of the state of the error and make visibility of the error message depending on this state.
  • In a form, revalidate all fields when the form is submitted and remove all error messages that are no longer relevant.
  • Add a “Dismiss” button to the error that makes the error message disappear.

plainEnglish.summary: Error messages stay on screen until the error is fixed or the user dismisses them - they do not time out on their own.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A message that disappears on a timer is gone before many people have finished reading it, particularly people who read slowly, use magnification, or are navigating with a screen reader.

title: Error Notifications Available
rawBody:
Errors that are programmatically determined are identified and the problem is described to the user in text.

:::example
- invalid form input
- server errors
- application errors
:::

examples:
• invalid form input
  • server errors
  • application errors
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each page/view:

  1. Trigger errors.
  2. For each error, check that the nature of the problem is identified and described.

Expected results

  • #2 is true for each error.

plainEnglish.summary: When the content can detect an error, it says so in text and describes what the problem is - not just that something went wrong.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Colour or an icon alone tells a screen reader user nothing, and 'invalid input' tells nobody what to change. A described error in text is what makes the problem fixable.

title: Error Suggestions Provided
rawBody:
Error messages include suggestions for corrections.

:::applies-when
- Errors require corrections by the user.
:::

:::except-when
- including suggestions would jeopardize the security or purpose of the content.
:::

appliesWhen: • Errors require corrections by the user.
exceptWhen: • including suggestions would jeopardize the security or purpose of the content.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each error message:

  1. Check that the error needs correction by the user.
  2. Check that the error message includes suggestions for how to fix the error.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where the user has to correct an error, the message suggests how - unless suggesting it would compromise security or defeat the purpose of the content.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Knowing that a field is wrong is not the same as knowing what it wants. Suggestions are what make a form completable for people with cognitive or learning disabilities.

title: Errors Associated
rawBody:
When input validation fails, the errors are visually and programmatically associated with the element that caused the error or that can resolve it.

:::example
Failing validation includes but is not limited to:

- when input is required and the field is left empty
- when the user input does not meet the requested format
:::

examples:
Failing validation includes but is not limited to:

  • when input is required and the field is left empty
  • when the user input does not meet the requested format
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each validation error:

  1. Check that the validation error is indicated visually.
  2. Check that the validation error is indicated programmatically.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: When validation fails, the error is tied both visually and programmatically to the element that caused it or that can fix it.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A programmatic association is what lets a screen reader announce the error when the user reaches the field, rather than leaving it stranded somewhere else on the page.

title: Errors Indicated In Multiple Ways
rawBody:
Error messages are visually indicated using at least two of the following:

* a symbol that is consistent throughout the conformance scope
* color that differentiates the error message from surrounding content
* a textual indication

:::example
An example of a "textual indication" would be to add  "Error: " before the error description.
:::

examples: An example of a “textual indication” would be to add “Error: ” before the error description.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each validation error:

  1. Check that it meets at least two of the listed indicators (symbol, color, or text).

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: An error has to be marked in at least two of three ways: a symbol used consistently throughout, a distinguishing colour, and a textual indication.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Colour alone is invisible to people with colour vision deficiencies and disappears in high-contrast modes. A second, redundant signal means the error still registers.

title: Data Entry Validated
rawBody:
Data entered is validated after the user enters data, either:

* when the user leaves the field, or 
* when the form is submitted

derived.tests:
Procedure

  1. Check that no validation has not occurred before data entry.
  2. Enter data.
  3. Check that validation is provided immediately after data entry or occurs before submission.

Expected results

  • #1 and #3 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: Data is validated either when the user leaves the field or when the form is submitted - not, for instance, mid-keystroke.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Validation that fires while someone is still typing produces errors for input that is merely unfinished, which is disorienting for screen reader users and discouraging for people who type slowly.

title: Error Prevention Review
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that: 

* For each form in the conformance claim, we have reviewed the form designs to reduce the possibility of users making mistakes. 

This review includes checking to make sure that we:

* Make the user enter as little information as possible.
* Clearly indicate required fields.
* For long numbers, divide input fields into chunks (supporting autocomplete across fields).
* Use an interface where only valid input can be selected.
* Use autocomplete and personalization of form controls.
* Use common words and metrics or units that users are likely to be familiar with.
* Automatically correct input errors when possible and reliable.
* Provide the user with known suggestions and corrections.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion
* date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

* documentation of which forms were reviewed
* documentation of any changes made as a result of the review
* date of usability testing, if applicable

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that it has reviewed its form designs to reduce mistakes - asking for less information, marking required fields, chunking long numbers, offering valid choices, supporting autocomplete, using familiar words and units, and correcting or suggesting where it reliably can.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Most form failures are design failures. Reviewing the design removes errors before anyone has to recover from them, which matters most for people with cognitive and learning disabilities.

title: Errors Preventable
rawBody:
Data entry interfaces allow for users to do at least one of the following before submission:

* Review, confirm, and correct all information.
* Review and correct input errors found during validation.

:::except-when
- entered data is auto-saved and/or reversible.
:::

:::ednote
Editors are looking at removing the grey area that may exist in this requirement due to interpretations of the word “submission“ (pressing “Submit” in the UI or receiving information server-side).
:::

exceptWhen: • entered data is auto-saved and/or reversible.
editorNotes: Editors are looking at removing the grey area that may exist in this requirement due to interpretations of the word “submission“ (pressing “Submit” in the UI or receiving information server-side).
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each data entry point:

  1. Check that users can return at any point in the process to correct data they entered.
  2. If it’s not possible to go back and correct the data during the process, check that the information being submitted can be reviewed and corrected before submission, or that it’s validated and can be fixed before submission.

Expected results

  • #1 or #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Before submitting, users can either review, confirm and correct everything they entered, or review and correct the errors validation found. Content that auto-saves or where submission is reversible is exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A mistake that can only be discovered after submission is expensive to undo. A review step is what makes an irreversible action safe for people who are more likely to mistype or misread.

title: Submission Status Notified
rawBody:
Data entry interfaces notify users of submission status at the time of submission.

:::applies-when
- data submission has succeeded or failed.
:::

appliesWhen: • data submission has succeeded or failed.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each data submission:

  1. Check that the user is notified about the submission immediately afterwards.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: When a submission succeeds or fails, the interface says so at the time it happens.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Without an announcement, a screen reader user has no way to know whether anything happened, and may submit again - or leave believing a task is done when it failed.

title: Feedback Mechanism Available
rawBody: A mechanism is available to provide feedback to authors.

derived.tests:
Procedure

Within the conformance scope:

  1. Check that a feedback mechanism exists.
  2. Check that the feedback is sent to authors.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: There is a way for users to send feedback to the people who made the content.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: When something is inaccessible, a feedback route is often the only way a disabled user can get it fixed. Its absence makes the barrier permanent.

title: Consistent Help Available
rawBody:
Help is labeled consistently and is available in a consistent location relative to other content.

:::applies-when
* human contact information, a human contact mechanism, a self-help option, or a fully automated contact mechanism is available.
:::

appliesWhen: • human contact information, a human contact mechanism, a self-help option, or a fully automated contact mechanism is available.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each help item in a page / view:

  1. Check that it is labeled consistently.
  2. Check that it remains in the same relative visual and programmatic location.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where help exists - a phone number, a contact form, a self-help option or an automated assistant - it is labelled the same way and sits in the same place relative to other content across pages.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Help that moves around is help that cannot be found in the moment it is needed, which is exactly when someone with a cognitive disability has least capacity to search for it.

title: Contextual Help Available
rawBody: Context-sensitive help is available.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each interactive element:

  1. Check for potentially confusing or difficult interactions such as formatting restrictions or interdependencies.
  2. For any element identified in #1, check that context-sensitive help is available.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Help is available that relates to what the user is doing at the time, rather than only as general documentation.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Generic help pages put the burden of translation on the user. Help tied to the current task is what lets people with cognitive and learning disabilities finish it.

title: Conversational Support Available
rawBody: Conversational support allowing both text and speech formats is available.

derived.tests:
Procedure

  1. Check that a conversational support mechanism is available.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: An exploratory requirement: support is available through conversation, in both text and speech, rather than only one of the two.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Some people cannot use speech and some cannot use typing. Offering both formats means the support route itself is not the barrier.

title: Data Visualizations
rawBody:
:::ednote
Editors are considering removal of this requirement.
:::

Help is available to understand and use data visualizations.

editorNotes: Editors are considering removal of this requirement.

plainEnglish.summary: An exploratory requirement: help is available for understanding and using data visualisations.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Charts encode meaning in position, colour and shape at once. Without an explanation or an alternative route to the data, that meaning is unavailable to screen reader users and to many people with cognitive disabilities.

title: Disabled Controls Explained
rawBody:
Information explaining why a visible interactive element is disabled is available and, if the user can take action(s) to enable the element, those action(s) are described.

:::example
When a submit button is disabled until all required fields are filled in, explain that this is the case.
:::

examples: When a submit button is disabled until all required fields are filled in, explain that this is the case.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each visible disabled control:

  1. Check that instructions are available that explain how to enable it.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: When a control is visible but disabled, the content explains why, and if the user can do something to enable it, says what.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A greyed-out button with no explanation is a dead end: the user cannot tell whether they have missed a step, lack permission, or hit a bug.

title: Help Usability Testing
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* Help and training was added based on usability testing with people with cognitive and mental health disabilities to identify gaps.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
* date of when the usability testing was conducted
* date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

* usability findings
* solutions added

:::example
Solutions include help with completing functionality such as data entry, task completion, search, and understanding complex ideas and visualizations.
:::

examples: Solutions include help with completing functionality such as data entry, task completion, search, and understanding complex ideas and visualizations.

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that it added help and training in response to usability testing with people with cognitive and mental health disabilities, and records when that testing happened.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Help written without testing tends to answer the questions the authors imagined. Testing with the people who rely on it is what finds the gaps that matter.

title: New Interfaces
rawBody:
A mechanism to learn a new interface or revert to the older design is available.

:::applies-when
- Interfaces dramatically change due to redesign.
:::

:::except-when
- The new interface is essential.
:::

appliesWhen: • Interfaces dramatically change due to redesign.
exceptWhen: • The new interface is essential.
derived.tests:
Procedure

  1. When an interface has been redesigned, check that a tutorial is available or that the user is given an opportunity to revert to the previous design.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: An exploratory requirement: when an interface changes dramatically in a redesign, there is a way to learn the new one or to go back to the old design - unless the new interface is essential.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A redesign resets the learned patterns people depend on. For users with cognitive disabilities that relearning cost can be severe enough to end their use of the product.

title: Personalizable Help
rawBody:
:::ednote
Editors are considering removal of this requirement.
:::

Help is adaptable and personalizable.

editorNotes: Editors are considering removal of this requirement.

plainEnglish.summary: An exploratory requirement: help can be adapted and personalised to the individual user.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: One fixed explanation suits one kind of reader. Being able to change the form of help - its length, its vocabulary, its medium - is what makes it usable across very different cognitive profiles.

title: Sensory Characteristics Not Relied On
rawBody:
Instructions and help do not rely on sensory characteristics.

:::example
Sensory characteristics include but are not limited to shape, color, size, visual location, orientation, or sound.
:::

examples: Sensory characteristics include but are not limited to shape, color, size, visual location, orientation, or sound.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each reference to shape, size, or position of an object:

  1. Check that the reference includes additional information that allows the item to be located and identified without any knowledge of its shape, size, or relative position.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Instructions and help do not depend on shape, colour, size, visual location, orientation or sound to make sense - 'the round button on the right' has to work for someone who cannot see it.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Directions given purely by appearance or position are unusable by screen reader users, and often by people with colour vision deficiencies or those using a reflowed, magnified layout.

title: Support Available
rawBody:
Support is available during data entry, task completion and search.

:::except-when
- the content does not include one or more of the mentioned processes.
:::

:::example
When the content does not include search, there is no requirement for support to be available for search.
:::

exceptWhen: • the content does not include one or more of the mentioned processes.
examples: When the content does not include search, there is no requirement for support to be available for search.

plainEnglish.summary: Support is available while the user is entering data, completing a task or searching, where the content includes those processes.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: These are the moments when people get stuck and abandon a task. Support offered at that point, rather than in a manual, is what keeps the task completable.

title: Supported decision-making review
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* We have conducted a review to identify when users need to make substantial decisions about money, privacy, or well-being. In these situations, additional support was provided, such as:
  * a clear layout of options advantages and disadvantages
  * aids for comprehension such as icons and graphics
  * reduced distractions

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
* date of when the policy was implemented
* date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

* results of review
* documentation of decisions and changes made as a result

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that it identified the places where users make substantial decisions about money, privacy or wellbeing, and added support there - a clear layout of advantages and disadvantages, comprehension aids such as icons and graphics, and reduced distractions.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: High-stakes decisions are where poor comprehension turns into real harm. Extra support at those points protects people with cognitive disabilities from consequences that are hard to reverse.

title: Accessible Audio Player Selected
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* We provide an audio player that supports appropriate media alternatives. The audio player includes the following features [list all that apply]:
  * turning audio descriptions on and off
  * changing the language of the audio descriptions

:::applies-when
- an audio format is used that does not play in standard browsers.
:::

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
* date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)
* feature included from the list

::assertion-recommended

* audio player documentation detailing functional support for media alternatives

appliesWhen: • an audio format is used that does not play in standard browsers.

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion, relevant when audio needs a player that standard browsers do not provide: the organisation states that its audio player supports the media alternatives it lists, such as turning audio descriptions on and off and changing their language.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A custom player can undo the accessibility of the media inside it. Naming the features it actually supports makes that checkable rather than assumed.

title: Accessible Video Player Selected
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* We provide a video player that supports appropriate media alternatives. The video player includes the following features [list all that apply]:
  * supports closed captions in a standard caption format
  * turning captions on and off
  * turning audio descriptions on and off
  * adjusting caption styles, including but not limited to: font size, font weight, font style, font color, background color, background transparency, and placement
  * changing the location of captions
  * changing the language of the audio descriptions

:::applies-when
- a video is used that does not play in standard browsers.
:::

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
* date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)
* feature included from the list

::assertion-recommended

* video player documentation detailing functional support for media alternatives

appliesWhen: • a video is used that does not play in standard browsers.

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion, relevant when video needs a player that standard browsers do not provide: the organisation states which media-alternative features its video player supports - closed captions in a standard format, turning captions and audio descriptions on and off, restyling and repositioning captions, and changing the audio description language.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Captions and descriptions only help if the player exposes them and lets people adjust them. Caption styling in particular is what makes them readable for people with low vision.

title: Audio Description Language Adjustable
rawBody: A mechanism is available that allows users to change the audio description language if multiple languages are available.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each media asset with audio content:

  1. Check that a version of the media has audio description available in alternative languages and the language of audio description can be changed by the user.
  2. Alternatively, check that alternative versions of the media exist that have audio description available in alternative languages.

Expected results

  • #1 or #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where audio descriptions exist in more than one language, there is a way for the user to choose between them.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A description in a language the viewer does not speak conveys nothing. This matters most for blind and low-vision users, who have no fallback to the picture.

title: Audio Description Volume Adjustable
rawBody: A mechanism is available that allows users to control the audio description volume independently from the audio volume of the video.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each media asset with visual content:

  1. Play the media with audio description on.
  2. Check that the volume of the audio description can be controlled separately from the main audio track of the media using all relevant inputs.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: An exploratory requirement: the audio description track can be adjusted in volume separately from the video's own audio.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: When description and soundtrack are locked together, one drowns out the other. Independent control is what makes both audible for people who rely on the description.

title: Audio descriptions available (live)
rawBody: Audio descriptions are available in live video for visual content needed to understand the media.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each live media broadcast:

  1. Check that a secondary audio option exists that provides live audio description of the broadcast.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Live video carries audio descriptions of the visual information needed to follow it.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Live events are exactly where a blind or low-vision viewer cannot catch up later. Without description, anything shown rather than said is lost.

title: Audio descriptions available (prerecorded)
rawBody:
Audio descriptions are available in prerecorded video for visual content needed to understand the media.

:::ednote
WCAG 3 needs to specify how to handle video content with audio that does not include gaps to insert audio descriptions. Two possible solutions are providing an exception that allows the content author(s) to use descriptive transcripts instead or requiring content authors to provide an extended audio description.
:::

:::except-when
the video content is an alternative for text and is clearly labeled as such.
:::

exceptWhen: the video content is an alternative for text and is clearly labeled as such.
editorNotes: WCAG 3 needs to specify how to handle video content with audio that does not include gaps to insert audio descriptions. Two possible solutions are providing an exception that allows the content author(s) to use descriptive transcripts instead or requiring content authors to provide an extended audio description.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For prerecorded video:

  1. Check that audio description is available for visual content needed to understand the media.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Prerecorded video carries audio descriptions of the visual information needed to follow it. Video that exists as an alternative to text and says so is exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Anything conveyed only by the picture - a document on screen, a gesture, who just entered the room - is simply absent for blind and low-vision viewers without description.

title: Audio Descriptions Controllable
rawBody:
A mechanism is available to turn audio descriptions on and off.

:::except-when
- Audio descriptions are hard-coded into the audio or video content.
:::

exceptWhen: • Audio descriptions are hard-coded into the audio or video content.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each audio description:

  1. Check that content with audio descriptions provides a mechanism to turn the audio descriptions on and off.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: There is a way to turn audio descriptions on and off, unless they are baked into the recording and cannot be separated.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Description is welcome to some listeners and intrusive to others sharing the same screen. Control is what lets both use the same content.

title: Audio descriptions equivalent (prerecorded)
rawBody: The information conveyed by audio descriptions is equivalent to the visual content needed to understand the media.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each audio description:

  1. Check that the content of the audio description is equivalent to the meaningful information in the media content.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Not just present, but equivalent: the description has to carry the same information as the visual content it stands in for.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A description that names what is on screen without conveying what it means leaves blind viewers with a thinner version of the content than everyone else gets.

title: Audio Descriptions Reviewed By Content Authors
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* We have reviewed the audio descriptions.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
* date of the review
* date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

* role of the creator
* number of creators (for each Role)
* date (Period) of review
* examples of fixed issues based on the review

:::example
* **Roles and numbers:** 3 creators
  * 1 director
  * 1 planner
  * 1 screenwriter/playwright
* **Period:** 10-21 October 2024
* **Examples of fixed issues:**
  * Provided more details based on feedback.
  * Rewrote some scripts to reflect the director's intent.
  * Added the description of the background shown in the video.
:::

examples:
• Roles and numbers: 3 creators
    • 1 director
    • 1 planner
    • 1 screenwriter/playwright
  • Period: 10-21 October 2024
  • Examples of fixed issues:
    • Provided more details based on feedback.
    • Rewrote some scripts to reflect the director’s intent.
    • Added the description of the background shown in the video.

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that it reviewed its audio descriptions, and records who reviewed them and when.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Descriptions produced at volume, or automatically, drift from what the picture actually shows. A recorded review is the check that they still match.

title: Audio Descriptions Style Guide
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* Our organization has a style guide that includes guidance on audio descriptions and a policy and/or processes that the style guide must be followed.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
* date of when the style guide was published
* date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

* summary of the needs of users involved
* identified issues and details of solutions applied
* copy or snapshot of the style guide


:::example
* **Name:** ABC Inc. Style Guide for Audio Descriptions
* **Version:** 1.2
* **Date:** October 2024
* **Description:** The style guide include sections such as:
  * What are audio descriptions?
  * Who needs audio descriptions?
  * Guideline provided by WCAG 3
  * Recommended style of audio descriptions
  * Resources
* **Example:** The style guide has requirements such as:
  * Explain reasons for no sound or long pause.
  * …
:::

examples:
• Name: ABC Inc. Style Guide for Audio Descriptions
  • Version: 1.2
  • Date: October 2024
  • Description: The style guide include sections such as:
    • What are audio descriptions?
    • Who needs audio descriptions?
    • Guideline provided by WCAG 3
    • Recommended style of audio descriptions
    • Resources
  • Example: The style guide has requirements such as:
    • Explain reasons for no sound or long pause.
    • …

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that it has a style guide covering audio descriptions, plus a policy or process requiring the guide to be followed.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Consistency across a library is what lets a regular listener build expectations. A style guide is how that consistency survives changes of author and vendor.

title: Audio Descriptions Synchronized
rawBody:
Audio descriptions are synchronized with video content without overlapping dialogue and meaningful audio content.

:::except-when
- There are no audio descriptions.
:::

exceptWhen: • There are no audio descriptions.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For synchronized media with audio description:

  1. Check that audio description is in sync with video content in synchronized media.
  2. Check that audio description doesn’t overlap with dialogue and meaningful audio content.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: Descriptions land in time with the video and do not talk over dialogue or other meaningful audio.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A description that collides with the dialogue costs the listener both. Timing is what keeps the described version coherent.

title: Audio Descriptions Usability Testing
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* We have conducted usability testing with users who need audio descriptions, and changes were made to fix or mitigate the issues found.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
* date of when the usability testing was conducted
* date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended
* scope
* types of disabilities each user had
* number of users (for each type of disability)
* date of testing
* identified issues and details of solutions applied

:::example
* **Scope:** videos on the following URLs:
  * "What is accessibility?" https://xxx.xxx/yyyy1
  * "About assistive technologies" https://xxx.xxx/yyyy2
  * "How to use WCAG" https://xxx.xxx/yyyy3
* **Type and number:** 8 users in total
  * 5 users who are deaf
  * 3 users who are hard of hearing
* **Dates:** 10-11 October 2024
* **Examples of fixed issues:**
  * Added description of action scene.
:::

examples:
• Scope: videos on the following URLs:
    • “What is accessibility?” https://xxx.xxx/yyyy1
    • “About assistive technologies” https://xxx.xxx/yyyy2
    • “How to use WCAG” https://xxx.xxx/yyyy3
  • Type and number: 8 users in total
    • 5 users who are deaf
    • 3 users who are hard of hearing
  • Dates: 10-11 October 2024
  • Examples of fixed issues:
    • Added description of action scene.

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that it tested with people who rely on audio descriptions and fixed or mitigated what the testing found.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Whether a description works can only be judged by someone using it without the picture. Testing is what turns that judgement into evidence.

title: Extended Audio Descriptions Available
rawBody:
The video pauses to extend the audio track and provides an extended audio description to describe visual information needed to understand the media.

:::applies-when
* the existing pauses in a soundtrack are not long enough.
:::

appliesWhen: • the existing pauses in a soundtrack are not long enough.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each media asset with visual content:

  1. Check that the video includes pauses to allow enough time for extended audio descriptions to describe visual information.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where the natural gaps in the soundtrack are too short to describe what is on screen, the video pauses so that a longer description can be given.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Dense visual content cannot be described in the pauses a soundtrack happens to leave. Pausing is the only way to convey it without cutting information.

title: Extended Audio Descriptions Equivalent
rawBody: The information conveyed by extended audio descriptions is equivalent to the visual content needed to understand the media.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each media asset with visual content:

  1. Play the media with the extended audio description on.
  2. Check that the extended audio description includes all important visual information that cannot be understood from the main soundtrack alone.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: The extended description must convey the same information as the visual content it describes, not just fill the pause.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: The pause is bought at the cost of the viewer's time; an inadequate description wastes it and still leaves the content incomplete.

title: Non-verbal cues identified in audio descriptions
issueLabel: Non-verbal cues identified in audio desc
rawBody: Nonverbal cues needed to understand the media are explained in audio descriptions.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each instance of audio content that includes nonverbal cues:

  1. Check that the audio descriptions explain audio nonverbal cues, such as tone of voice, facial expressions, body gestures, or music with emotional meaning.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: An exploratory requirement: nonverbal cues needed to follow the media - expressions, gestures, reactions - are explained in the audio description.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Meaning frequently sits in what nobody says. Without it, a blind listener gets the words of a scene and not its sense.

title: Sounds Identified In Audio Descriptions
rawBody:
Sounds needed to understand the media are identified or described in captions and transcripts.

:::ednote
This includes sound effects and other non-spoken audio content.
:::

:::applies-when
- there is sound.
:::

:::except-when
- the video is decorative.
:::

appliesWhen: • there is sound.
exceptWhen: • the video is decorative.
editorNotes: This includes sound effects and other non-spoken audio content.
derived.tests:
Meaningful sounds in audio descriptions

Procedure

For all audio content:

  1. Identify meaningful non-verbal audio (sounds).
  2. Check that audio descriptions include a description of the meaningful non-verbal audio.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where sound carries meaning and the video is not decorative, that sound is named or described in the captions and transcript rather than left to be heard.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A door closing offscreen or an alarm can carry the plot. Deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers only get it if it is written down.

title: Speaker Language Identified In Audio Descriptions
issueLabel: Speaker language identified in audio desc
rawBody:
When more than one language is spoken in audio content, the language spoken by each speaker is identified in all audio descriptions.

:::except-when
- Words are used incidentally.
:::

exceptWhen: • Words are used incidentally.
derived.tests:
Language identified in audio descriptions

Procedure

For each audio description that includes multiple languages:

  1. Check that part(s) using a language different from the original language is programmatically determined in the audio description.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where more than one language is spoken, every audio description identifies which language each speaker is using. Incidental words are exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Without it, a listener cannot tell whether they have missed something or the speaker has simply switched language - and may not know a translation exists.

title: Speakers Identified In Audio Descriptions
rawBody:
Speakers are identified understandably within all audio descriptions.

:::applies-when
- There are multiple speakers in the video.
:::

:::except-when
- The speaker has a hidden identity as part of narrative structure.
- Identity is identifiable within the context of use.
:::

:::example
Initially using "Maya Angelou" within the context of a story regarding poetry and then using "Angelou".
:::

appliesWhen: • There are multiple speakers in the video.
exceptWhen:
• The speaker has a hidden identity as part of narrative structure.
  • Identity is identifiable within the context of use.
examples: Initially using “Maya Angelou” within the context of a story regarding poetry and then using “Angelou”.
derived.tests:
Consistent speaker name in audio descriptions

Procedure

For each audio description:

  1. Check that each speaker in the audio or video is consistently identified.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: When a video has several speakers, the audio description makes clear who is speaking - except where the speaker's identity is deliberately hidden or is already obvious from context.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Voices alone are hard to tell apart without the picture, particularly for listeners with hearing loss as well as sight loss.

title: Visual Information Identified In Audio Descriptions
issueLabel: Visual information identified in audio desc
rawBody:
Visual information needed to understand the media is described in audio descriptions.

:::ednote
* This includes actions, charts or informative visuals, scene changes, and on-screen text,
:::

editorNotes: • This includes actions, charts or informative visuals, scene changes, and on-screen text,
derived.tests:
Meaningful visual information in audio descriptions

Procedure

For each audio description:

  1. Check that the audio description includes a description of any visual information needed to understand the content of the audio or video.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Whatever the picture carries and the soundtrack does not - actions, documents, expressions, on-screen text - is spoken in the audio description.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: This is the core of the technique: what the picture carries and the soundtrack does not is exactly what a blind viewer would otherwise lose.

title: Caption Features Available
rawBody:
Enhanced features that allow users to interact with captions are available.

:::ednote
* Needs additional research.
:::

:::example
A link to review a glossary term or a labeled diagram.
:::

editorNotes: • Needs additional research.
examples: A link to review a glossary term or a labeled diagram.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each media asset with audio content that provides enhanced features to allow users to interact with captions:

  1. Play the media with captions on.
  2. Check that a mechanism is available so that users can interact with the captions using all relative input methods.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: An exploratory requirement: captions offer enhanced features that let users interact with them rather than only read them.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Being able to search, pause on or re-read a caption gives deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers the same control over pace that hearing viewers get from replaying audio.

title: Caption Language Adjustable
rawBody: A mechanism is available that allows users to change the caption language if multiple languages are available.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each media asset with audio content:

  1. Check that a version of the media has captions available in alternative languages and the language of captions can be changed by the user.
  2. Alternatively, check that alternative versions of the media exist that have captions available in alternative languages.

Expected results

  • #1 or #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where captions exist in more than one language, there is a way for the user to choose between them.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Captions in the wrong language are no more use than no captions. This matters most where an audience shares a region but not a first language.

title: Captions Adjustable
rawBody: The appearance of captions, including associated visual indicators, is adaptable including font size, font weight, font style, font color, background color, background transparency, and placement.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each caption:

  1. Check that the appearance of captions and associated visual indicators is adaptable including font size, font weight, font style, font color, background color, background transparency, and placement.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Caption appearance can be adapted - font size, weight, style and colour, background colour and transparency, and where they sit on screen - along with any associated visual indicators.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Fixed captions are unreadable for many low-vision viewers. Size, contrast and position are the settings that make the difference between legible and not.

title: Captions available (live)
rawBody: Captions are available for all live audio content.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For all live audio content:

  1. Check that captions are provided.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Everything spoken in live audio is captioned as it happens, for the whole of the content rather than parts of it.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Live is where there is no catching up afterwards. Without captions, a deaf or hard-of-hearing participant is excluded from the event as it happens.

title: Captions available (prerecorded)
rawBody:
Captions are available for all prerecorded audio content.

:::except-when
- The audio content is an alternative for text and is clearly labeled as such.
:::

exceptWhen: • The audio content is an alternative for text and is clearly labeled as such.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each prerecorded media asset:

  1. If the captions format is closed captions:
    • Turn on the closed caption feature of the media player
    • View the synchronized media content
    • Check that captions (of all dialogue and important sounds) are visible and in the human language of the video
  2. If the captions format is open captions:
    • Check that captions (of all dialogue and important sounds) are visible and in the human language of the video

Expected results

  • #1 or #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: All prerecorded audio content is captioned, unless the audio is an alternative to text and is clearly labelled as such.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Captions are the primary route into spoken content for deaf and hard-of-hearing users, and the route many other people use in noisy or silent settings.

title: Captions centered (immersive)
rawBody:
In 360-degree digital environments, captions remain directly in front of the user.

:::applies-when
- the position of the captions is controlled by the user.
:::

appliesWhen: • the position of the captions is controlled by the user.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each caption in 360-degree environments:

  1. Check that captions remain directly in front of the user.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: In 360-degree environments where the user controls where captions sit, the captions stay directly in front of the user as they look around.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Captions anchored to a fixed point in the scene vanish the moment the viewer turns their head, which in an immersive environment is constantly.

title: Captions Consistent
rawBody: Captions are presented consistently throughout the media, and across related productions, unless exceptions are essential. This includes consistent styling and placement of the captions text and consistent methods for identifying speakers, languages, and sounds.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each media asset with audio content:

  1. Play the media with captions on.
  2. Check that the captions are presented consistently throughout the audio content.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: An exploratory requirement: captions look and behave the same way through a production and across related productions - styling, placement, and how speakers, languages and sounds are marked - unless a difference is essential.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Reading captions is already a divided-attention task. Consistent conventions mean the viewer spends attention on the content rather than on decoding the captions.

title: Captions Controllable
rawBody:
A mechanism is available to turn captions on and off.

:::except-when
- Captions are hard-coded into the video content.
:::

exceptWhen: • Captions are hard-coded into the video content.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each caption:

  1. Check that content with captions provides a mechanism to turn the captions on and off.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: There is a way to turn captions on and off, unless they are burned into the video.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Captions cover part of the picture and are a distraction to viewers who do not need them, so the choice has to sit with the viewer.

title: Captions equivalent (prerecorded)
rawBody:
Equivalent captions are available for audio and video content.

:::except-when
- The audio or video has no spoken content and serves only as background.
:::

exceptWhen: • The audio or video has no spoken content and serves only as background.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each caption:

  1. Check that the content of the caption is equivalent to the meaningful information in the media content.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Captions have to be equivalent to the audio, not an approximation of it. Audio or video with no spoken content that serves only as background is exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Auto-generated captions routinely drop names, technical terms and negations. An approximate caption can change the meaning of what was said.

title: Captions Reviewed By Content Authors
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* We have reviewed the captions.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
* date of the review
* date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

* role of the creator
* number of creators (for each Role)
* date (Period) of review
* examples of fixed issues based on the review

:::example
* **Roles and numbers:** 3 creators
  * 1 director
  * 1 planner
  * 1 screenwriter/playwright
* **Period:** 10-21 October 2024
* **Examples of fixed issues:**
  * Provided more details based on feedback.
  * Rewrote some scripts to reflect the director's intent.
  * Added the description of the background shown in the video.
:::

examples:
• Roles and numbers: 3 creators
    • 1 director
    • 1 planner
    • 1 screenwriter/playwright
  • Period: 10-21 October 2024
  • Examples of fixed issues:
    • Provided more details based on feedback.
    • Rewrote some scripts to reflect the director’s intent.
    • Added the description of the background shown in the video.

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that it reviewed its captions, and records who did so and when.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Machine captioning is now the default, and its errors are systematic. A recorded review is what catches them before publication.

title: Captions Style Guide
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* Our organization has a style guide that includes guidance on captions and a policy and/or processes that the style guide must be followed.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
* date of when the style guide was published
* date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

* summary of the needs of users involved
* identified issues and details of solutions applied
* copy or snapshot of the style guide

:::example
* **Name:** ABC Inc. Style Guide for Captions
* **Version:** 1.2
* **Date:** October 2024
* **Description:** The style guide include sections such as:
  * What are captions?
  * Who needs captions?
  * Guideline provided by WCAG 3
  * Recommended style of captions
  * Resources
* **Example:** The style guide has requirements such as:
  * Never use more than two lines.
  * Use parentheses for sound representation.
  * Identify no sound or long pause.
  * …
:::

examples:
• Name: ABC Inc. Style Guide for Captions
  • Version: 1.2
  • Date: October 2024
  • Description: The style guide include sections such as:
    • What are captions?
    • Who needs captions?
    • Guideline provided by WCAG 3
    • Recommended style of captions
    • Resources
  • Example: The style guide has requirements such as:
    • Never use more than two lines.
    • Use parentheses for sound representation.
    • Identify no sound or long pause.
    • …

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that it has a style guide covering captions, plus a policy or process requiring it to be followed.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Caption conventions - how speakers are named, how sounds are written - only help if they are stable. A style guide is how they stay stable across teams.

title: Captions Synchronized
rawBody: Captions are synchronized with the audio content of synchronized media.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each caption:

  1. Check if the caption is in sync with video content.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Captions are timed to the audio they represent.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Captions that run ahead of or behind the speech break the link between the words and who is saying them, and make dialogue hard to follow.

title: Captions Unobstructed
rawBody: Captions are placed on the screen so that they do not hide visual information needed to understand the video content.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each caption:

  1. Check if the caption doesn’t hide visual information needed to understand the video content.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Captions are positioned so they do not cover visual information needed to understand the video.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Captions sitting over on-screen text or a speaker's face force a deaf viewer to choose between two pieces of the same content.

title: Captions Usability Testing
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* We have conducted usability testing with users who need captions, and changes were made to fix or mitigate the issues found.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
* date of when the usability testing was conducted
* date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended
* scope
* types of disabilities each user had
* number of users (for each type of disability)
* date of testing
* identified issues and details of solutions applied

:::example
* **Scope:** videos on the following URLs:
  * "What is accessibility?" https://xxx.xxx/yyyy1
  * "About assistive technologies" https://xxx.xxx/yyyy2
  * "How to use WCAG" https://xxx.xxx/yyyy3
* **Type and number:** 8 users in total
  * 5 users who are deaf
  * 3 users who are hard of hearing
* **Dates:** 10-11 October 2024
* **Examples of fixed issues:**
  * Identified where the speaker changed.
  * Described background music.
  * Indicated that a dog was barking.
:::

examples:
• Scope: videos on the following URLs:
    • “What is accessibility?” https://xxx.xxx/yyyy1
    • “About assistive technologies” https://xxx.xxx/yyyy2
    • “How to use WCAG” https://xxx.xxx/yyyy3
  • Type and number: 8 users in total
    • 5 users who are deaf
    • 3 users who are hard of hearing
  • Dates: 10-11 October 2024
  • Examples of fixed issues:
    • Identified where the speaker changed.
    • Described background music.
    • Indicated that a dog was barking.

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that it tested with people who rely on captions and fixed or mitigated what the testing found.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Caption quality problems - timing, reading speed, speaker attribution - show up in use rather than in a checklist.

title: Direction indicated (immersive)
rawBody:
In 360-degree digital environments, the direction of a sound or speech is indicated when audio is heard from outside the current view. 

:::example
* **Visual indicators:** An arrow with an outline pointing to the speaker or the direction of a sound
* **Customizable styles:** Users can select various arrow sizes, colors, and outline colors
:::

examples:
• Visual indicators: An arrow with an outline pointing to the speaker or the direction of a sound
  • Customizable styles: Users can select various arrow sizes, colors, and outline colors
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each instance of audio that is heard from outside the current view in a 360-degree digital environment:

  1. Check that the captions indicate the direction of a sound or speech.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: In 360-degree environments, when a sound or speech comes from outside the current view, its direction is indicated.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Spatial audio is the usual cue for where to look, and it is unavailable to deaf and hard-of-hearing users. A visual direction cue restores it.

title: Non-verbal cues identified in captions
rawBody: Nonverbal cues needed to understand the media are explained in captions.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each instance of audio content that includes nonverbal cues:

  1. Check that the captions explain audio nonverbal cues, such as tone of voice, facial expressions, body gestures, or music with emotional meaning.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: An exploratory requirement: nonverbal cues needed to understand the media are explained in the captions.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Tone, sarcasm and emotion carry meaning that the words alone do not. Captions that omit them can invert what a scene means.

title: Sounds Identified In Captions
rawBody:
Sounds needed to understand the media are identified or described in captions.

:::ednote
This includes sound effects and other non-spoken audio content.
:::

:::applies-when
- there is sound.
:::

:::except-when
- the video is decorative.
:::

appliesWhen: • there is sound.
exceptWhen: • the video is decorative.
editorNotes: This includes sound effects and other non-spoken audio content.
derived.tests:
Meaningful sounds in captions

Procedure

For all audio content:

  1. Identify meaningful non-verbal audio (sounds).
  2. Check that captions include a description of the meaningful non-verbal audio.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where sound carries meaning and the video is not decorative, the captions say what the sound is - not only what is spoken.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Significant sounds - a phone, a knock, music signalling a change - are part of the content, not decoration around it.

title: Speaker Language Identified In Captions
rawBody:
When more than one language is spoken in audio content, the language spoken by each speaker is identified in all captions.

:::except-when
- Words are used incidentally.
:::

exceptWhen: • Words are used incidentally.
derived.tests:
Language identified in captions
