Procedure

For each caption that includes multiple languages:

  1. Check that part(s) using a language different from the original language is programmatically determined in the captions.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where more than one language is spoken, the captions identify which language each speaker is using. Incidental words are exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A deaf viewer cannot hear the switch. Naming the language is what prevents a translated line from reading as the speaker's own words.

title: Speakers Identified In Captions
rawBody:
Speakers are identified understandably within all captions.

:::applies-when
- There are multiple speakers in the video.
:::

:::except-when
- The speaker has a hidden identity as part of narrative structure.
- Identity is identifiable within the context of use.
:::

:::example
Initially using "Maya Angelou" within the context of a story regarding poetry and then using "Angelou".
:::

appliesWhen: • There are multiple speakers in the video.
exceptWhen:
• The speaker has a hidden identity as part of narrative structure.
  • Identity is identifiable within the context of use.
examples: Initially using “Maya Angelou” within the context of a story regarding poetry and then using “Angelou”.
derived.tests:
Consistent speaker name in captions

Procedure

For each caption:

  1. Check that each speaker in the audio or video is consistently identified.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where a video has several speakers, the captions make clear who is speaking - except where identity is deliberately hidden or already clear from context.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Captions strip out voice, accent and volume, which is how hearing viewers tell speakers apart. Without attribution, a conversation becomes a block of text.

title: Figure Captions Persistent
rawBody: Figure captions persist or a mechanism is available to make figure captions persist, even if the focus moves away.

plainEnglish.summary: An exploratory requirement: figure captions stay visible, or there is a way to make them stay, even after focus moves elsewhere.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A caption that vanishes when focus moves cannot be read alongside the figure it explains - which is exactly how people using magnification or a screen reader read it.

title: Alternative Text Editable
rawBody: Automatically generated text descriptions are editable by the content creator.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each image that has automatically generated text descriptions, check that:

  1. The image’s text description can be updated; and
  2. The image can be marked as decorative.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: An exploratory requirement: where text descriptions are generated automatically, the content creator can edit them.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Generated descriptions miss what the image is for in its context. Editability is what lets the person who knows the purpose correct it.

title: Decorative Images Hidden
rawBody: Decorative images are programmatically hidden.

derived.tests:
(General) No accessible name

Procedure

  1. Check for any images that add no information to the content.
  2. Check that the image has no accessible name.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

(HTML) Using an empty alt attribute for an image element

Procedure

For any image that adds no information to the content:

  1. Check that title, aria-label, aria-labelledby is either absent or empty.
  2. Check that an alt attribute is present and empty.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: Images that are purely decorative are hidden from assistive technology.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Announcing every decorative image buries the content in noise, and for a screen reader user that noise costs real time on every pass through the page.

title: Image Alternatives Available
rawBody: Text alternatives are available for non-decorative images.

derived.tests:
Provide a text alternative for the image in a way that conveys the equivalent meaning or content that’s displayed visually.

(General) Equivalent text alternative

Procedure

For each non-decorative image:

  1. Remove, hide, or mask the image.
  2. Replace it with the text alternative.
  3. Check that the meaningful content in the image is described by the text alternative.
  4. If the image includes words that are important to understanding the content, check that those words are included in the text alternative.

Expected results

  • #3 is true.
  • #4 is also true, if the image includes words that are important to understanding the content.

plainEnglish.summary: Every image that is not decorative has a text alternative.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Without one, a screen reader user gets a filename or silence where the content is - and if the image is a link or a control, may not be able to use it at all.

title: Image Alternatives Equivalent
rawBody: Text alternatives for non-decorative images convey the equivalent purpose to the image.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each text alternative:

  1. Check that the content of the text alternative is equivalent to the meaningful information in the image.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: The text alternative has to serve the same purpose as the image, not merely describe its appearance.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: "Photo of a chart" tells a blind reader that information exists and withholds it. The alternative has to carry what the image is there to convey.

title: Image Alternatives Style Guide
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* Our organization has a style guide that includes guidance on image text alternatives and a policy and/or processes that the style guide must be followed.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
* date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

* section labels relevant to image alternatives
* copy or snapshot of the style guide

:::example
* Name: ABC Inc. Style Guide for text alternatives
* Version 1.2
* Date: 9 October 2024
* Description: The style guide includes sections such as:
  * What are text alternatives?
  * Who needs text alternatives?
  * Guideline provided by WCAG 3
  * Recommended style of text alternatives
  * Resources
  * The style guide has requirements such as:
    * Provide equivalent information.
    * Write text on the image as it is.
    * Don't omit information provided by the image.
:::

examples:
• Name: ABC Inc. Style Guide for text alternatives
  • Version 1.2
  • Date: 9 October 2024
  • Description: The style guide includes sections such as:
    • What are text alternatives?
    • Who needs text alternatives?
    • Guideline provided by WCAG 3
    • Recommended style of text alternatives
    • Resources
    • The style guide has requirements such as:
      • Provide equivalent information.
      • Write text on the image as it is.
      • Don’t omit information provided by the image.

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that it has a style guide covering image text alternatives, plus a policy or process requiring it to be followed.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Alt text is written by many hands over time. A style guide is what keeps it purposeful rather than decorative or duplicative.

title: Image Types Identified
rawBody:
The image types are indicated.

:::except-when
* An image is a link or a part of a link.
* An image is a button or a part of a button.
* An image is purely decorative (such as an icon used alongside text, or a thumbnail image within a link).
:::

:::example
Types include, but are not limited to:

* photograph
* illustration
* chart
* infographic
* map
* graph
* screenshot
* headshot
* diagram
:::

exceptWhen:
• An image is a link or a part of a link.
  • An image is a button or a part of a button.
  • An image is purely decorative (such as an icon used alongside text, or a thumbnail image within a link).
examples:
Types include, but are not limited to:

  • photograph
  • illustration
  • chart
  • infographic
  • map
  • graph
  • screenshot
  • headshot
  • diagram
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each image:

  1. Check if the image is not a link, a button, any other interactive element nor purely decorative.
  2. Check that the image type is described by the text alternative.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: An exploratory requirement: the type of an image is indicated - a photo, a chart, an illustration. Images that are links, buttons, or purely decorative are exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Knowing the kind of image sets expectations about what the alternative will contain and whether a longer description is worth seeking out.

title: Images Detectable
rawBody:
Non-decorative images are detectable.

:::applies-when
- content includes non-decorative images.
:::

appliesWhen: • content includes non-decorative images.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each non-decorative image:

  1. Check the code to see if it has been marked up in a way that makes it detectable; or
  2. For technologies where the code cannot be checked, use a screen reader to test that the image is detectable.

Expected results

  • #1 or #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where a page contains non-decorative images, those images can be detected - a user can tell that an image is there.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Knowing an image exists is what lets someone decide to seek out its description. An undetectable image is invisible even to a user who would want it.

title: Non-text content not relied on
rawBody: All non-text content that is not decorative includes a programmatically determinable equivalent text alternative.

derived.tests:
HTML alternative text for images

Procedure

  1. Examine the source code of the HTML document to identify all non-decorative img elements.
  2. Each img element has an alt attribute.
  3. The alt attribute provides a text alternative which conveys meaning or content that is displayed visually.
  4. If the image includes words that are important to understanding the content, the words are included in the text alternative.

Expected results

  • #2, #3, and #4 are true.

(Mobile) Videos include accessible name

Procedure

For each instance of non-text content:

  1. Using native mobile screen reader to review all videos in the app.
  2. When videos are navigated to an accessible name is read out.
  3. The accessible name includes the title of the video.

Expected results

  • #2 and #3 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: All non-decorative non-text content - not only images, but audio, icons, controls and the rest - has a programmatically determinable text equivalent.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Text is the one form that can be rendered as speech, braille, larger type or a different colour. It is what makes content translatable to any user's needs.

title: Sign language available (prerecorded)
rawBody:
Sign language interpretation is provided for all prerecorded audio content in the primary sign language that is most appropriate for each intended audience or region.

:::except-when
- The audio content is an alternative for visual content and is clearly labeled as such.
- The audio content is decorative background sound.
- The audio is an interface sound effect.
:::

:::example
Audio description is an example of audio content that is an alternative for visual content.
:::

exceptWhen:
• The audio content is an alternative for visual content and is clearly labeled as such.
  • The audio content is decorative background sound.
  • The audio is an interface sound effect.
examples: Audio description is an example of audio content that is an alternative for visual content.
derived.tests:
Sign language for audio only

Procedure

For each instance of prerecorded audio content:

  1. Check that sign language interpretation is available either as picture-in-picture or in a video closely associated with the audio controls.
  2. Check that sign language interpretation uses a version of sign language appropriate for the intended audience or region.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: Prerecorded audio content is interpreted into the primary sign language most appropriate for its audience or region. Audio that is an alternative to visual content and labelled as such, decorative background sound and interface sound effects are exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: For many deaf people a sign language is their first language and the written language of the page is a second one, so captions are not an equivalent route.

title: Sign Language Controllable
rawBody:
A mechanism is available to show and hide sign language interpretation. 

:::except-when
- Sign language interpretation is hard-coded into the video content.
- A sign language interpreted version is provided as a separate video.
:::

:::example
Hard-coded sign language interpretation would include video content where the interpreter is standing next to the speaker in the video.
:::

exceptWhen:
• Sign language interpretation is hard-coded into the video content.
  • A sign language interpreted version is provided as a separate video.
examples: Hard-coded sign language interpretation would include video content where the interpreter is standing next to the speaker in the video.
derived.tests:
Sign language control mechanism

Procedure

For each audio and video player where sign language is not hard-coded:

  1. Check that a mechanism is provided to switch on sign language interpretation.
  2. Check that a mechanism is provided to switch off sign language interpretation.
  3. Check that a link to a sign language interpreted version of the content is provided.

Expected results

  • Either #1 and #2 are true, or #3 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: There is a way to show and hide sign language interpretation, unless it is burned into the video or supplied as a separate interpreted version.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: An interpreter window occupies part of the picture. Viewers who do not use it need it out of the way, and viewers who do need it present.

title: Sign language policy (live)
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that: 

* Our organization has a policy to provide sign language interpretation for live in-person, hybrid, and fully online events/meetings.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion (with contact information)
* date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)
* date the policy was last reviewed/updated
* how sign language interpretation can be requested
    * format: email, phone, contact form
    * timeline/deadline for requesting (maybe just the average timeline)

::assertion-recommended

* approved vendors and contact information
* steps for hosting on each platform used
* versioned communications guide for announcing sign language availability for each meeting/event

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that it has a policy of providing sign language interpretation at live in-person, hybrid and online events, and publishes how and by when interpretation can be requested.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Live interpretation has to be booked ahead. A published route and deadline is what makes attendance possible rather than a matter of luck.

title: Graphical Object Contrast Sufficient
rawBody:
Parts of graphical objects required to understand the content meet a minimum contrast ratio test

:::except-when
* a particular presentation of graphical objects is essential to the information being conveyed.
:::

exceptWhen: • a particular presentation of graphical objects is essential to the information being conveyed.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each part of a graphical object that conveys information:

  1. Check that these parts meet the minimum contrast ratio with adjacent colors.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: The parts of a graphic you need in order to understand it must meet a minimum contrast ratio. Where a particular presentation is essential to the information itself, the requirement does not apply.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Icons, chart lines and diagram strokes carry meaning the same way text does. At low contrast that meaning disappears for people with low vision, and for anyone on a dim or glare-hit screen.

title: Hue Not Relied On
rawBody:
Information is not conveyed by hue alone.

:::note
Information conveyed includes but is not limited to presenting data or meaning, indicating an action, prompting a response, distinguishing between items, conveying boundaries. Artistic expression is not part of information conveyed.
:::

:::except-when
* Content is artistic or expressive.
* Content is designed only for a device that is limited to presenting hues.
:::

exceptWhen:
• Content is artistic or expressive.
  • Content is designed only for a device that is limited to presenting hues.
notes: Information conveyed includes but is not limited to presenting data or meaning, indicating an action, prompting a response, distinguishing between items, conveying boundaries. Artistic expression is not part of information conveyed.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each instance where information is conveyed by hue:

  1. Check that at least one additional visual indicator is present that conveys the same information.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Hue alone cannot be the only carrier of information. Artistic or expressive content, and content made for a device that can only present hues, are exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Around one in twelve men has a colour vision deficiency, and hue is also lost in greyscale printing, high-contrast modes and bright sunlight.

title: Sound Not Relied On
rawBody:
Information is not conveyed by sound alone.

:::except-when
* Content is audio-based media.
:::

:::note
Information conveyed includes but is not limited to presenting data or meaning, indicating an action, prompting a response, distinguishing between items, conveying boundaries. Artistic expression is not part of information conveyed.
:::

exceptWhen: • Content is audio-based media.
notes: Information conveyed includes but is not limited to presenting data or meaning, indicating an action, prompting a response, distinguishing between items, conveying boundaries. Artistic expression is not part of information conveyed.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each instance where information is conveyed by sound:

  1. Check that the information is also conveyed in a way that does not use sound, for instance with a visual, text, or haptic indicator.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Sound alone cannot be the only carrier of information, except where the content is itself audio-based media.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A beep signalling success or an error is silent for deaf users, for anyone with the volume down, and for anyone in a noisy place.

title: Spatial Audio Not Relied On
rawBody:
Information is not conveyed by spatial audio alone.

:::note
Information conveyed includes but is not limited to presenting data or meaning, indicating an action, prompting a response, distinguishing between items, and conveying boundaries. Artistic expression is not part of information conveyed.
:::

notes: Information conveyed includes but is not limited to presenting data or meaning, indicating an action, prompting a response, distinguishing between items, and conveying boundaries. Artistic expression is not part of information conveyed.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each instance where information is conveyed by spatial audio:

  1. Check that the information is also conveyed in a way that does not use sound, for instance with a visual text, or haptic indicator.

Expected results

  • #1 is true for all instances.

plainEnglish.summary: Where sound is positioned in space to convey information, that positioning cannot be the only way the information is given.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Spatial cues require hearing in both ears. They are unavailable to people with single-sided deafness or asymmetric hearing loss, and to anyone listening on one earbud or a mono speaker.

title: Visual Depth Not Relied On
rawBody: Information is not conveyed through visual depth perception alone.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each instance where information is conveyed by visual depth:

  1. Check that at least one additional visual indicator is present that conveys the same information.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Depth perception cannot be the only way information is conveyed.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Stereoscopic depth needs usable vision in both eyes. People with monocular vision or amblyopia get no depth cue at all, and flat displays remove it for everyone.

title: Descriptive Transcripts Available
rawBody:
Descriptive transcripts are provided for prerecorded audio and video content.

:::except-when
* The media is purely decorative.
* The media is already a media alternative for text and is clearly labeled as such.
* The visual track includes no information that is not already conveyed in the audio track (for example, a "talking head" video where only the speaker is visible against a static background).
:::

:::example
* actions
* charts or informative visuals
* scene changes
* on-screen text
:::

exceptWhen:
• The media is purely decorative.
  • The media is already a media alternative for text and is clearly labeled as such.
  • The visual track includes no information that is not already conveyed in the audio track (for example, a “talking head” video where only the speaker is visible against a static background).
examples:
• actions
  • charts or informative visuals
  • scene changes
  • on-screen text

plainEnglish.summary: Prerecorded audio and video have a descriptive transcript - one that covers the visuals as well as the speech. Purely decorative media, media that is already an alternative for text and labelled as such, and video whose picture adds nothing to the audio are exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A transcript is the one format that can be read at any speed, searched, translated, and rendered in braille. It serves deafblind users, who have no route through either captions or audio description.

title: Dialogue transcripts available (live)
rawBody:
Dialogue transcripts are available for all live audio and video content.

:::except-when
* The audio or video content is an alternative for text and is clearly labeled as such.
* The audio or video has no spoken content and serves only as background.
:::

exceptWhen:
• The audio or video content is an alternative for text and is clearly labeled as such.
  • The audio or video has no spoken content and serves only as background.

plainEnglish.summary: Live audio and video have a transcript of the dialogue. Media that is an alternative for text and labelled as such, and media with no spoken content that serves only as background, are exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A live transcript is what lets someone catch up on a point they missed, which captions scrolling in real time do not allow.

title: Dialogue transcripts available (prerecorded)
rawBody:
Dialogue transcripts are available for all prerecorded audio and video content.

:::except-when
* The audio or video content is an alternative for text and is clearly labeled as such.
* The audio or video has no spoken content and serves only as background.
:::

exceptWhen:
• The audio or video content is an alternative for text and is clearly labeled as such.
  • The audio or video has no spoken content and serves only as background.
derived.tests:
(General) Transcript is available

Procedure

For each instance of audio or video:

  1. Check that a transcript is available.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Prerecorded audio and video have a transcript of the dialogue, with the same exemptions for text alternatives and background-only media.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Reading at one's own pace is the difference between following a recording and merely playing it, particularly for people with cognitive or processing disabilities.

title: Non-verbal cues identified in transcripts
rawBody: Nonverbal cues needed to understand the media are explained in transcripts.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each instance of audio content that includes nonverbal cues:

  1. Check that the transcripts explain audio nonverbal cues, such as tone of voice, facial expressions, body gestures, or music with emotional meaning.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: An exploratory requirement: nonverbal cues needed to understand the media are explained in the transcript.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A transcript of words alone loses the tone and reaction that told the audience how to read those words.

title: Sounds Identified In Transcripts
rawBody:
Sounds needed to understand the media are identified or described in transcripts.

:::ednote
This includes sound effects and other non-spoken audio content.
:::

:::applies-when
- there is sound.
:::

:::except-when
- the video is decorative.
:::

appliesWhen: • there is sound.
exceptWhen: • the video is decorative.
editorNotes: This includes sound effects and other non-spoken audio content.
derived.tests:
Meaningful sounds in transcripts

Procedure

For all audio content:

  1. Identify meaningful non-verbal audio (sounds).
  2. Check that transcripts include a description of the meaningful non-verbal audio.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where sound carries meaning and the video is not decorative, the transcript records what the sound was, alongside the dialogue.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: For a reader who never hears the audio, an unmarked sound is simply an event that did not happen.

title: Speaker Language Identified In Transcripts
rawBody:
When more than one language is spoken in audio content, the language spoken by each speaker is identified in all transcripts.

:::except-when
- Words are used incidentally.
:::

exceptWhen: • Words are used incidentally.
derived.tests:
Language identified in transcripts

Procedure

For each transcript that includes multiple languages:

  1. Check that part(s) using a language different from the original language is programmatically determined in the transcripts.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where more than one language is spoken, the transcript identifies which language each speaker is using. Incidental words are exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Without the marker, a reader cannot tell a translated passage from the speaker's own words, or know that a second-language version exists.

title: Speakers Identified In Transcripts
rawBody:
Speakers are identified understandably within all transcripts.

:::applies-when
- There are multiple speakers in the video.
:::

:::except-when
- The speaker has a hidden identity as part of narrative structure.
- Identity is identifiable within the context of use.
:::

:::example
Initially using "Maya Angelou" within the context of a story regarding poetry and then using "Angelou".
:::

appliesWhen: • There are multiple speakers in the video.
exceptWhen:
• The speaker has a hidden identity as part of narrative structure.
  • Identity is identifiable within the context of use.
examples: Initially using “Maya Angelou” within the context of a story regarding poetry and then using “Angelou”.
derived.tests:
Consistent speaker name in transcripts

Procedure

For each transcript:

  1. Check that each speaker in the audio or video is consistently identified.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where there are several speakers, the transcript makes clear who is speaking - except where identity is deliberately hidden or clear from context.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: An unattributed transcript reads as one continuous voice, and the argument in a conversation becomes impossible to follow.

title: Transcripts equivalent (prerecorded)
rawBody:
Equivalent transcripts are available for audio and video content.

:::except-when
- The audio or video has no spoken content and serves only as background.
:::

exceptWhen: • The audio or video has no spoken content and serves only as background.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each transcript:

  1. Check that the content of the transcript is equivalent to the meaningful information in the media content.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Transcripts have to be equivalent to the media, not a partial record of it. Media with no spoken content that serves only as background is exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A transcript that summarises rather than conveys gives its readers less than everyone else receives from the same content.

title: Transcripts Findable
rawBody:
A text transcript is adjacent to audio and video content.

:::except-when
* The audio or video content has no spoken dialogue.
* The audio or video is decorative.
* The media is already a media alternative for text and is clearly labeled as such.
:::

exceptWhen:
• The audio or video content has no spoken dialogue.
  • The audio or video is decorative.
  • The media is already a media alternative for text and is clearly labeled as such.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each instance of audio or video:

  1. Check that a transcript or link to a transcript is provided for each audio or video.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: The transcript sits next to the audio or video it belongs to, not on a separate page someone has to hunt for. Media with no spoken dialogue, decorative media and labelled text alternatives are exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A transcript nobody can find is not an alternative. Adjacency is what makes it a real choice at the moment the media is encountered.

title: Transcripts Reviewed By Content Authors
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* We have reviewed the transcripts.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
* date of the review
* date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

* role of the creator
* number of creators (for each Role)
* date (Period) of review
* examples of fixed issues based on the review

:::example
* **Roles and numbers:** 3 creators
  * 1 director
  * 1 planner
  * 1 screenwriter/playwright
* **Period:** 10-21 October 2024
* **Examples of fixed issues:**
  * Provided more details based on feedback.
  * Rewrote some scripts to reflect the director's intent.
  * Added the description of the background shown in the video.
:::

examples:
• Roles and numbers: 3 creators
    • 1 director
    • 1 planner
    • 1 screenwriter/playwright
  • Period: 10-21 October 2024
  • Examples of fixed issues:
    • Provided more details based on feedback.
    • Rewrote some scripts to reflect the director’s intent.
    • Added the description of the background shown in the video.

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that it reviewed its transcripts, and records who did so and when.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Automatic transcription errors cluster on exactly the words that carry meaning - names, terms, numbers. Review is what catches them.

title: Transcripts Style Guide
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* Our organization has a style guide that includes guidance on transcripts and a policy and/or processes that the style guide must be followed.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
* date of when the style guide was published
* date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

* summary of the needs of users involved
* identified issues and details of solutions applied
* copy or snapshot of the style guide

:::example
* **Name:** ABC Inc. Style Guide for Transcripts
* **Version:** 1.2
* **Date:** October 2024
* **Description:** The style guide include sections such as:
  * What are transcripts?
  * Who needs transcripts?
  * Guideline provided by WCAG 3
  * Recommended style of transcripts
  * Resources
* **Example:** The style guide has requirements such as:
  * Never use more than two lines.
  * Use parentheses for sound representation.
  * Identify no sound or long pause.
  * …
:::

examples:
• Name: ABC Inc. Style Guide for Transcripts
  • Version: 1.2
  • Date: October 2024
  • Description: The style guide include sections such as:
    • What are transcripts?
    • Who needs transcripts?
    • Guideline provided by WCAG 3
    • Recommended style of transcripts
    • Resources
  • Example: The style guide has requirements such as:
    • Never use more than two lines.
    • Use parentheses for sound representation.
    • Identify no sound or long pause.
    • …

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that it has a style guide covering transcripts, plus a policy or process requiring it to be followed.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Transcripts are only easy to read when their conventions hold steady across a library.

title: Transcripts Usability Testing
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* We have conducted usability testing with users who need transcripts, and changes were made to fix or mitigate the issues found.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
* date of when the usability testing was conducted
* date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended
* scope
* types of disabilities each user had
* number of users (for each type of disability)
* date of testing
* identified issues and details of solutions applied

:::example
* **Scope:** videos on the following URLs:
  * "What is accessibility?" https://xxx.xxx/yyyy1
  * "About assistive technologies" https://xxx.xxx/yyyy2
  * "How to use WCAG" https://xxx.xxx/yyyy3
* **Type and number:** 8 users in total
  * 5 users who are deaf
  * 3 users who are hard of hearing
* **Dates:** 10-11 October 2024
* **Examples of fixed issues:**
  * Identified where the speaker changed.
  * Described background music.
  * Indicated that a dog was barking.
:::

examples:
• Scope: videos on the following URLs:
    • “What is accessibility?” https://xxx.xxx/yyyy1
    • “About assistive technologies” https://xxx.xxx/yyyy2
    • “How to use WCAG” https://xxx.xxx/yyyy3
  • Type and number: 8 users in total
    • 5 users who are deaf
    • 3 users who are hard of hearing
  • Dates: 10-11 October 2024
  • Examples of fixed issues:
    • Identified where the speaker changed.
    • Described background music.
    • Indicated that a dog was barking.

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that it tested with people who rely on transcripts and fixed or mitigated what the testing found.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Whether a transcript is usable depends on its structure and labelling, which shows up in use rather than in a spot check.

title: Visual Information Identified In Transcripts
rawBody:
Visual information needed to understand the media is described in transcripts.

:::ednote
* This includes actions, charts or informative visuals, scene changes, and on-screen text,
:::

editorNotes: • This includes actions, charts or informative visuals, scene changes, and on-screen text,
derived.tests:
Meaningful visual information in transcripts

Procedure

For each transcript:

  1. Check that the transcript includes a description of any visual information needed to understand the content of the audio or video.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Whatever the picture carries and the dialogue does not is written into the transcript, so the transcript stands alone as a record of the media.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: This is what separates a descriptive transcript from a dialogue list, and what makes the transcript a complete substitute for the media.

title: Biometrics Not Relied On
rawBody:
Biometric identification is not the only way to identify or authenticate.

:::note
Biometrics includes facial recognition software, fingerprinting, vocal patterns and other voice characteristics.
:::

notes: Biometrics includes facial recognition software, fingerprinting, vocal patterns and other voice characteristics.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each method of biometric user authentication:

  1. Check that there is at least one other method of non-biometric authentication.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.
derived.methods: • When requiring biometric information for authentication, provide an additional way to authenticate that is not biometric. For example, if a fingerprint is required for authentication, then a password must also be supported.

plainEnglish.summary: Biometric identification cannot be the only way to identify or authenticate - there has to be another route in.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Fingerprint and face recognition fail for people whose bodies the sensors were not designed around, including people with tremor, limb differences, facial differences or certain eye conditions. A failed scan with no alternative locks the account.

title: Multiple Biometrics Available
rawBody: Authentication does not rely solely on a single type of biometrics.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each method of user authentication:

  1. Check that there is at least one other method of authentication (biometric or non-biometric).

Expected results

  • #1 is true.
derived.methods: • When requiring biometric information for authentication, provide an additional way to authenticate (this may include using a different type of biometrics — for example, if a fingerprint is required for authentication, then voice authentication or a password must also be supported).

plainEnglish.summary: An exploratory requirement: authentication does not depend on a single type of biometric.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A person who cannot use one biometric may well be able to use another; offering only one turns a single sensor's limits into a lockout.

title: Voice Identification Not Relied On
rawBody: Voice identification is not the only way to identify or authenticate.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each place where voice is used for identification:

  1. Check that there is an alternative way to achieve authentication.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Voice identification cannot be the only way to identify or authenticate.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Voice recognition fails for people who are non-speaking, who have dysarthria or a speech difference, or whose voice changes with a condition or treatment.

title: Body Movements Not Relied On
rawBody:
Functionality does not rely solely on full or gross body movement.

:::except-when
- Full or gross body movement is essential to the functionality.
:::

:::note
This includes both detection of body movement and actions to the device, such as shaking, that require body movement.
:::

exceptWhen: • Full or gross body movement is essential to the functionality.
notes: This includes both detection of body movement and actions to the device, such as shaking, that require body movement.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each instance of functionality that uses body movement:

  1. Check that the body movement is not the only way to achieve any functionality.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Functionality cannot depend solely on full or gross body movement, unless that movement is essential to what the function is.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Requiring someone to move their whole body excludes wheelchair users, people with limited mobility and anyone seated at a fixed workstation.

title: Eye Tracking Not Relied On
rawBody:
Content and functionality does not rely solely on eye tracking.

:::except-when
- Eye tracking is essential. 
:::

:::note
This is primarily aimed at ensuring there is an alternative for people who cannot use eye tracking (but do have sight) due to eye conditions.
:::

:::note
Some platforms may only allow eye tracking. Ideally the platforms allow additional mechanisms for control. 
:::

exceptWhen: • Eye tracking is essential.
notes: This is primarily aimed at ensuring there is an alternative for people who cannot use eye tracking (but do have sight) due to eye conditions.
Some platforms may only allow eye tracking. Ideally the platforms allow additional mechanisms for control.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For platforms that use eye-tracking for pointer use:

  1. Check that an alternative, such as using a switch control, is available.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Content and functionality cannot rely solely on eye tracking, unless eye tracking is essential.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Eye tracking assumes steady, controllable gaze. Nystagmus, strabismus, low vision and blindness all make it unreliable or impossible.

title: Hover Content Persistent
rawBody:
If pointer hover can trigger content, then the pointer can be moved over the additional content without the additional content disappearing.

:::applies-when
- Receiving and then removing pointer hover or keyboard focus triggers additional content to become visible and then hidden, and the visual presentation of the additional content is controlled by the author and not by the user agent.
:::

:::note
This applies to content that appears in addition to the triggering of the interactive element itself. Since hidden interactive elements that are made visible on keyboard focus (such as links used to skip to another part of a page/view) do not present additional content, they are not covered by this requirement.
:::

:::example
Additional content controlled by the user agent includes browser tooltips created through use of the HTML `title` attribute.
:::

:::example
Custom tooltips, sub-menus, and other non-modal popups that display on hover and keyboard focus.
:::

appliesWhen: • Receiving and then removing pointer hover or keyboard focus triggers additional content to become visible and then hidden, and the visual presentation of the additional content is controlled by the author and not by the user agent.
notes: This applies to content that appears in addition to the triggering of the interactive element itself. Since hidden interactive elements that are made visible on keyboard focus (such as links used to skip to another part of a page/view) do not present additional content, they are not covered by this requirement.
examples: Additional content controlled by the user agent includes browser tooltips created through use of the HTML title attribute.
Custom tooltips, sub-menus, and other non-modal popups that display on hover and keyboard focus.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For additional content that appears on hover:

  1. Check that the pointer can be moved over the additional content without the additional content disappearing.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where hovering makes extra content appear, the pointer can be moved onto that content without it vanishing. This applies when the author, rather than the browser, controls how the extra content looks.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A tooltip that disappears when you move toward it cannot be read by anyone who uses magnification, has a tremor, or simply moves the pointer slowly.

title: Hover Or Focus Content Dismissible
rawBody:
A mechanism is available to dismiss content that appears on pointer hover or keyboard focus without moving pointer hover or keyboard focus, unless the additional content does not obscure or replace other content.

:::applies-when
- Receiving and then removing pointer hover or keyboard focus triggers additional content to become visible and then hidden, and the visual presentation of the additional content is controlled by the author and not by the user agent.
:::

:::note
This applies to content that appears in addition to the triggering of the interactive element itself. Since hidden interactive elements that are made visible on keyboard focus (such as links used to skip to another part of a page/view) do not present additional content, they are not covered by this requirement.
:::

:::example
Additional content controlled by the user agent includes browser tooltips created through use of the HTML `title` attribute.
:::

:::example
Custom tooltips, sub-menus, and other non-modal popups that display on hover and keyboard focus.
:::

appliesWhen: • Receiving and then removing pointer hover or keyboard focus triggers additional content to become visible and then hidden, and the visual presentation of the additional content is controlled by the author and not by the user agent.
notes: This applies to content that appears in addition to the triggering of the interactive element itself. Since hidden interactive elements that are made visible on keyboard focus (such as links used to skip to another part of a page/view) do not present additional content, they are not covered by this requirement.
examples: Additional content controlled by the user agent includes browser tooltips created through use of the HTML title attribute.
Custom tooltips, sub-menus, and other non-modal popups that display on hover and keyboard focus.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For additional content that appears on hover:

  1. Check that the content can be closed without moving the pointer way from the trigger. Either by pressing Esc, by pressing another documented keyboard shortcut, or by activating the trigger.

For additional content that appears on focus:

  1. Check that the content can be closed without moving the focus away from the trigger. Either by pressing Esc, by pressing another other documented keyboard shortcut, or by activating the trigger.

Expected results

  • For additional content that appears on hover: #1 is true.
  • For additional content that appears on focus: #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Content that appears on hover or keyboard focus can be dismissed without moving the pointer or the focus, unless it does not cover or replace anything else.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A popup covering the field you are typing in is a trap for magnification users - dismissing it by moving away means losing your place.

title: Hover Or Focus Content Persistent
rawBody:
Content that appears on pointer hover or keyboard focus remains visible until the hover or keyboard focus trigger is removed, the user dismisses it, or its information is no longer valid.

:::applies-when
- Receiving and then removing pointer hover or keyboard focus triggers additional content to become visible and then hidden, and the visual presentation of the additional content is controlled by the author and not by the user agent.
:::

:::note
This applies to content that appears in addition to the triggering of the interactive element itself. Since hidden interactive elements that are made visible on keyboard focus (such as links used to skip to another part of a page/view) do not present additional content, they are not covered by this requirement.
:::

:::example
Additional content controlled by the user agent includes browser tooltips created through use of the HTML `title` attribute.
:::

:::example
Custom tooltips, sub-menus, and other non-modal popups that display on hover and keyboard focus.
:::

appliesWhen: • Receiving and then removing pointer hover or keyboard focus triggers additional content to become visible and then hidden, and the visual presentation of the additional content is controlled by the author and not by the user agent.
notes: This applies to content that appears in addition to the triggering of the interactive element itself. Since hidden interactive elements that are made visible on keyboard focus (such as links used to skip to another part of a page/view) do not present additional content, they are not covered by this requirement.
examples: Additional content controlled by the user agent includes browser tooltips created through use of the HTML title attribute.
Custom tooltips, sub-menus, and other non-modal popups that display on hover and keyboard focus.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For additional content or focus that appears on hover:

  1. Check that the additional content stays visible and does not automatically close after a time.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Content shown on hover or focus stays visible until the trigger is removed, the user dismisses it, or its information stops being valid.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Content that times out on its own is gone before slower readers, screen magnifier users and people using switch input have finished with it.

title: Input Method Flexible
rawBody:
The ability to switch between input methods is available at any time.

:::note
This does not mean that all input technologies (pointer, keyboard, voice, gesture) need to be supported, but if an input modality is supported, it is supported everywhere in the content except where a particular input method is essential to the functionality.
:::

notes: This does not mean that all input technologies (pointer, keyboard, voice, gesture) need to be supported, but if an input modality is supported, it is supported everywhere in the content except where a particular input method is essential to the functionality.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each input:

  1. Set up multiple input types (for example, pointer, keyboard, voice, gesture)
  2. Check that you can switch between inputs and complete functionality.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: The user can switch between input methods at any time, rather than being locked into the one they started with.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Many people move between keyboard, pointer, voice and touch during one session, often because of fatigue or pain. Being locked in forces them to stop.

title: Path-based gesture not relied on
rawBody:
Path-based gestures are not the only way of achieving any functionality.

:::except-when
- A path-based gesture is essential to the functionality.
:::

exceptWhen: • A path-based gesture is essential to the functionality.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each path-based gesture:

  1. Check that the functionality is available without a path-based gesture.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: A gesture that has to follow a particular path - a swipe, a drag along a line - cannot be the only way to do something, unless the path is essential.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Path gestures require fine motor control and a pointer that can be dragged accurately, which rules out switch users, many voice users and people with tremor.

title: Pointer Accessible
rawBody:
Pointer selection of elements moves the keyboard focus to that element, even if the user selects an interactive element and drags away from the element without activation.

:::applies-when
- Content can interfere with pointer or keyboard focus behavior.
:::

:::example
A user scrolls a document down six screens, then clicks on a paragraph with their pointer. The user then presses the <kbd>Tab</kbd> key, which moves the focus to the first interactive component after the position on the screen that was clicked, rather than from the previous position, six screens up the document.
:::

appliesWhen: • Content can interfere with pointer or keyboard focus behavior.
examples: A user scrolls a document down six screens, then clicks on a paragraph with their pointer. The user then presses the Tab key, which moves the focus to the first interactive component after the position on the screen that was clicked, rather than from the previous position, six screens up the document.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For every interactive element that allows pointer selection (including click events on non-interactive elements):

  1. Check that the keyboard focus moves when the pointer selects the element.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Selecting an element with a pointer moves keyboard focus to it, including when the user presses down on an interactive element and then drags away without activating it.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: When focus and pointer disagree, a user who alternates between mouse and keyboard loses their place, and a screen reader announces somewhere other than where the user is working.

title: Bidirectional Navigation
rawBody:
The keyboard interface can always move forward to the next interactive element and back to the previous interactive element.

:::note
Although keyboard navigation is required to be bidirectional, it is not required that it be symmetrical, even though this is usually recommended practice.
:::

:::example
Tabbing through menus, hitting <kbd>space</kbd> to open a menu, tabbing off the end of the menu lands you on the next menu. A <kbd><kbd>shift</kbd>+<kbd>tab</kbd></kbd> may go back to the last item in the previous menu (symmetrical) or to the last menu (not symmetrical but also does not fail this requirement).
:::

notes: Although keyboard navigation is required to be bidirectional, it is not required that it be symmetrical, even though this is usually recommended practice.
examples: Tabbing through menus, hitting space to open a menu, tabbing off the end of the menu lands you on the next menu. A shift+tab may go back to the last item in the previous menu (symmetrical) or to the last menu (not symmetrical but also does not fail this requirement).
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each interactive element:

  1. Check that when tabbing forwards, you can navigate to the interactive element and then to the next interactive element.
  2. Check that when tabbing backwards, you can navigate to the interactive element and then to the previous interactive element.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.
derived.methods: • Use standard HTML to create interactive elements.
derived.recommendedPractices: • Avoid modifying the tab order to be in only one direction.

plainEnglish.summary: The keyboard interface can always move on to the next interactive element and back to the previous one.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: One-way navigation means a mistake can only be corrected by starting the page over, which for a keyboard-only user can mean dozens of keystrokes.

title: Custom Keys Documented
rawBody: Documentation for each custom keyboard command is actively available on the page/view to which it applies, or within the applicable process.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each custom keyboard command that works on a page/view:

  1. Check that documentation for the keyboard commands exists.
  2. Check that the documentation is actively available on the page/view to which it applies.
  3. Check that the documentation is actively available within the applicable process.

Expected results

  • #1 is true, and #2 or #3 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where a page defines its own keyboard commands, the documentation for them is available on the page or within the process where they apply.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: An undocumented shortcut may as well not exist, and a user who discovers one by accident cannot tell what else is available.

title: Focus Movement Relevant
rawBody:
Except for skip links and other elements that are hidden but specifically added to aid keyboard navigation, tabbing does not move the keyboard focus onto content that was not visible before the tab action.

:::note
Accordions, dropdown menus, and [ARIA tab panels](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/tabs/) are examples of expandable content. According to this requirement, these would not expand simply because they include an element in the tab-order contained in them. They would either not expand or would not have any tab-order elements in them.
:::

:::example
A menu that expands when you tab to it, but then uses arrow keys to navigate in it would pass. But a menu that expands and then requires you to tab through all the newly-visible elements to navigate past it would fail.
:::

notes: Accordions, dropdown menus, and ARIA tab panels are examples of expandable content. According to this requirement, these would not expand simply because they include an element in the tab-order contained in them. They would either not expand or would not have any tab-order elements in them.
examples: A menu that expands when you tab to it, but then uses arrow keys to navigate in it would pass. But a menu that expands and then requires you to tab through all the newly-visible elements to navigate past it would fail.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For any interactive element:

  1. Check that keyboard focus does not disappear into content that is not visible.
  2. Check that hidden element does not automatically expand (become visible) when the keyboard focus is on it (unless it is a visually hidden element specifically added to aid keyboard navigation) (for example, skip to main content).

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: Tabbing does not move focus onto content that was not visible before the tab press, apart from skip links and similar hidden aids to keyboard navigation.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Focus landing on something invisible strands sighted keyboard users, who can see the focus indicator disappear but not where it went.

title: Focus Placed
rawBody:
When keyboard focus moves from one context to another within a page/view, whether automatically or by user request, the keyboard focus is preserved so that, when the user returns to the previous context, the keyboard focus is restored to its previous location unless that location no longer exists.

:::example
When a user closes a modal dialog or other popup, keyboard focus is returned to the element that caused the dialog or popup to open.
:::

:::example
When there are tags, with a delete button on each tag, the keyboard focus needs to be moved to a meaningful location after a tag is deleted.
:::

examples: When a user closes a modal dialog or other popup, keyboard focus is returned to the element that caused the dialog or popup to open.
When there are tags, with a delete button on each tag, the keyboard focus needs to be moved to a meaningful location after a tag is deleted.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each situation where elements that have or contain keyboard focus are removed:

  1. Check that the keyboard focus moves to its previous location, or, if that no longer exists, to another meaningful location.

Expected results

  • #1 is true for each situation.
derived.methods: • When removing interactive elements such as filters, dialogs, or popups that currently contain focus, actively place the focus back on the element that led to that element, the previous element within the focus order, or another meaningful location.
derived.recommendedPractices: • Conduct usability testing with screen reader users to evaluate the focus movement.

plainEnglish.summary: When keyboard focus moves between contexts within a page, returning to the previous context restores focus to where it was - unless that place no longer exists.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Being dumped back at the top of a long page after closing a dialog can mean re-traversing the entire page, which is slow and disorienting for keyboard and screen reader users.

title: Focus user-controlled
rawBody:
The keyboard focus only moves as a result of user interaction.

:::except-when
- The keyboard focus automatically moves to the next interactive elements in keyboard navigation order on completion of some user action, such when the focus moves between the fields for a time-based one-time password (TOTP) code.
- The keyboard focus results from security or emergency situations, such as warning about an imminent session timeout that would cause the user to lose their work.
- The user is informed of the potential keyboard focus move before it happens and given the chance to avoid the move.
:::

exceptWhen:
• The keyboard focus automatically moves to the next interactive elements in keyboard navigation order on completion of some user action, such when the focus moves between the fields for a time-based one-time password (TOTP) code.
  • The keyboard focus results from security or emergency situations, such as warning about an imminent session timeout that would cause the user to lose their work.
  • The user is informed of the potential keyboard focus move before it happens and given the chance to avoid the move.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each time the keyboard focus changes:

  1. Check that one of the following is true:
    • The focus was moved under direct user control
    • A new page / view such as a dialog is introduced and the focus is moved to it
    • The user is informed of the potential move and given the chance to avoid the move
    • The keyboard focus moves to the next item in keyboard navigation order

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Keyboard focus moves only because the user did something. The draft allows narrow exceptions, such as advancing between the boxes of a one-time code and security or emergency situations like an imminent session timeout.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Focus that moves on its own takes control away mid-task: a screen reader starts reading somewhere else, and typed input can land in a field the user never chose.

title: Keyboard Accessible
rawBody:
All content that can be accessed by other input modalities can be accessed using keyboard interface only.

:::note
All content includes content made available via mechanisms including but not limited to hovers, right clicks.
:::

:::note
Other input modalities include pointing devices, voice and speech recognition, gesture, camera, and any other means of input or control.
:::

:::note
The ["Keyboard operable" requirement](#keyboard-operable) allows you to navigate to all actionable elements, but if the next element is 5 screens down, you also need to be able to access all the content. Also, if the content is in expanding sections, you need to not only open them but also access all of the content, not just its actionable elements.
:::

notes: All content includes content made available via mechanisms including but not limited to hovers, right clicks.
Other input modalities include pointing devices, voice and speech recognition, gesture, camera, and any other means of input or control.

The “Keyboard operable” requirement allows you to navigate to all actionable elements, but if the next element is 5 screens down, you also need to be able to access all the content. Also, if the content is in expanding sections, you need to not only open them but also access all of the content, not just its actionable elements.
derived.tests:
Procedure For all content on the page/view:

  1. Check that the content can be viewed using the keyboard and keyboard actions in the Standard Keyboard Navigation & Operation Keys and Techniques;
  2. Check that the content can be viewed using keyboard actions described on the page where it is required or on a page earlier in the process where it is required.

Expected results

  • #1 or #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Anything reachable with another input method has to be reachable with the keyboard interface alone.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: The keyboard interface is what screen readers, switch devices, sip-and-puff systems and voice control all drive. Content it cannot reach is content those users cannot reach.

title: Keyboard Operable
rawBody: All components on the page/view that can be operated by pointer, audio (voice or other), gesture, camera, or other means can be operated using keyboard interface only.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each interactive element:

  1. Check that it can be operated using only the keyboard and keyboard actions in the Standard Keyboard Navigation & Operation Keys and Techniques or described on the page where it is required or on a page earlier in the process where it is required.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Anything operable by pointer, voice, gesture, camera or any other means has to be operable with the keyboard interface alone.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Reaching a control is not the same as being able to use it. A custom widget that only responds to a mouse event is a dead end for every keyboard-driven assistive technology.

title: No Keyboard Conflicts
rawBody: Custom keyboard commands do not conflict with standard platform keyboard commands or they can be remapped.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each custom keyboard command:

  1. Check that it does not conflict against the standard platform keyboard commands.
  2. Check that it can be remapped.

Expected results

  • #1 or #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Custom keyboard commands must not clash with standard platform commands, or they must be remappable.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A single-key shortcut that overrides a platform command can disable an assistive technology's own keys, which is worse than having no shortcut at all.

title: No Keyboard Traps
rawBody:
Components that can be activated or entered using the keyboard interface, can be deactivated or exited using a standard keyboard navigation-operation technique, standard platform keyboard commands.

:::except-when
- The non-standard keyboard navigation technique is described in the page/view or earlier in the process.
:::

:::example
* Ensuring that users can exit a modal dialog, menu, or calendar picker after entering it.
* Ensuring that users can deactivate an animation, video, drop down menu, or carousel after activating it.
:::

exceptWhen: • The non-standard keyboard navigation technique is described in the page/view or earlier in the process.
examples:
• Ensuring that users can exit a modal dialog, menu, or calendar picker after entering it.
  • Ensuring that users can deactivate an animation, video, drop down menu, or carousel after activating it.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each interface element:

  1. Check that you can exit from it in a forward or backward direction.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Anything you can enter or activate with the keyboard, you can leave using standard keyboard techniques - unless a non-standard way out is described on the page or earlier in the process.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A keyboard trap ends the session: the user cannot move on, cannot go back, and often cannot reach the browser's own controls.

title: Keyboard Effort Comparable
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

- A review has been conducted and changes made (when necessary) to ensure that there is minimal difference between the number of input commands required when using the keyboard interface only and the number of commands when using other input modalities.

:::note
Other input modalities include pointing devices, voice and speech recognition, gesture, camera, and any other means of input or control.
:::

::assertion-required

- title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
- date of when the review was conducted
- date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)
- scope of assertion (if different from the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

- copy of the review implementing the use of user interface design principles that include minimizing the difference between the number of input commands required when using the keyboard interface only and the number of commands when using other input modalities
- whether training was provided for authors
- date training was provided
- number or proportion of authors who completed the training
- copy of the user interface design principles document

notes: Other input modalities include pointing devices, voice and speech recognition, gesture, camera, and any other means of input or control.

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that it reviewed its content, and made changes where needed, so that doing a task with the keyboard alone takes a comparable number of commands to doing it another way.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Content can be technically keyboard-operable and still take five times as many keystrokes. That gap is a fatigue and pain cost for people with motor disabilities and RSI.

title: Navigation Keys Described
rawBody:
If any keyboard action needed to navigate, perceive, and operate the full content of the page/view is not a common keyboard navigation technique, then it is described in the page/view where it is required or on a page/view earlier in the process where it is used. 

:::note
Any platform-related functions are not the responsibility of the author as long as they are not overridden by the content. Examples:

- <kbd>Tab</kbd> and <kbd><kbd>Shift</kbd> + <kbd>Tab</kbd></kbd> to move through elements
- Sticky Keys functionality that allows single key activation of multi-key commands
:::

notes:
Any platform-related functions are not the responsibility of the author as long as they are not overridden by the content. Examples:

  • Tab and Shift + Tab to move through elements
  • Sticky Keys functionality that allows single key activation of multi-key commands
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each keyboard command needed to operate functionality:

  1. Check that it is in the list of common keyboard navigation techniques.
  2. Check that it is described on the page / view where it is required or on a page / view earlier in the process where it is used.

Expected results

  • #1 or #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: If understanding or operating the page needs a keyboard action that is not a common navigation technique, it is described on that page or earlier in the process.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Custom interaction models are not discoverable by exploration. Without a description, a keyboard user has no way to know the technique exists.

title: No Repetitive Adjacent Interactive Elements
rawBody:
Adjacent interactive elements that achieve the same outcome are not included in the page/view.

:::except-when
- That outcome is a form of dismissal.
:::

:::note
A common pattern is having a component that includes a linked image and some linked text, where both links go to the same content. Someone using screen reading software can be disoriented from the unnecessary chatter, and a keyboard user has to navigate through more tab stops than should be necessary. Combining adjacent links that go to the same content improves the user experience.
:::

exceptWhen: • That outcome is a form of dismissal.
notes: A common pattern is having a component that includes a linked image and some linked text, where both links go to the same content. Someone using screen reading software can be disoriented from the unnecessary chatter, and a keyboard user has to navigate through more tab stops than should be necessary. Combining adjacent links that go to the same content improves the user experience.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For adjacent interactive elements that achieve the same outcome:

  1. Check that only one of the elements is focusable and available to assistive technology.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.
derived.methods:
• When repetitive interactive elements are used, remove them from the focus and reading order.
  • Use a single link instead of multiple links to the same destination.
derived.recommendedPractices: • Combine repetitive links into a single interactive element.

plainEnglish.summary: Adjacent interactive elements that do the same thing are not both included - unless the outcome is a form of dismissal.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Duplicated links and buttons double the tab stops and the screen reader announcements for no added function, which is pure cost for keyboard and screen reader users.

title: Consistent Pointer Cancellation
rawBody:
The method of pointer cancellation is consistent for each type of interaction within a set of pages/views.

:::except-when
- It is essential to be different.
:::

:::note
Where it is essential to be different, it can be helpful to alert the user.
:::

exceptWhen: • It is essential to be different.
notes: Where it is essential to be different, it can be helpful to alert the user.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each type of pointer interaction:

  1. Check that it can be canceled with a consistent interaction.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: How a pointer action is cancelled stays the same for each type of interaction across a set of pages, unless a difference is essential.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Cancelling an accidental press is a skill users learn once. Changing the rule between pages means accidental activations stick.

title: Pointer Activation Controllable
rawBody:
At least one of the following is true for functionality that can be activated using a simple pointer input:

No down event
: The down event of the pointer is not used to execute any part of the function.

Cancel or undo
: Completion of the function is on the up event and a mechanism is available to cancel the function before completion, or there is a mechanism to undo the function after completion.

Up reversal
: The up event reverses any outcome of the preceding down event.

:::except-when
- Completing the function on the down event is essential.
:::

:::example
An example of Cancel would be dragging where there is a pickup action on button down, but it can be canceled by dropping anywhere other than the drop area.
:::

:::example
Examples of places where action on down event may be essential include a descending-price auction or a game trigger.
:::

exceptWhen: • Completing the function on the down event is essential.
examples: An example of Cancel would be dragging where there is a pickup action on button down, but it can be canceled by dropping anywhere other than the drop area.
Examples of places where action on down event may be essential include a descending-price auction or a game trigger.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each element that can be activated with a simple pointer:

  1. Check that the down-event of the pointer is not used to execute any part of the function.
  2. Check that completion of the function is on the up-event, and a mechanism is available to abort the function before completion or to undo the function after completion.
  3. Check that the up-event reverses any outcome of the preceding down-event.
  4. Check that completing the function on the down-event is essential.

Expected results

  • Any of #1, #2, #3, or #4 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: For anything activated by a simple pointer input, at least one of these has to hold: nothing happens on the down event; the action completes on the up event and can be cancelled beforehand or undone afterwards; or the up event reverses whatever the down event did. Only an essential need to act on the down event is exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: People with tremor, limited dexterity or an imprecise pointer press the wrong thing regularly. Acting on release rather than press is what makes a mis-press recoverable.

title: Pointer Pressure Not Relied On
rawBody:
Specific pointer pressure is not the only way of achieving any functionality.

:::except-when
- Specific pressure is essential to the functionality.
:::

:::example
Specific pressure would be essential to a paintbrush feature or advanced signature verification.
:::

exceptWhen: • Specific pressure is essential to the functionality.
examples: Specific pressure would be essential to a paintbrush feature or advanced signature verification.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each instance of interactive content:

  1. Check that pointer pressure is not the only way to achieve any functionality.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.
derived.methods: • When building in functionality that relies on pointer pressure, add a slider or other control that can complete the same functionality.

plainEnglish.summary: Requiring a particular pointer pressure - a force press, for instance - cannot be the only way to do something, unless that pressure is essential.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Pressure-sensitive input assumes controlled force, which is not available to people with weakness, tremor, or those using a head pointer, stylus or switch.

title: Pointer Speed Not Relied On
rawBody:
Functionality does not rely solely on specific pointer speed.

:::except-when
- Specific pointer speed is essential to the functionality.
:::

:::example
Specific pointer speed would be essential to a paintbrush feature, advanced signature verification, or time-constrained gaming.
:::

exceptWhen: • Specific pointer speed is essential to the functionality.
examples: Specific pointer speed would be essential to a paintbrush feature, advanced signature verification, or time-constrained gaming.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each instance of functionality that uses a pointer:

  1. Check that pointer speed is not the only way to achieve any functionality.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Functionality cannot depend on moving the pointer at a particular speed, unless that speed is essential.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Speed requirements like double-click timing or a fast flick exclude people whose movements are slow or variable, including many older users.

title: Simple Pointer Input Available
rawBody:
All functionality and content available using complex pointer inputs is also available using a simple pointer input, or a sequence of simple pointer inputs that do not require timing.

:::example
Complex pointer inputs include but are not limited to:

- double clicks
- dragging movements
- swipe gestures
- multipoint gestures such as pinching, split tap, or two-finger rotor
- variable pressure or timing
:::

:::note
Complex pointer inputs are not banned, but they cannot be the only way to accomplish an action.
:::

:::note
Simple pointer input is different than single pointer input and is more restrictive than simply using a single pointer.
:::

notes: Complex pointer inputs are not banned, but they cannot be the only way to accomplish an action.
Simple pointer input is different than single pointer input and is more restrictive than simply using a single pointer.
examples:
Complex pointer inputs include but are not limited to:

  • double clicks
  • dragging movements
  • swipe gestures
  • multipoint gestures such as pinching, split tap, or two-finger rotor
  • variable pressure or timing
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each functionality that uses pointer input other than simple pointer input:

  1. Check that it can also be operated by a simple pointer input or a sequence of simple pointer inputs that do not require timing.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Anything you can do with a complex pointer input - multi-finger, multi-point, path-based - can also be done with a simple pointer input, or a series of them that does not depend on timing.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Multi-point and timed gestures are unavailable to people using a head pointer, switch, stylus or single finger, and to anyone whose movements are slow or imprecise.

title: Generated Speech Testing
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

- We have tested voice input and communication systems with generated speech to ensure the systems work with artificial speech as well as human speech.

::assertion-required

- title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
- date of when the policy was implemented
- date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

- systems tested
- accuracy rates
