plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that it tested its voice input and communication systems with synthetic speech, not only human speech.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Many non-speaking people communicate through a speech-generating device. A system tuned only to human voices rejects them at the door.

title: Real-time text available
rawBody: A real-time text option is available for real-time bidirectional voice communication.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each place where speech is used for communication (with human or AI):

  1. Check that there is an alternative way to achieve the same function using real-time text.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.
derived.methods: • Provide a chat option for any voice communication.

plainEnglish.summary: Two-way live voice communication also offers real-time text - text that transmits as it is typed rather than when a message is sent.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Real-time text lets a deaf or non-speaking person hold a live conversation at conversational pace, including in emergencies where a voice call is the default channel.

title: Speech Not Relied On
rawBody:
Content or functionality does not rely on speech alone.

:::except-when
- Speech input is essential to the functionality.
:::

exceptWhen: • Speech input is essential to the functionality.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each functionality or content that is accessed using speech input:

  1. Check that there is another way to complete the functionality.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.
derived.methods: • When speech input is supported, an additional way of providing input is also supported.

plainEnglish.summary: Content and functionality cannot depend on speech alone, unless speech input is essential to what the function is.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Requiring speech excludes people who are non-speaking, who have a speech difference, who use a communication device, or who are in a setting where they cannot speak.

title: Changes To Elements Notified
rawBody: Changes to interactive element names, roles, values, or states are visually and programmatically indicated.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each interactive element:

  1. Confirm that the role, value, and state (when applicable) are visually indicated in all states.
  2. Inspect the code and accessibility tree (when available) to confirm that the name, role, value and state (when applicable) are indicated.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.
derived.methods:
• Add code that clearly defines the name, role, value and state.
  • Visually indicate the names, roles, and values of the interactive element.
  • HTML: HTML tags or ARIA

plainEnglish.summary: When an interactive element's name, role, value or state changes, that change is indicated both visually and programmatically.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A state change nobody announces - a button that has become pressed, a field now marked invalid - leaves screen reader users acting on stale information.

title: Input Constraints Used
rawBody:
Field constraints and conditions are available.

:::example
* required line length
* date format
* password format
:::

examples:
• required line length
  • date format
  • password format
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each input:

  1. Confirm it has a visual information that describes the constraint.
  2. Inspect the code and accessibility tree (when applicable) and confirm that the constraint is programmatically listed in the code and associated with the input.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.
derived.methods: • HTML: To programmatically indicate, use the pattern attribute or write the information in a label; to visually indicate, add the requirements to the page near the input.

plainEnglish.summary: The constraints and conditions on a field - required format, length, allowed values - are made available to the user.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Constraints discovered only by failing are a guessing game, which is costly for people with cognitive disabilities and for anyone whose input is slow or effortful.

title: Interactive Element Contrast Sufficient
rawBody:
Visual information required to identify interactive elements and states meet a minimum contrast ratio test.

:::except-when
* The interactive element is inactive, or
* The appearance of the component is determined by the user agent and not modified by the content author.
:::

exceptWhen:
• The interactive element is inactive, or
  • The appearance of the component is determined by the user agent and not modified by the content author.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each interactive element:

  1. Identify which visual information defines the boundaries of the interactive area.
  2. Check if the visual information meets the minimum contrast ratio test.
  3. For each possible state, repeat step 1 and 2.

Expected results

  • #2 is true for each state.

plainEnglish.summary: The visual information needed to identify an interactive element and its states has to meet a minimum contrast ratio. Inactive elements, and components whose appearance the browser supplies unmodified, are exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: If the boundary of a control or the mark showing it is selected is too faint to see, the control is effectively invisible to people with low vision, even though its label is readable.

title: Interactive Element Importance Indicated
rawBody: The importance of interactive components is indicated.

plainEnglish.summary: An exploratory requirement: the relative importance of interactive components is indicated.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: When every control looks equally weighted, users have to read all of them to find the one that matters - a real cost for people with cognitive disabilities or limited screen area.

title: Interactive Element Names Available
rawBody:
Persistent names (including labels) that identify the purpose of the interactive element are visually and programmatically available. 

:::note
Visible labels can be text or non-text, for instance icons.
:::

notes: Visible labels can be text or non-text, for instance icons.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each interactive element:

  1. Confirm it has a visual label that describes the element.
  2. Confirm the visual label persists during use.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.
derived.methods: • Provide unique, descriptive text or image (icon) for each interactive element.
derived.recommendedPractices:
• To ensure clarity, pair an icon with a persistent visible text label, or only use a persistent visible text label.
  • When an icon is the only visual label, provide a tooltip (hover label) with the text description.

plainEnglish.summary: Every clickable or interactive element (buttons, links, form fields, tabs) must have a persistent visual and programmatic name so users know what it does.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Users rely on labels to know what will happen when they click or tap. Screen readers need programmatic names to announce controls accurately.

title: Interactive Elements Distinguishable
rawBody: Interactive elements are visually distinguishable without interaction from static content and include visual cues on how to use them.

derived.methods: • Add visual indicators, such as shading, border, drop-down arrow, or placement, to interactive elements.
derived.recommendedPractices: • Document interactive indicators and designs in a style guide.

plainEnglish.summary: Interactive elements look different from static content before anyone interacts with them, and carry visual cues about how to use them.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Flat design that removes button edges and link underlines makes people hunt by hovering, which is impossible on touch and unreliable for anyone with low vision or a cognitive disability.

title: Label Included In Programmatic Name
rawBody: The programmatic name includes the visual label.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each interactive element:

  1. Identify the interactive elements’ programmatic name.
  2. Identify the interactive element’s visual name.
  3. Check that #1 includes all of #2.

Expected results

  • #3 is true.
derived.methods: • Code the same name as you display.
derived.recommendedPractices: • Use unique names and keep the programmatic and visual names the same.

plainEnglish.summary: The programmatic name of a control contains the visible label text.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Voice control users say what they see. When the accessible name does not contain the visible words, the command simply fails.

title: Roles, values, states, properties available
rawBody: Accurate names, roles, values, and states are available for interactive elements.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each interactive element:

  1. Inspect the code and accessibility tree (when available) to confirm that the role, value, state, and properties (when applicable) are indicated.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.
derived.methods:
• HTML: Use HTML elements according to specification.
  • ARIA: Add roles, values, states, and properties according to specification.

plainEnglish.summary: Interactive elements expose accurate names, roles, values and states.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: This is what assistive technology reads. An element with a wrong role is announced as the wrong kind of thing, and a missing state hides whether it is on, off, expanded or selected.

title: Consistent Control Location
rawBody:
Where an interactive element with the same purpose is used across pages/views, its visual position in the layout is maintained.

:::except-when
- The location changes due to a page variation or viewport change, or
- The layout changes due to being part of a process.
:::

:::example
An e-commerce checkout is an example of where the layout might change within a longer process.
:::

exceptWhen:
• The location changes due to a page variation or viewport change, or
  • The layout changes due to being part of a process.
examples: An e-commerce checkout is an example of where the layout might change within a longer process.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each interactive component in a set of pages/views:

  1. Check that components appear in the same relative visual position across pages/views, except when exceptions apply.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.
derived.methods:
• Establish a design system with documented rules for consistent placement of common interactive components (for example, navigation menus, search bars, and action buttons).
  • Reuse the same components across pages/views instead of recreating them.
derived.recommendedPractices: • If a visual position must change, document why and consider providing cues (for example, animations and labels) to reduce confusion.

plainEnglish.summary: A control that serves the same purpose across pages keeps the same visual position - except where the position changes because of a page variation, a change of viewport, or a step in a process.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Spatial memory is how most people find familiar controls quickly. Moving them costs the most for magnification users, who see only a fraction of the screen at once.

title: Consistent Interactions
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

- A review has been conducted and changes made (when necessary) to ensure that Components with the same functionality behave consistently:
  - Components that perform the same function behave in the same way and use the same visual indicators.
  - Within the component, interactive elements with the same function have consistent labels.
  - Standard user interface designs for the platform are used when applicable.

::assertion-required

- title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
- date of when the review was completed
- date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

- results from the review
- process or policy for maintaining the review

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that it reviewed its components so that things with the same function behave the same way, use the same visual indicators and the same labels, and follow standard platform patterns where they apply.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Inconsistent behaviour forces relearning at every encounter, which is exactly the cost people with cognitive disabilities can least absorb.

title: Conventional Pattern Used
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

- A review has been conducted and changes made (when necessary) to ensure that Components follow established conventions:
  - Each component follows applicable platform conventions for how users interact with that type of component.
  - If a component library is used, then each component in the library: 
    - is tested for accessibility before being used
    - follows applicable platform conventions for how users interact with that type of component

::assertion-required

- title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
- date of when the review was completed
- date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

- results from the review
- process or policy for maintaining the review

:::note
A component library specifies a set of standardized components used in a product or products. It can include code to use, but at a minimum would define how the component is used and define pointer, keyboard, and assistive technology interactions.

Using a component library can help larger teams and organizations provide a consistent experience. 

Examples of component libraries include [GDS](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/), [Carbon Design System](https://www.carbondesignsystem.com/), and [Lion](https://lion.js.org/).

Examples of platform patterns are [ARIA Platform Authoring Guide](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/) (web), [Apple human interface guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/components), and [Android Material Design](https://m2.material.io/components?platform=android).
:::

notes:
A component library specifies a set of standardized components used in a product or products. It can include code to use, but at a minimum would define how the component is used and define pointer, keyboard, and assistive technology interactions.

Using a component library can help larger teams and organizations provide a consistent experience.

Examples of component libraries include GDS, Carbon Design System, and Lion.

Examples of platform patterns are ARIA Platform Authoring Guide (web), Apple human interface guidelines, and Android Material Design.

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that its components follow established platform conventions, and that any component library it uses is tested for accessibility before use.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Assistive technologies are built around conventional patterns. A custom component that ignores them may be unusable even when it is technically labelled.

title: Default Focus Indicator Used
rawBody: The focusable item uses the user agent default focus indicator.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For user agents that allow the customization of focus indicators:

  1. Use the keyboard to move focus onto the item.
  2. Check that the focus indicator is the user agent’s default indicator.
  3. For platform display changes, check that the focus indicator’s color is correct for the type of element.

Expected results

  • #2 and #3 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: The focusable element uses the browser's own default focus indicator rather than a replacement.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: The default indicator is designed to be visible against unknown backgrounds and is what users already recognise. Replacing it is where most focus indicators become invisible.

title: Focus Indicator Contrast Sufficient
rawBody:
If a custom focus indicator is used, it has sufficient adjacent contrast and change of contrast.

:::applies-when
* the user agent's default focus indicator is replaced by a custom focus indicator.
:::

appliesWhen: • the user agent’s default focus indicator is replaced by a custom focus indicator.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each element able to attain focus:

  1. Using a keyboard, tab to the component.
  2. Check that the focus indicator contrast meets the minimum contrast ratio test.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where a custom focus indicator replaces the browser default, it has to have sufficient contrast against what is next to it and sufficient change of contrast from the unfocused state.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: An indicator that cannot be distinguished from the background tells a sighted keyboard user nothing about where they are on the page.

title: Focus Indicator Size Sufficient
rawBody:
If a custom focus indicator is used, it has sufficient size and adjacency.

:::applies-when
* the user agent's default focus indicator is replaced by a custom focus indicator.
:::

appliesWhen: • the user agent’s default focus indicator is replaced by a custom focus indicator.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each custom focus indicator:

  1. Check that the focus indicator is at least as large as the area of a 2 CSS pixel thick perimeter of the unfocused component or sub-component, and
  2. Check that the focus indicator has a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 between the same pixels in the focused and unfocused states.

Except when

  • the focus indicator is determined by the user agent and cannot be adjusted by the author, or the focus indicator and the indicator’s background color are not modified by the author.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where a custom focus indicator replaces the browser default, it has to be large enough and close enough to what it marks.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A hairline outline is easy to lose on a busy page, particularly for people with low vision or when the page is magnified.

title: Focus Indicator Style Guide
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

- Our organization has a style guide that includes guidance on focus indicators and a policy and/or processes that the style guide must be followed.

::assertion-required

- title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
- date of when the design style guide was published
- date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

- copy of the policy implementing the use of design style guide on focus style
- whether training was provided for authors
    - date training was provided
    - number or proportion of authors who completed the training
- copy of the design style guide (if any) where focus style has been defined

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that it has a style guide covering focus indicators, plus a policy or process requiring it to be followed.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Focus styling is usually removed by accident, one component at a time. A style guide is what keeps it from eroding across a product.

title: Focus Order Meaningful
rawBody:
The keyboard focus moves sequentially through content in an order and way that preserves meaning and operability.

:::note
- The Common Keyboard Navigation Techniques are considered logical by default.
- Having the navigation follow a consistent pattern on the page would be an indication of logic (if it is not consistently random).
- A strictly start-to-end order is not required.
- Linear means in a single direction (forward/backward) - and is not required as long the non-linear (x-y) technique is in the Common Keyboard Navigation Techniques or is described on the page or where the user will encounter it prior.
:::

notes:
• The Common Keyboard Navigation Techniques are considered logical by default.
  • Having the navigation follow a consistent pattern on the page would be an indication of logic (if it is not consistently random).
  • A strictly start-to-end order is not required.
  • Linear means in a single direction (forward/backward) - and is not required as long the non-linear (x-y) technique is in the Common Keyboard Navigation Techniques or is described on the page or where the user will encounter it prior.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each page/view:

  1. Determine the logical order of the interactive elements.
  2. Starting with the first focusable element in the page/view, tab through the interactive elements in the content.
  3. Check that the focus order of the interactive elements in the content is the same as the logical order in #1.

Expected results

  • #3 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Keyboard focus moves through content in an order that preserves the meaning of the content and keeps it operable.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: When focus order and reading order disagree, keyboard and screen reader users get the page in an order it was never written to be read in.

title: Focus Relevant
rawBody: The focus order does not include hidden, static, or groups of repeated interactive elements.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For groups of repeated interactive elements (for example, a site-wide navigation bar on a website):

  1. Check that a method of skipping them is available.
  2. Check that hidden interactive elements do not receive focus.
  3. Check that static elements do not receive focus.

Expected results

  • #1, #2, and #3 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: The focus order leaves out hidden elements, static content and groups of repeated interactive elements.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Tabbing through invisible or repeated stops wastes keystrokes and makes the focus indicator seem to vanish - a common reason keyboard users abandon a page.

title: Focus Retained
rawBody: A user can focus on a content "area", such as a modal or popup, then resume their view of all content using a limited number of steps.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each situation where the keyboard focus is removed:

  1. Check that the keyboard focus moves to its previous location, or, if that no longer exists, to another meaningful location.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: A user can move focus into an area such as a modal or popup and get back to the rest of the content in a small number of steps.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Escaping an overlay by tabbing through everything inside it is slow enough that many keyboard users give up on the task.

title: Default Pointer Used
rawBody:
The user can ensure that the appearance of the pointer is not overridden by the authored interface.

:::except-when
- Changing the pointer appearance is essential.
:::

exceptWhen: • Changing the pointer appearance is essential.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each pointer indicator:

  1. Check that the pointer uses the standard platform indicator.
  2. Check for a setting that the user can enable to use the standard platform indicator.

Expected results

  • #1 or #2 is true.
derived.methods:
• No scripting or styling overrides the pointer indicator appearance.
  • Provide a setting that removes any overrides to the pointer indicator appearance.

plainEnglish.summary: The user can keep the pointer looking the way their system draws it, rather than having the page override it - unless changing the pointer is essential.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: People who have enlarged or recoloured their cursor did so because they lose it otherwise. A custom cursor undoes that setting without asking.

title: Enhanced Pointer Available
rawBody: Provide a more visible pointer indicator than the platform default. The enhanced pointer indicator can be enabled in a setting, and be visible temporarily (for a few seconds) or permanently.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each pointer indicator:

  1. Check for a setting that increases the visibility.
  2. Check that it works in the conformance scope of web pages/views.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.
derived.methods: • Provide a setting to adjust the pointer indicator.

plainEnglish.summary: A more visible pointer indicator than the platform default is offered, switchable on in a setting, shown either temporarily or permanently.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Finding the pointer is a recurring problem for people with low vision, attention-related disabilities and anyone on a large or high-resolution display.

title: Pointer activation indicated (enhanced)
rawBody:
The user can choose to always have a visible pointer indicator.

:::applies-when
- The platform does not use a visible pointer indicator.
:::

:::note
This is primarily aimed at eye-tracking and touch-screens, where it is useful for the user to be able to have a visible indicator, but it wouldn't be universal. This aims to avoid it being in the way for some users.
:::

appliesWhen: • The platform does not use a visible pointer indicator.
notes: This is primarily aimed at eye-tracking and touch-screens, where it is useful for the user to be able to have a visible indicator, but it wouldn’t be universal. This aims to avoid it being in the way for some users.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each pointer indicator:

  1. Check the settings of the platform or conformance scope for the ability to have an always-visible pointer indicator.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where the platform itself does not show a visible pointer indicator, the user can choose to have one shown at all times.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: On touch and immersive platforms there is often no cursor at all, leaving no feedback about where an action will land.

title: Pointer activation indicated (minimum)
rawBody:
There is a visible indication of the activation of an interactive element when selected by the pointer.

:::applies-when
- The platform does not use a visible pointer indicator.
:::

:::note
This is primarily aimed at touch-interfaces and VR where you don’t have a pointer indicator, but do need to know when something has been selected.
:::

appliesWhen: • The platform does not use a visible pointer indicator.
notes: This is primarily aimed at touch-interfaces and VR where you don’t have a pointer indicator, but do need to know when something has been selected.
derived.tests:
Procedure

Where the platform does not use a visible pointer indicator, for each interactive element:

  1. Check that there is an indicator of activation.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where the platform does not show a pointer indicator, activating an interactive element by pointer produces a visible indication that it happened.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Without confirmation, users repeat the action - which on a form or a payment is worse than no feedback at all.

title: Pointer Contrast Sufficient
rawBody:
The default pointer meets the @@[non-text-contrast] requirement, and is at least as large as the platform default.

:::applies-when
* the pointer indicator appearance can be adjusted from the platform default.
:::

:::note
There can be multiple types of pointer indicator. For example, arrow, hand, caret. The size requirement applies to whichever type of indicator would be the default for that scenario.
:::

appliesWhen: • the pointer indicator appearance can be adjusted from the platform default.
notes: There can be multiple types of pointer indicator. For example, arrow, hand, caret. The size requirement applies to whichever type of indicator would be the default for that scenario.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each custom pointer indicator:

  1. Identify which visual information defines the boundaries of the interactive area.
  2. Check if the visual information meets the minimum contrast ratio test.
  3. For each possible state, repeat step 1 and 2.

Expected results

  • #2 is true for each state.

plainEnglish.summary: Where the pointer's appearance can be changed from the platform default, it must meet the non-text contrast requirement and be at least as large as the default.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A custom cursor that is smaller or fainter than the system one is harder to track for exactly the people who most need to track it.

title: Pointer Focus Indicated
rawBody:
There is a visible pointer indicator.

:::except-when
- The pointer is on a video - it can be hidden if there is a pointer mechanism to un-hide the pointer indicator.
- The pointer controls the direction of view in a virtual or real world environment.
:::

:::note
Examples of pointers which do not always show the pointer indicator:

- A touch-screen interface does not need to have an indicator as the pointer is not on an element before activating it.
- An eye-tracking interface highlights the element under the gaze of the user, but otherwise does not have a pointer indicator. 
- A game where you use the pointer to move the entire view around a virtual environment.
:::

exceptWhen:
• The pointer is on a video - it can be hidden if there is a pointer mechanism to un-hide the pointer indicator.
  • The pointer controls the direction of view in a virtual or real world environment.
notes:
Examples of pointers which do not always show the pointer indicator:

  • A touch-screen interface does not need to have an indicator as the pointer is not on an element before activating it.
  • An eye-tracking interface highlights the element under the gaze of the user, but otherwise does not have a pointer indicator.
  • A game where you use the pointer to move the entire view around a virtual environment.
derived.tests:
Procedure

With appropriate user settings enabled:

  1. Move the pointer (mouse, eye tracker, hand gesture in VR space, …).
  2. Check that there is some form of indication of where the user is pointing to.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.
derived.methods: • Interactive elements are highlighted when the pointer is on the element. For example, a set of image links are shown, and the one under the pointer is highlighted with an outline or change in size.

plainEnglish.summary: There is a visible pointer indicator - except over video, where it may hide as long as there is a way to bring it back, and where the pointer is steering the direction of view in a virtual or real-world environment.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Losing the pointer means losing your place. The exceptions cover the cases where a visible cursor would obscure the content itself.

title: Pointer Visible
rawBody:
The pointer indicator is always visible.

:::except-when
- The pointer is on a video and is not moving.
- The pointer controls the direction of view in a virtual or real world environment.
:::

exceptWhen:
• The pointer is on a video and is not moving.
  • The pointer controls the direction of view in a virtual or real world environment.
derived.tests:
Procedure

If the pointer is ever not visible:

  1. Check that it meets one of the exceptions.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.
derived.methods: • No styling or scripting hides the pointer indicator.

plainEnglish.summary: The pointer indicator stays visible, with the same narrow exceptions for a stationary pointer over video and for a pointer controlling the direction of view.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Auto-hiding cursors force users to move the pointer to find it, which is a real cost for people with motor disabilities and for anyone with low vision.

title: Infinite Scrolling Controllable
rawBody: Where content includes infinite scrolling, a mechanism is provided prior to the scrolling content that allows users to switch off infinite scrolling. No content should be rendered unavailable as a result of switching on this option.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each instance of infinite scrolling:

  1. Check that the preceding content includes a mechanism to allow infinite scrolling to be switched off.
  2. Check that all content that was available via infinite scrolling is also available without relying on it.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: An exploratory requirement: where content scrolls infinitely, a control before the scrolling content lets the user switch that behaviour off, and nothing becomes unreachable when they do.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Infinite scroll can put the footer permanently out of reach and makes a page impossible to get to the end of - a particular problem for screen reader and keyboard users.

title: Overlay Content Dismissible
rawBody: When new content becomes visible and covers the main content, a mechanism is available to dismiss the new content.

derived.tests:
Modal dialogs on interaction

Procedure

For each element that opens a modal dialog when interacted with:

  1. Open the dialog.
  2. Check that the dialog includes a mechanism to allow the dialog to be dismissed.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.
derived.methods:
• The ‘Escape’ (Esc) key closes new content.
  • An accessible ‘close’ button is provided to close the new content.

plainEnglish.summary: When new content appears over the main content, there is a way to dismiss it.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A cookie banner or chat widget with no reachable close button can cover the content permanently for keyboard users and for anyone using magnification.

title: Conventional Layout Review
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* We have reviewed layout conventions for similar products or processes.
* The layout used follows a conventional pattern or a tested non-conventional pattern was used.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
* date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

* report covering review of layouts for similar products or processes
* design log capturing decision to use specific layouts
* if a non-conventional layout is used, usability testing results that demonstrate the utility of the approach taken

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that it reviewed layout conventions for comparable products and either followed a conventional pattern or tested a non-conventional one.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Conventional layouts are what let people apply what they already know. Departing from them without testing shifts the learning cost onto users with cognitive disabilities.

title: Blocks of content available (enhanced)
rawBody: Styling is used to enhance the visual separation between meaningful blocks of content.

derived.tests:
Visually identifiable meaningful blocks of content

Procedure

For each meaningful block of content in the page/view:

  1. Check that each meaningful block of content is grouped by one or more of the following characteristics:
    • Color or lightness — the same color scheme is used (Note that this should also meet requirements for ‘Color alone’ and ‘Contrast’)
    • Borders — blocks are contained within the same borders
    • Spacing — blocks are grouped based on their proximity to others within the same area, while spacing is used to separate different sections of content
    • Font — blocks are presented with similar font families
    • Position — blocks are located in the same area of the page/view (for example, header, navigation, footer)
    • Repeated visual feature — blocks contain a consistent visual feature (for example, bullets in a list, checkbox)

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Styling is used to strengthen the visual separation between meaningful blocks of content.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Clear visual grouping is how readers find their way without reading everything, and it is what keeps a page navigable when magnified or reflowed.

title: Blocks of content available (minimum)
rawBody: Meaningful blocks of content are programmatically determinable and visually presented with sufficient surrounding space.

derived.tests:
HTML sufficient space

Procedure

  1. Identify meaningful blocks of content in the page/view that are not bounded by a visual border.
  2. Examine the computed style to determine the total of margin, padding and border spacing.
  3. Check that the spacing between all adjacent meaningful blocks of content is sufficient.

Expected results

  • #3 is true.

Programmatically identifiable meaningful blocks of content

Procedure

For each meaningful blocks of content in the page/view:

  1. Check that an appropriate role is being used for the meaningful blocks of content in the source code.
  2. Check using assistive technology that an appropriate role is being used for the meaningful blocks of content.

Expected results

  • #1 or #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: The page is divided into meaningful blocks that software can identify, and each block is given enough surrounding space to be seen as a block.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: The programmatic part is what lets a screen reader jump between sections; the spacing is what lets a sighted reader see where one ends and the next begins.

title: Clear Structure Review
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* Our organization has a process and policy for reviewing written content for clear structure before publication. The process includes confirming:
    * all of the core requirements in the Structure guideline are met
    * content sections are as concise as possible
    * icons are considered as possible ways to help users understand the content structure and identify key parts
    * authors consider when to turn sentences into lists to make the information easier to understand and remember
* If a style guide is used by authors, it must provide guidance on these aspects of clear structure.
* If author training is provided, it must provide guidance on these aspects of clear structure.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
* date of when the policy was implemented
* date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

* copy of the policy implementing the clear structure review
* whether training was provided for authors:
    * date training was provided
    * number or proportion of authors who completed the training
* copy of the style guide (if any) where clear structure review has been defined

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that it has a process and policy for reviewing written content for clear structure before publication - checking the Structure guideline's core requirements, keeping sections concise, considering icons as structural cues, and turning sentences into lists where that helps - and that any style guide or author training covers these.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Structure is decided while writing, not afterwards. A review process is what keeps clear structure from depending on which author happened to write the page.

title: Heading Structure Available
rawBody:
Meaningful blocks of content are organized with a logical hierarchy of headings.

:::except-when
* The technology does not support heading levels.
:::

exceptWhen: • The technology does not support heading levels.
derived.tests:
Headings set at right level

Procedure

For the hierarchy of headings:

  1. Check that headings for sibling content blocks have the same heading level.
  2. Check that headings for immediate child content blocks are at most one level higher than parent content blocks.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.

HTML heading levels not skipped

Procedure

For each page/view:

  1. Review the hierarchy of headings.
  2. Check that each heading level is at most one numerical level higher than the preceding heading.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Meaningful blocks of content are organised under a logical hierarchy of headings, where the technology supports heading levels.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Headings are the primary way screen reader users navigate a long page; a flat or scrambled hierarchy removes that route entirely.

title: Key Information Usability Testing
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* We conducted usability testing to ensure that a diverse group of users, including people with cognitive and mental health challenges, understand the site's information hierarchy and menu organization and are able to find key information.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion
* date of assertion
* date of the testing

::assertion-recommended

* documentation of usability testing and results
* scope of testing
* number of participants and disabilities represented
* documentation of changes made as a result of usability findings

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that it ran usability testing with a diverse group including people with cognitive and mental health disabilities, checking that they understood the information hierarchy and menu organisation and could find key information.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Whether an information architecture works is not something its authors can judge - they already know where everything is.

title: Order Detectable
rawBody:
Ordered content includes programmatically determinable markers that indicate the position of each item.

:::except-when
* The nature of the ordering of the content is presented immediately prior.
:::

:::note
This includes lists and processes.
:::

exceptWhen: • The nature of the ordering of the content is presented immediately prior.
notes: This includes lists and processes.
derived.tests:
Process steps

Procedure

For each ordered process:

  1. Check that each step in the process includes an indicator of its position within the process.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

HTML ordered lists

Procedure

For each ordered list:

  1. Examine the HTML code and check that each ordered list is marked up with an <ol> element.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where content is ordered, programmatically determinable markers indicate each item's position - unless the nature of the ordering is stated immediately before it.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Without position markers a screen reader user hears a list of items with no sense of sequence, which matters when the order is the information.

title: Relationships Detectable
rawBody: Relationships of meaning between elements are conveyed programmatically.

derived.tests:
HTML hierarchical relationship

Procedure

  1. Determine the contextual hierarchy of the content either visually or through the meaning of the content.
  2. Examine the source code of the HTML document to identify each hierarchical section.
  3. Check that each section uses an appropriate semantic HTML element that reflects its position in the hierarchy.

Expected results

  • #3 is true.

HTML input field/label relationship

Procedure For each input field within the unit of conformance:

  1. Check that each <input>, <select>, and <textarea> in the source code has a programmatically-associated <label> using for and id attributes.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

HTML list relationship

Procedure

For each list within the unit of conformance:

  1. Check that each list consists of a <ul>, <ol>, or <dl>.
  2. Check that each list item within the list is contained within an <li> element (for <ul> and <ol>) or <dt>/<dd> pair (for <dl>).
  3. Check that the immediate child element of the list is an <li> element (for <ul> and <ol>) or <dt>/<dd> pair (for <dl>).

Expected results

  • #1, #2, and #3 are true.

HTML nested list relationship

Procedure

For each nested list within the unit of conformance:

  1. Check that all child lists are contained within a <li> of the parent list.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where two things are related in meaning - a label and its field, a heading and its section, a cell and its column - the relationship is marked up, not just implied by position or styling.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A label beside a field, a cell under a column header, a caption under a figure - all of these are obvious by sight and invisible to assistive technology unless the relationship is marked up.

title: Sections Labeled
rawBody:
Meaningful blocks of content have a semantically appropriate label that defines their purpose.

:::except-when
* A label is not needed to understand the purpose of the content within the context of use.
:::

:::ednote
* Add example(s) of labels and heading usage
:::

exceptWhen: • A label is not needed to understand the purpose of the content within the context of use.
editorNotes: • Add example(s) of labels and heading usage
derived.tests:
Meaningful label

Procedure

  1. Review content and identify meaningful blocks with labels.
  2. Check that each label correctly describes the block.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

Label exists

Procedure

  1. Review content and identify meaningful blocks.
  2. Check that each block has a label that describes the block.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

HTML heading semantics

Procedure

  1. Visually identify each meaningful block.
  2. Check that heading text is marked up using an <h?> element.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Meaningful blocks of content carry a semantically appropriate label that says what they are for - unless the purpose is already clear from the context of use.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Labelled regions are what let a screen reader user skip to navigation, search or main content instead of reading through the page to find them.

title: All Steps Listed
rawBody:
A list of all steps in a multi-step process is visually and programmatically available at each step.

:::except-when
- The total number of steps is unknown, or the sequence of steps depends on user actions.
:::

exceptWhen: • The total number of steps is unknown, or the sequence of steps depends on user actions.
derived.tests:
Visual multi-step listing

Procedure

For each multi-step process:

  1. Review the content within each stage of a multi-step process.
  2. Check that a list of steps in the process is included on each stage.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

HTML multi-step listing

Procedure

For each multi-step process:

  1. Examine the HTML source code for each step of the process.
  2. Check that an <ol> is included with a <li> for each step of the process at each step.
  3. Check that the <ol> is included in the accessibility tree.

Expected results

  • #2 and #3 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: In a multi-step process, the full list of steps is available visually and programmatically at every step - unless the number of steps is unknown or the sequence depends on what the user does.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Knowing how much is left is what lets someone decide whether they can finish now, which matters for people with fatigue, pain or limited time on a shared device.

title: Current Step Indicated
rawBody: The current step within a multi-step process is visually and programmatically indicated.

derived.tests:
ARIA current

Procedure

For each multi-step process:

  1. Examine the source code of the HTML document.
  2. Check that the process navigation steps are included.
  3. Check that the current process step is identified using aria-current="step".

Expected results

  • Check #2 and #3 are true.

Current step visually identifiable

Procedure

For each multi-step process:

  1. Visually examine the content.
  2. Check that the process navigation steps are viewable.
  3. Check that the current process step is visually distinguishable from other steps.

Expected results

  • Check #2 and #3 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: The current step in a multi-step process is indicated both visually and programmatically.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Without it, a user who is interrupted cannot tell where they are on returning, and a screen reader user may not be able to tell at all.

title: Location Within Product Review
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* We have reviewed conventions for presenting current location within the conformance scope.
* The presentation of current location within the conformance scope uses appropriate visually and programmatically patterns.

:::note
It is often helpful for users to understand where within a digital product they are. There are many ways to achieve this, for example, a breadcrumb. Ideally this is consistently presented throughout the conformance scope but for some pages/views it may make less sense to include. For example, including a breadcrumb trail on the homepage or on pages that sit outside the hierarchy, for example a shopping cart.
:::

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
* date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

* design log capturing decision to use specific approaches to current location patterns used within the conformance scope
* if a non-conventional design pattern is used, usability testing results that demonstrate the utility of the design approach taken

notes: It is often helpful for users to understand where within a digital product they are. There are many ways to achieve this, for example, a breadcrumb. Ideally this is consistently presented throughout the conformance scope but for some pages/views it may make less sense to include. For example, including a breadcrumb trail on the homepage or on pages that sit outside the hierarchy, for example a shopping cart.

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that it reviewed the conventions for showing the user's current location and used patterns that work both visually and programmatically.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Knowing where you are is the precondition for deciding where to go next; it is easily lost in deep or dynamic interfaces.

title: Page/view change notified
rawBody: When content triggers a change of page/view there is a visual change within the view and programmatic notification of the change.

derived.tests:
Opening new page

Procedure

For each change of page/view triggered by content:

  1. Check that the change is conveyed in the view.
  2. Check that the change is conveyed programmatically using the assistive technology in the accessibility support set.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: When content causes a change of page or view, there is a visible change within the view and a programmatic notification of it.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: In a single-page application nothing reloads, so a screen reader user may not be told anything happened and can continue reading content that is no longer there.

title: Page/view title available
rawBody:
The page/view has a title that describes its name, topic, or purpose.


:::except-when
- The technology has no way to include a title.
:::

exceptWhen: • The technology has no way to include a title.
derived.tests:
Ensure the page/view title is meaningful

Procedure

For each page/view:

  1. Examine the source code of the HTML document and check that the first title element is not-empty.
  2. Check that the title element describes the document.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.

Verify that the page/view has no available mechanism to define a title

Procedure

For each page/view where no title element is present:

  1. Determine whether the current page/view allows setting the HTML document title element.
  2. If the page/view is rendered within the current document context (for example, modal dialog or popup) and does not provide a mechanism to set a document-level title, the exception applies.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: Each page or view has a title describing its name, topic or purpose - unless the technology has no way to carry one.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: The title is the first thing a screen reader announces and how users tell tabs, windows and history entries apart.

title: Return To Start Prominent
rawBody:
Mechanisms that return the user to the starting point of the conformance scope are available in prominent positions both programmatically and visually.

:::note
For HTML, a good programmatic positioning of such a mechanism would be early in the DOM.
:::

:::example
* Common design practices place the homepage link for websites in the top-left corner on the site logo.
* Common design patterns for mobile applications is to include a sticky navigation at the bottom of the viewport which often includes a control to return to the starting point.
:::

notes: For HTML, a good programmatic positioning of such a mechanism would be early in the DOM.
examples:
• Common design practices place the homepage link for websites in the top-left corner on the site logo.
  • Common design patterns for mobile applications is to include a sticky navigation at the bottom of the viewport which often includes a control to return to the starting point.

plainEnglish.summary: A recommended practice: ways to get back to the starting point of the conformance scope are prominent, both visually and programmatically.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A reliable way home is what makes exploring safe. Without it, getting lost means starting over.

title: Return To Start Supported
rawBody:
A visual and programmatically available mechanism exists that allows users to return to the starting point of the conformance scope.

:::except-when
* The page/view is the starting point of the conformance scope.
* It is essential to the functionality not to provide this mechanism.
:::

:::note
Where the conformance scope is a sub-part of larger digital product, then the starting point should be the conformance scope starting point. For example, an organization's careers website that is separate from the main website.
:::

exceptWhen:
• The page/view is the starting point of the conformance scope.
  • It is essential to the functionality not to provide this mechanism.
notes: Where the conformance scope is a sub-part of larger digital product, then the starting point should be the conformance scope starting point. For example, an organization’s careers website that is separate from the main website.
derived.tests:
HTML homepage link

Procedure

For each page/view that is not the website’s home page:

  1. Check that there is a link that points to the website’s home page.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: There is a mechanism, available both visually and programmatically, to get back to the starting point of the conformance scope. Pages that are themselves the starting point are exempt, as is content where withholding the mechanism is essential.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A dependable route home is what makes it safe to explore an unfamiliar interface, and it is what a disoriented user reaches for first.

title: Inclusive Data Set
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* Content author(s) train AI models using representative and unbiased disability-related information that is proportional to the general population.

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that its authors train AI models on representative, unbiased disability-related data, in proportion to the general population.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Models trained on data where disabled people are rare or stereotyped reproduce that in their output - and increasingly that output is the interface.

title: No Harm From Algorithms
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:
* Content author(s) conduct usability testing and ethics reviews to minimize the possibility that algorithms disadvantage people with disabilities.

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that its authors run usability testing and ethics reviews to reduce the chance that algorithms disadvantage disabled people.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Algorithmic decisions about ranking, moderation or eligibility can disadvantage disabled people invisibly, without any individual decision looking wrong.

title: Algorithm Inclusivity Review
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* We have a policy and process to review — and have reviewed — the data set, results, and/or algorithm in order to minimize the possibility that algorithms are disadvantageous for people with disabilities.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion
* date of assertion
* disabilities considered
* what was reviewed (data set, results, or algorithm itself)
* review scope

::assertion-recommended

* results
* copy of any process and policy
* copy of usability testing, if conducted
* steps taken to resolve the issues found

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that it has a policy and process for reviewing the data set, the results or the algorithm itself to reduce disadvantage to disabled people, and records which disabilities were considered and what was reviewed.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Naming what was reviewed and which disabilities were in scope is what turns a general claim of fairness into something that can be checked.

title: Consequences Explained Before Agreement
rawBody:
Legal, financial, privacy, and security consequences are provided before finalizing an agreement.

:::applies-when
- Entering an agreement is required.
:::

appliesWhen: • Entering an agreement is required.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For any agreements being made by the user:

  1. Identify any potential legal, financial, privacy and security consequences to the user as a result of the agreement.
  2. Check that the consequences are provided before the user enters into the agreement.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where entering an agreement is required, the legal, financial, privacy and security consequences are given before it is finalised.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Consequences disclosed after the fact are not a choice. Presenting them beforehand is what makes consent meaningful for people who need time to process them.

title: Consequences Of Choices Explained
rawBody: Choices with legal, financial, privacy, or security consequences are accompanied by a description of the benefits, risks, and potential consequences when users make the choice.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For any choices being made by the user:

  1. Identify any potential legal, financial, privacy and security consequences to the user as a result of the choice.
  2. Check that the consequences are provided when the user makes the choice.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Choices with legal, financial, privacy or security consequences come with a description of the benefits, the risks and what may follow.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Interfaces routinely present consequential choices as routine ones. An explicit description is what protects people who take the interface at its word.

title: Diverse Disabilities Considered
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* When considering the safety and security of our users, we considered use cases of people with diverse disabilities. For example, people with cognitive or learning disabilities are sometimes targeted on social media for sexual exploitation and other bad intent.
* Research has been conducted on risks to safety, wellbeing, and mental health for users with diverse disabilities and, when risks are found, all reasonable practical steps have been identified and taken to mitigate the risk.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion
* date of assertion

::assertion-recommended

* list of steps that have been taken
* list of use cases used

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that it considered the safety and security of users with diverse disabilities - noting, for example, that people with cognitive or learning disabilities are sometimes targeted for exploitation - researched the risks, and took reasonable practical steps to mitigate what it found.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Safety design usually assumes an average user. Disabled users are disproportionately targeted, and a threat model that leaves them out leaves them unprotected.

title: Risk Comparable
rawBody:
Use of assistive technology, accessible alternative versions, accessibility-related modifications of content, and accessibility-related settings do not expose people with disabilities to additional risk. 

:::applies-when
- The content displays or requires entry of personal or sensitive information.
:::

:::note
Additional risk includes risk to privacy, finances and personal safety — for example, unintentional exposure of a password or bank account number. 
:::

appliesWhen: • The content displays or requires entry of personal or sensitive information.
notes: Additional risk includes risk to privacy, finances and personal safety — for example, unintentional exposure of a password or bank account number.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For information that is personal or sensitive:

  1. Check that personal or sensitive information is visually hidden by default.
  2. Check that the personal or sensitive information is programmatically hidden by default.
  3. Check that the use of AT, accessibility settings and accessibility-related modifications does not expose any personal or sensitive information.
  4. Check whether any accessible alternative versions or modifications of the digital content exist.
  5. Check that the accessible alternative or modification of the digital content does not include additional risk beyond what’s in the inaccessible alternative.

Expected results

  • #1, #2, and #3 are true.
  • If #4 is true, then #5 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: An exploratory requirement: where content shows or asks for personal or sensitive information, using assistive technology, an accessible alternative version, an accessibility modification or an accessibility setting must not expose the user to extra risk.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: If turning on accessibility features marks a user out, weakens their security, or discloses their disability, the price of access is exposure.

title: No Time Limits
rawBody:
The completion of a process does not include time limits. 

:::except-when 
- the time limit is essential. 
:::

:::example
Essential time limits would include but are not limited to auctions, ticket sales, or timed exams.
:::

:::note
Implying to a user that they will lose a benefit if they don’t act immediately is not an essential time limit.
:::

exceptWhen: • the time limit is essential.
notes: Implying to a user that they will lose a benefit if they don’t act immediately is not an essential time limit.
examples: Essential time limits would include but are not limited to auctions, ticket sales, or timed exams.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each page/view:

  1. Check if content includes time limits.

Expected results

  • #1 is false.

plainEnglish.summary: Completing a process does not involve time limits, unless a limit is essential.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Time limits assume a typical speed of reading, typing and decision-making. People using screen readers, switch input or voice, and people with cognitive disabilities, routinely need longer.

title: No Unnecessary Time Limits
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* Products and processes in scope have no non-essential time limits for engagement or completion.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
* date of assertion

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that the products and processes in scope have no non-essential time limits for engagement or completion.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Most time limits are implementation convenience rather than necessity, and each one silently excludes whoever cannot work at that pace.

title: Time Limits Conveyed
rawBody:
Users are informed at the start of the process or session that a time limit exists, its length, and that it can be adjusted.

:::applies-when 
- pages/views within the conformance scope have a time limit.
:::

:::except-when 
- hiding the existence of the time limit is essential.
:::

appliesWhen: • pages/views within the conformance scope have a time limit.
exceptWhen: • hiding the existence of the time limit is essential.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each time limit:

  1. Check that a notification is provided to the user at the start of a process that the time limit exists, its length, and that it can be adjusted.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where a time limit exists, the user is told at the start of the process or session that there is one, how long it is, and that it can be adjusted - unless hiding its existence is essential.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A limit nobody mentions is discovered by losing work. Knowing about it in advance is what lets someone adjust it or plan around it.

title: Timeout Adjustable
rawBody:
A mechanism exists to extend the time limit before timeout, or the time limit can be disabled.

:::applies-when
- Time limit(s) exist.
:::

:::except-when
- The time limit is essential.
:::

appliesWhen: • Time limit(s) exist.
exceptWhen: • The time limit is essential.
derived.tests:
Extend or disable at timeout

Procedure

For each time limit:

  1. Check if there is a way to disable it.
  2. Wait for the timeout.
  3. Check that before the timeout, an option is given to extend the time limit.

Expected results

  • #3 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where time limits exist, there is a way to extend the limit before it expires or to switch it off - unless the limit is essential.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Without an extension, a session that times out mid-form destroys work, and the people most likely to hit it are those who were already working hardest to complete it.

title: Deceptive Practices Usability Testing
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that: 

* We conducted a usability test that included participants with cognitive disabilities and/or mental health based disabilities to evaluate content for misleading wording, artificial pressure, misdirection, and other deceptive practices.
* We removed any deceptive practices found.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
* date of assertion

::assertion-recommended

* number of participants
* the deceptive practices evaluated
* maintained records of usability testing protocol, and results
* disabilities represented within the group of participants

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that it ran a usability test including participants with cognitive or mental health disabilities to look for misleading wording, artificial pressure and misdirection, and removed what it found.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Deceptive patterns work by exploiting the gap between what an interface appears to offer and what it does - a gap that is widest for users who read it literally.

title: Deceptive messaging expert review
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* We conducted an expert review to evaluate content for misleading wording, artificial pressure, misdirection, and other deceptive practices.
* We removed any deceptive practices found.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion
* date of assertion

::assertion-recommended

* the deceptive practices evaluated
* maintained records of deceptive practices found, and resolutions

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that an expert review looked for misleading wording, artificial pressure, misdirection and other deceptive practices, and that what was found was removed.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Expert review catches patterns that individual users experience as their own mistake rather than as a design decision.

title: No Artificial Time Limits
rawBody:
The completion of a process does not include artificial time limits. 

:::except-when
* The time limit is essential.
:::

:::example
Essential time limits would include but are not limited to auctions, ticket sales, or timed exams.
:::

exceptWhen: • The time limit is essential.
examples: Essential time limits would include but are not limited to auctions, ticket sales, or timed exams.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each time limit:

  1. Check that it does not restart or reset immediately.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: An exploratory requirement: completing a process does not involve artificial time limits - countdowns manufactured to create urgency - unless the limit is essential.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Manufactured urgency pushes people into decisions before they have understood them, and hits hardest anyone who needs longer to read or decide.

title: Preselections Visible
rawBody: During the completion of a process, preselected options that impact finance, privacy or safety are visibly and programmatically available to the user by default.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For all options that affect finance, privacy and safety:

  1. Check that the options are visible when completing a process.
  2. Check that they are programmatically available before completing the process.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: During a process, any preselected option affecting finance, privacy or safety is visible and programmatically available to the user by default.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A pre-ticked box is a decision made on the user's behalf. If it is not announced, a screen reader user may agree to it without ever encountering it.

title: Automated Entry Allowed
rawBody:
Automated input of personal information from user agents, third-party tools, or paste is not prevented.

:::note
Personal information includes but is not limited to names and passwords.
:::

notes: Personal information includes but is not limited to names and passwords.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each form that requests personal information:

  1. Ensure there is a test identity set up in the browser.
  2. Navigate to a form requiring the input of personal information.
  3. Check that the browser tools automatically populate personal information into the form.

Expected results

  • #3 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Automated entry of personal information is not blocked - whether from the browser, a third-party tool, or pasting.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Blocking paste or autofill forces manual transcription of exactly the data that is longest and least memorable, which is a barrier for password manager users and people with cognitive or motor disabilities.

title: Cognitive Test Alternatives Available
rawBody:
Processes can be completed without a cognitive function test.

:::example
User authentication or login.
:::

examples: User authentication or login.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each form requiring the completion of a complex test, such as a puzzle, image identification, gesture reproduction, math question, or character recognition/entry:

  1. Check that there is an alternative provided that does not require completion of a cognitive function test.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Users must not be forced to solve puzzles, recall passwords, or perform mental math to complete tasks unless an alternative login or verification method exists.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Cognitive tests like CAPTCHAs lock out users with memory loss, dyslexia, or brain injuries.

title: Copying Supported
rawBody: Copying of content is not prevented.

plainEnglish.summary: An exploratory requirement: copying content is not prevented.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Copying is how people move text into a translator, a reader, a note or a password manager. Blocking it removes an adaptation the user had already made for themselves.

title: No Memorization
rawBody: Processes can be completed without memorizing and recalling information from previous stages of the process.

plainEnglish.summary: An exploratory requirement: a process can be completed without having to memorise and recall information from an earlier stage.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Requiring recall turns a task into a memory test, which excludes people with memory impairments, and is harder for anyone interrupted mid-process.

title: Information Requirements Available At Start
rawBody:
Information and resources that are needed to complete a multi-step process are provided at the start of the process, including the:

- number of steps it might take (if known in advance),
- details of any resources needed to perform the task, and
- overview of the process and next step.

:::applies-when
- the user needs to complete a multi-step process.
:::

appliesWhen: • the user needs to complete a multi-step process.
derived.tests:
Procedure

At the start of each process:

  1. Identify any multi-step processes.
  2. If it can be determined in advance, check that the number of steps it will take to complete the process is provided at the start of the process.
  3. Check that the details of any information and resources that are needed to perform the task are provided at the start of the process.
  4. Check that an overview of the process and next steps are provided at the start of the process.

Expected results

  • #2, #3, and #4 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where a user has to complete a multi-step process, the information and resources needed are given up front: how many steps it may take if that is known, what will be needed to do it, and an overview of the process and the next step.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Discovering halfway through that a document is needed means abandoning the task. Knowing in advance is what lets people with limited time, energy or attention start at the right moment.

title: Process Instructions Available
rawBody:
The instructions needed to complete a multi-step process are available.

:::applies-when
- The user needs to complete a multi-step process.
:::

appliesWhen: • The user needs to complete a multi-step process.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each multi-step process:

  1. Check that the steps and instructions needed to complete a multi-step process are provided.
  2. Check that any breadcrumb navigation correctly communicates the current step in the process.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where a task runs across several steps, the instructions for completing it are there to be found - the process does not assume the user already knows how it works.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Processes that assume prior knowledge exclude first-time users, and disproportionately those who cannot infer the missing steps from the layout alone.

title: Required Action Available
rawBody:
The interface indicates when user input or action is required in order to proceed to the next step.

:::applies-when
- the user needs to complete an action in order to proceed to the next step.
:::

:::example
This would apply when the user needs to agree to the terms and conditions before they can submit the form.
:::

appliesWhen: • the user needs to complete an action in order to proceed to the next step.
examples: This would apply when the user needs to agree to the terms and conditions before they can submit the form.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For any parts of a process that cannot be completed without the user doing a required action:

  1. Enter in all the information except for the required action(s).
  2. Try to complete the process.
  3. Check that there is a notification that explains what the user needs to do before the process can be completed.

Expected results

  • #3 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where the user must do something to move to the next step, the interface says so.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A process that stalls without saying why reads as a broken page. The user most likely to give up is the one who cannot see the unfilled field.

title: Going Back Supported
rawBody:
In a multi-step process, the interface supports stepping backwards in a process and returning to the current point without data loss.

:::except-when
- It is essential that the user cannot step back in a process.
:::
 
:::example
Certain tests in education may require that the student cannot go back through previously-submitted responses and change them.
:::

exceptWhen: • It is essential that the user cannot step back in a process.
examples: Certain tests in education may require that the student cannot go back through previously-submitted responses and change them.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For multi-step processes:

  1. Check that the user is prompted to review and confirm data.
  2. Check that the user is allowed to return to previous steps to review and change the data.
  3. Check that if a summary of all data input by the user is provided before the transaction is committed, and that a method is provided to correct errors, if necessary.

Expected results

  • #1, #2, or #3 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: In a multi-step process the user can step backwards and return to where they were without losing data - unless it is essential that they cannot go back.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Correcting an earlier answer should not cost the whole form. Losing data on going back punishes exactly the users who most often need to check their work.

title: No Redundant Entry
rawBody:
Information previously entered by or provided to the user that is required to be entered again in the same process is either auto-populated, or available for the user to select.

:::except-when
- Re-entering the information is essential,
- The information is required to ensure the security of the content, or
- Previously entered information is no longer valid.
:::

exceptWhen:
• Re-entering the information is essential,
  • The information is required to ensure the security of the content, or
  • Previously entered information is no longer valid.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For any process that requires the user to enter information:

  1. Check whether the information has already been requested in a previous step of the process.
  2. Check that the information entered previously is prepopulated in the respective field(s) or is displayed on the page for copying.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Information the user already entered or was already given, if required again in the same process, is either filled in automatically or offered for selection. Re-entry that is essential, needed for security, or where the earlier information is no longer valid, is exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Re-typing the same data is effort and a new chance to make a mistake, which is costly for people with motor and cognitive disabilities and slow for anyone using speech input.

title: Progress Saved
rawBody:
Data entry and other task completion processes allow saving and resuming from the current step in the task.

:::except-when
- The task completion is part of a real-time event, and no alternative to the time limit is possible.
:::

:::example
Real-time events would include but are not limited to auctions or ticket sales.
:::

exceptWhen: • The task completion is part of a real-time event, and no alternative to the time limit is possible.
examples: Real-time events would include but are not limited to auctions or ticket sales.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For any processes that require the user to enter information:

  1. Log in, if needed, and begin the timed activity.
  2. Allow the session to time out.
  3. Submit or save the data.
  4. Log out if logged in.
  5. Re-authenticate and log back in.
