  6. Check that the process can continue from where you left off and be completed without loss of data, including the original data and any changes made after re-authentication.
  7. Check that the process used to save the information submitted in step 3 is not stored on the server. (Note: This requires knowledge of the technology and features used to implement the technique.)

Expected results

  • #6 and #7 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: Data entry and task completion can be saved and resumed from the current step - unless the task is part of a real-time event where no alternative to the time limit is possible.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Being able to stop and come back is what makes a long task possible for people with fatigue, pain, attention-related disabilities, or an unreliable connection.

title: Usability Testing For Unnecessary Steps
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* Usability testing has been conducted to review for unnecessary steps in the process or unnecessary information being requested.
* The sample of test participants included people with cognitive disabilities and/or mental health based disabilities.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion
* date of assertion

::assertion-recommended

* maintained records of usability testing protocol, scope of the testing, and results
* number of participants and disabilities represented within the group of participants
* record of actions taken to address identified issues

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that it ran usability testing, including participants with cognitive or mental health disabilities, to find unnecessary steps and unnecessary requests for information.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Every extra step is a place to give up. Which steps are unnecessary is visible in testing and invisible from inside the design.

title: Abbreviations Explained
rawBody:
Explanations of abbreviations are available when first used. 

:::except-when
- the abbreviation is:
    * used so often it has become a word with its own dictionary entry, such as "scuba," "info," and "HTML",
    * used in a logo, or
    * included in a longer phrase, such as "brand DNA," whose meaning needs to be defined to meet the [non-literal language requirement](#non-literal-language-explained).
:::

:::example
Abbreviation is introduced after first expanded use of the term.

> "He has Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID)."

Abbreviation is linked to a glossary entry or tooltip.

> "He has [ARFID]."
:::

exceptWhen:
• the abbreviation is:
    • used so often it has become a word with its own dictionary entry, such as “scuba,” “info,” and “HTML”,
    • used in a logo, or
    • included in a longer phrase, such as “brand DNA,” whose meaning needs to be defined to meet the non-literal language requirement.
examples:
Abbreviation is introduced after first expanded use of the term.

“He has Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID).”

Abbreviation is linked to a glossary entry or tooltip.

“He has [ARFID].”
derived.tests:
Procedure

For any abbreviation in the content:

  1. Check that an explanation is available for the first use of the abbreviation.
  2. For an abbreviation that has no explanation available, check that it is included in a dictionary intended for the general public.

Expected result

  • #1 or #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: An abbreviation is explained where it is first used - unless it has become a dictionary word in its own right (such as "scuba" or "HTML"), appears in a logo, or sits inside a longer phrase that the non-literal language requirement already covers.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Unexplained abbreviations stop readers who are new to a domain, reading in a second language, or have a language or learning disability - and screen readers often pronounce them as words.

title: Clear Language Review
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* Our organization has a process and policy to review text content for clear language before publication. The process includes confirming:
  * All of the core requirements in the ‘Clear Language’ guideline are met.
  * Verb tense is chosen for ease of understanding.
  * Content uses short paragraphs.
  * Paragraphs that convey information begin with a sentence stating the main point or purpose (often called a topic sentence).
  * If a style guide is used by content authors, it must provide guidance on these aspects of clear language. 
  * If author training is provided, it must provide guidance on these aspects of clear language.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
* date of when the policy was implemented
* date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

* copy of the policy implementing the clear language review
* date author training was provided (if any)
* number or proportion of authors who completed the training
* copy of the style guide (if any) where clear language review has been defined

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that it has a process and policy for reviewing text for clear language before publication - meeting the Clear Language guideline's core requirements, choosing verb tense for ease of understanding, keeping paragraphs short, and opening informative paragraphs with a topic sentence - and that any style guide or author training covers these.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Clarity is a property of how content is produced. A review policy is what makes it survive deadlines and changes of author.

title: Common Words Used
rawBody: Common words are used, and definitions are available for uncommon words. :::applies-when * human languages have more than 1,500 words. ::: :::except-when * the words are for names of people or places, or * the language does not have a high-frequency corpus. ::: :::note This is not a core requirement because a list of common words would not cover terms that are known by specific audiences, such as accounting terms on an accounting site. However, in future guidance for policymakers, it is an example of a supplemental requirement that could be made mandatory for public service and education providers. Lists of common words are called high-frequency corpora. They exist for many languages including Arabic, Hindi, Mandarin, and Russian as well as American English, British English, and Canadian English. ::: :::ednote Research shows that using common words and defining uncommon words improves understanding. Making Content Usable for People with Cognitive and Learning Disabilities recommends using the 1,500 highest-frequency words or phrases because people with severe language impairments are most likely to know these terms. However, more research is needed to confirm if the same threshold applies to many languages for distinguishing common from uncommon words. :::

appliesWhen: • human languages have more than 1,500 words.
exceptWhen:
• the words are for names of people or places, or
  • the language does not have a high-frequency corpus.
notes:
This is not a core requirement because a list of common words would not cover terms that are known by specific audiences, such as accounting terms on an accounting site. However, in future guidance for policymakers, it is an example of a supplemental requirement that could be made mandatory for public service and education providers.

Lists of common words are called high-frequency corpora. They exist for many languages including Arabic, Hindi, Mandarin, and Russian as well as American English, British English, and Canadian English.
editorNotes: Research shows that using common words and defining uncommon words improves understanding. Making Content Usable for People with Cognitive and Learning Disabilities recommends using the 1,500 highest-frequency words or phrases because people with severe language impairments are most likely to know these terms. However, more research is needed to confirm if the same threshold applies to many languages for distinguishing common from uncommon words.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each word:

  1. Check that the word appears in the 1,500 most common words in a high-frequency corpus for the language used.
  2. If the word is not in the list of the 1,500 most common words, check that it has a definition available within the page/view.
  3. Check that a technology in the accessibility support set meets ‘Common words used.’

Expected results

  • #1, #2, or #3 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Common words are used, and uncommon ones come with definitions. This applies to languages with more than 1,500 words; names of people and places are exempt, as are languages with no high-frequency corpus.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Vocabulary is the most common barrier in text. Uncommon words stop readers with cognitive and learning disabilities, and readers working in a second language.

title: Diacritics Available
rawBody: Diacritics required to identify the correct meaning of each word are available. :::applies-when * a human language has a version that removes diacritics for proficient readers. ::: :::note A diacritic is a small mark that is added to a letter or character that changes how it is pronounced or what it means. Diacritics may appear above, below, within, or between letters or characters. ::: :::note Hebrew and Arabic are examples of human languages that omit diacritics for proficient readers. ::: :::example The Hebrew word אמר, with three consonants and no diacritics * Without diacritics to represent the vowels, אמר can represent different verb and noun forms of “to say.” * Readers must rely on context to determine the intended pronunciation and meaning. ::: :::example The Hebrew word אָמַר, with diacritics under two of the three consonants * A diacritic (whose unicode looks similar to an uppercase T) under the א makes an “ah” sound. * A horizontal mark under the מ makes a short “a” sound. * Pronunciation: ah-mar * Meaning: "He said" ::: :::example The Hebrew word יֹאמַר, with diacritics in front of the first consonant and under another * A mark (that looks similar to a floating comma) in front of the word indicates future tense, masculine. * A dot above the prefix makes an "o" sound. * A horizontal mark under the מ makes a short “a” sound. * Pronunciation: yo-mar * Meaning: "He will say" ::: :::example The Hebrew word אֹמֶר, with a different set of diacritics above one consonant and under another * A dot above the first letter makes an “o” sound. * Three dots forming a small triangle under the מ make a short “e” sound. * Pronunciation: oh-mer * Meaning: "utterance; saying" (noun) :::

appliesWhen: • a human language has a version that removes diacritics for proficient readers.
notes: A diacritic is a small mark that is added to a letter or character that changes how it is pronounced or what it means. Diacritics may appear above, below, within, or between letters or characters.
Hebrew and Arabic are examples of human languages that omit diacritics for proficient readers.
examples:
The Hebrew word אמר, with three consonants and no diacritics

  • Without diacritics to represent the vowels, אמר can represent different verb and noun forms of “to say.”
  • Readers must rely on context to determine the intended pronunciation and meaning.

The Hebrew word אָמַר, with diacritics under two of the three consonants

  • A diacritic (whose unicode looks similar to an uppercase T) under the א makes an “ah” sound.
  • A horizontal mark under the מ makes a short “a” sound.
  • Pronunciation: ah-mar
  • Meaning: “He said”

The Hebrew word יֹאמַר, with diacritics in front of the first consonant and under another

  • A mark (that looks similar to a floating comma) in front of the word indicates future tense, masculine.
  • A dot above the prefix makes an “o” sound.
  • A horizontal mark under the מ makes a short “a” sound.
  • Pronunciation: yo-mar
  • Meaning: “He will say”

The Hebrew word אֹמֶר, with a different set of diacritics above one consonant and under another

  • A dot above the first letter makes an “o” sound.
  • Three dots forming a small triangle under the מ make a short “e” sound.
  • Pronunciation: oh-mer
  • Meaning: “utterance; saying” (noun)
derived.tests:
Procedure

For all text content:

  1. Check for content that has missing diacritics.
  2. Check that an alternative version to text identified in #1 is provided that includes diacritics needed to identify the correct meaning of each word.
  3. Check that the accessibility support set meets ‘Diacritics available’.

Expected results

  • #2 or #3 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where a language has a form that drops diacritics for proficient readers, the diacritics needed to identify each word's correct meaning are available.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Without them, a word can be read several ways. Readers who are still learning the language, or who have a reading disability, cannot reliably pick the right one from context.

title: No Nested Clauses
rawBody:
Sentences do not include nested clauses.

:::except-when
- text content:
    * is poetic, scriptural, artistic, or expressive rather than informational, or
    * provides legal information.
:::

:::example
The sentence:

> "The teacher was surprised that the student who did well on yesterday's test was absent today."

Includes the nested clause "who did well on yesterday's test" of the clause "was surprised that the student ... was absent today".

This could be written without the nested clause as:

> "The teacher was surprised that the student was absent today. This was unexpected because he did well on yesterday's test."
:::

exceptWhen:
• text content:
    • is poetic, scriptural, artistic, or expressive rather than informational, or
    • provides legal information.
examples:
The sentence:

“The teacher was surprised that the student who did well on yesterday’s test was absent today.”

Includes the nested clause “who did well on yesterday’s test” of the clause “was surprised that the student … was absent today”.

This could be written without the nested clause as:

“The teacher was surprised that the student was absent today. This was unexpected because he did well on yesterday’s test.”
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each sentence: For all nested clauses in the sentence (introduced by nesting conjunctions such as ‘because’, ‘although’, ‘if’, ‘that’, ‘which’, ‘who’, ‘when’, and ‘where’).

  1. Check that each initial nested clause does not contain other nested clauses within it.
  2. Check that a technology in the accessibility support set meets ‘No nested clauses’.

Expected results

  • #1 or #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Sentences avoid nested clauses. Poetic, scriptural, artistic and expressive content is exempt, as is legal information.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Each nested clause is something the reader has to hold in mind while the sentence finishes. That load is what makes otherwise simple information unreadable for people with cognitive disabilities.

title: No Unnecessary Words
rawBody:
Sentences do not include unnecessary words.

:::except-when
- text content is:
  * poetic,
  * scriptural,
  * artistic, or
  * expressive rather than informational.
:::

:::example
* redundant modifiers such as ‘free gift’ and ‘past history’ 
* double negatives to express a positive such as ‘She didn't see nothing’ (which can be shortened to ‘She saw nothing’)
* indirect phrasing such as ‘at this point in time’ (which can be shortened to ‘now’)
* noun versions of verbs, such as ‘take into consideration’ (which can be shortened to ‘consider’)
:::

:::note 
Automated tools can help content authors identify unnecessary words in many languages, including Arabic, English, Hindi, Mandarin, and Russian.
:::

exceptWhen:
• text content is:
    • poetic,
    • scriptural,
    • artistic, or
    • expressive rather than informational.
notes: Automated tools can help content authors identify unnecessary words in many languages, including Arabic, English, Hindi, Mandarin, and Russian.
examples:
• redundant modifiers such as ‘free gift’ and ‘past history’
  • double negatives to express a positive such as ‘She didn’t see nothing’ (which can be shortened to ‘She saw nothing’)
  • indirect phrasing such as ‘at this point in time’ (which can be shortened to ‘now’)
  • noun versions of verbs, such as ‘take into consideration’ (which can be shortened to ‘consider’)
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each sentence:

  1. Identify any words that may be unnecessary.
  2. Remove or replace the phrase with a simpler alternative.
  3. Check that no meaning is lost.
  4. Check that a technology in the accessibility support set meets ‘No unnecessary words.’

Expected results

  • #3 or #4 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Sentences avoid unnecessary words. Poetic, scriptural, artistic and expressive content is exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Padding lengthens the path to the meaning, which costs the most for people who read slowly, use text-to-speech, or have limited working memory.

title: Non-literal language explained
rawBody:
Explanations or unambiguous alternatives are available in text content for non-literal language, such as idioms and metaphors.

:::except-when
* text content is:
  * poetic,
  * scriptural,
  * artistic, or
  * expressive rather than informational.
:::

:::ednote
Translation software and other tools can aid content authors in identifying non-literal language.
:::

exceptWhen:
• text content is:
    • poetic,
    • scriptural,
    • artistic, or
    • expressive rather than informational.
editorNotes: Translation software and other tools can aid content authors in identifying non-literal language.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each phrase of non-literal language in text content:

  1. Check that access is provided to an unambiguous alternative or to an explanation of the non-literal text.
  2. Check that the non-literal text is presented in a way that is available to user agents, including assistive technologies (AT).
  3. Check that the accessibility support set meets ‘Non-literal language explained’.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true, or
  • #3 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Idioms, metaphors and other non-literal language come with an explanation or an unambiguous alternative in text. Poetic, scriptural, artistic and expressive content is exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Non-literal language is routinely read literally by people with some cognitive disabilities and by autistic readers, and it rarely survives translation.

title: Numerical Alternatives Available
rawBody:
Explanations or alternatives are provided for complex numerical information such as statistics.

:::note
Complex numerical information can increase cognitive load, especially for users with a limited ability to understand and work with numbers. Providing written explanations or visualizations can aid understanding.
:::

:::example
Instead of:

> "The stadium holds 60,000 people."

Use:

> "The stadium holds 60,000 people, which is about the size of a small city."

Or:

> "The stadium holds many people."
:::

notes: Complex numerical information can increase cognitive load, especially for users with a limited ability to understand and work with numbers. Providing written explanations or visualizations can aid understanding.
examples:
Instead of:

“The stadium holds 60,000 people.”

Use:

“The stadium holds 60,000 people, which is about the size of a small city.”

Or:

“The stadium holds many people.”
derived.tests:
Procedure

For any complex numerical information in the content:

  1. Check that an alternative is available that is not presented as complex numerical information.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: An exploratory requirement: complex numerical information, such as statistics, comes with an explanation or an alternative.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Statistics compress a lot of meaning into a form many readers cannot unpack, and a misread number can change a decision about health or money.

title: Summaries Available
rawBody:
A summary is available for long-form text content and:
* is identifiable visually and programmatically,
* uses concise sentences, and
* provides access to explanations of any uncommon words that are used in the summary.

:::ednote

Research is needed to determine the number of words that trigger the summary requirement and whether this threshold varies for different languages. If you are aware of research in this area, please email public-agwg-comments@w3.org.
:::

:::applies-when
* a page/view with continuous long-form text content that is organized in paragraphs and has 300 or more words.
:::

:::except-when
* long-form text content continues on multiple pages/views, only the first page/view requires a summary.
:::

appliesWhen: • a page/view with continuous long-form text content that is organized in paragraphs and has 300 or more words.
exceptWhen: • long-form text content continues on multiple pages/views, only the first page/view requires a summary.
editorNotes: Research is needed to determine the number of words that trigger the summary requirement and whether this threshold varies for different languages. If you are aware of research in this area, please email public-agwg-comments@w3.org.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For long-form text content that has 300 or more words:

  1. Check that a summary is present.
  2. Check that the summary can be identified visually and programmatically.
  3. Check that the summary explains uncommon words and uses concise sentences.

Expected results

  • #1, #2, and #3 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: Long-form text - a page of continuous prose in paragraphs of 300 words or more - has a summary that is identifiable both visually and programmatically, uses concise sentences, and gives access to explanations of any uncommon words it uses. Where the text runs across several pages, only the first needs one.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A summary is how a reader decides whether to spend the effort, and for people with cognitive disabilities or limited reading stamina it is often the only part they can get through.

title: Visual Aids Review
rawBody:
[Title, role, or organization] asserts that:

* Our organization has a process and policy for reviewing text content to identify complex ideas such as processes, workflows, relationships, or chronological information, and adding visual aids to help readers understand them.

::assertion-required

* title, role, or organization making the assertion (if different from the conformance claim)
* date of when the policy was implemented
* date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)

::assertion-recommended

* copy of the policy implementing the use of visual aids
* date author training was provided (if any)
* number or proportion of authors who completed the training
* copy of the style guide (if any) where visual aids have been defined

plainEnglish.summary: An organisational assertion: the organisation states that it has a process and policy for finding complex ideas in its text - processes, workflows, relationships, chronology - and adding visual aids to help readers understand them.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Some relationships are far easier to see than to read. A diagram is often the difference between a process being followable and being merely described.

title: Blocks Of Text Adjustable
rawBody:
The presentation of blocks of text can be adjusted, without loss of content or functionality, to meet the @@ [values to be determined] for:
* inline margin
* block margin
* line length
* line height
* justification

:::note
The requirement is that the text is manipulable and the style attributes can be overridden.
:::

:::except-when
* the style attribute is hard-coded, such as raw text that is capitalized or hyphenated.
:::

:::ednote
If you are aware of research in this area, especially involving non-Latin scripts, please email public-agwg-comments@w3.org.
:::

exceptWhen: • the style attribute is hard-coded, such as raw text that is capitalized or hyphenated.
notes: The requirement is that the text is manipulable and the style attributes can be overridden.
editorNotes: If you are aware of research in this area, especially involving non-Latin scripts, please email public-agwg-comments@w3.org.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each block of text:

  1. Apply the highest level of change of each attribute specified in the provision.
  2. Check that the text is changed by the override.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: The presentation of blocks of text can be adjusted without losing content or functionality - inline margin, block margin, line length, line height and justification. The exact values are still to be determined in the draft. Hard-coded styling, such as raw text that is already capitalised or hyphenated, is exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Readers with dyslexia, low vision or attention-related disabilities often need wider spacing or shorter lines. Layouts that break when those change force a choice between reading comfortably and reading at all.

title: Blocks of text readable (enhanced)
rawBody:
The default/authored presentation of blocks of text meets the enhanced @@ [values to be determined] for:
* inline margin
* block margin
* line length
* line height

:::ednote
If you are aware of research in this area, especially involving non-Latin scripts, please email public-agwg-comments@w3.org.
:::

editorNotes: If you are aware of research in this area, especially involving non-Latin scripts, please email public-agwg-comments@w3.org.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each block of text:

  1. HTML: Check CSS to confirm that relevant style attributes (such as line height, letter spacing, word spacing, text align) are set within the values specified in the provision.
  2. Non-web apps: Check GUI toolkit settings (or defaults) to confirm that they apply values within the designated range.

Expected results

  • #1 or #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: The text as authored - before any user adjustment - meets enhanced values for inline margin, block margin, line length and line height. The values themselves are still to be determined.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Setting readable defaults means users do not have to know that adjustment is possible, which is most of them.

title: Blocks of text readable (minimum)
rawBody:
The default/authored presentation of blocks of text meets the minimum @@ [values to be determined] for:
* inline margin
* block margin
* line length
* line height

:::ednote
If you are aware of research in this area, especially involving non-Latin scripts, please email public-agwg-comments@w3.org.
:::

editorNotes: If you are aware of research in this area, especially involving non-Latin scripts, please email public-agwg-comments@w3.org.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each block of text:

  1. Check that the attributes of the block of text are within the attributes specified in this provision.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: The same as the enhanced version but at a minimum level: the authored presentation of text blocks meets baseline values for inline margin, block margin, line length and line height, still to be determined.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Long lines and tight leading cause readers to lose their place on the return sweep - a problem for everyone, and a barrier for people with dyslexia or low vision.

title: Text Color Adjustable
rawBody:
The foreground and background color of text can be adjusted without losing content or functionality.

:::note
The requirement is that the text is manipulable and the colors can be overridden. That could be achieved by the user-agent (including operating system, browser, and assistive technology), or provided by the content author.
:::

:::applies-when
* text is presented, including text embedded in an image format.
:::

:::except-when
* the text is:
  * also present elsewhere in the page/view which meets the requirement
  * part of an inactive interactive element
  * pure decoration
  * not visible to anyone
  * part of a picture that includes significant other visual content
  * part of a logo
:::

appliesWhen: • text is presented, including text embedded in an image format.
exceptWhen:
• the text is:
    • also present elsewhere in the page/view which meets the requirement
    • part of an inactive interactive element
    • pure decoration
    • not visible to anyone
    • part of a picture that includes significant other visual content
    • part of a logo
notes: The requirement is that the text is manipulable and the colors can be overridden. That could be achieved by the user-agent (including operating system, browser, and assistive technology), or provided by the content author.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each block of text:

  1. Adjust the foreground and background color to a high-contrast light-on-dark theme.
  2. Check that content and functionality is not lost.
  3. Adjust the foreground and background color to a high-contrast dark-on-light theme.
  4. Check that content and functionality is not lost.

Expected results

  • #2 and #4 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: The foreground and background colour of text can be changed without losing content or functionality. The exceptions mirror the contrast requirement: text also present elsewhere in a conforming form, text in an inactive control, pure decoration, invisible text, text within a substantive picture, and logos.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Many people read only with a specific colour combination - light text on dark, or a tinted background for scotopic sensitivity. Content that resists recolouring blocks the adaptation they depend on.

title: Text contrast sufficient (enhanced)
rawBody:
The default visual presentation of text meets @@[contrast measure to be determined, at a higher level than the core requirement for Text contrast sufficient (minimum)].

:::ednote
The contrast algorithm used in WCAG 3 is yet to be determined. For this draft, the requirement assumes the algorithm will include a size/weight factor. If the algorithm does not include size/weight, it will need to be added to this requirement text.
:::

:::applies-when
* text is presented, including text embedded in an image format.
:::

:::except-when
- the text is:
    * also present elsewhere in the page/view which meets the requirement
    * part of an inactive interactive element
    * pure decoration
    * not visible to anyone
    * part of a picture that includes significant other visual content
    * part of a logo
:::

appliesWhen: • text is presented, including text embedded in an image format.
exceptWhen:
• the text is:
    • also present elsewhere in the page/view which meets the requirement
    • part of an inactive interactive element
    • pure decoration
    • not visible to anyone
    • part of a picture that includes significant other visual content
    • part of a logo
editorNotes: The contrast algorithm used in WCAG 3 is yet to be determined. For this draft, the requirement assumes the algorithm will include a size/weight factor. If the algorithm does not include size/weight, it will need to be added to this requirement text.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each foreground and background combination of text:

  1. Identify the foreground color.
  2. Identify the background color.
  3. Check the contrast of text meets the [TBD algorithm].

Expected results

  • #3 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: A higher contrast bar than the minimum requirement, with the same scope and exceptions. The measure itself is still to be determined in the draft.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: The minimum level is a floor, not a comfortable reading level. The enhanced level is aimed at people whose contrast sensitivity is significantly reduced.

title: Text contrast sufficient (minimum)
rawBody:
The default visual presentation of text meets @@[contrast measure to be determined].

:::applies-when
* text is presented, including text embedded in an image format.
:::

:::except-when
- the text is:
  * also present elsewhere in the page/view which meets the requirement
  * part of an inactive interactive element
  * pure decoration
  * not visible to anyone
  * part of a picture that includes significant other visual content
  * part of a logo or brand name
:::

:::note
Transparency can cause testing issues, but should be tested as the rendered color.
:::

:::ednote
The contrast algorithm used in WCAG 3 is yet to be determined. For this draft, the requirement assumes the algorithm will include a size/weight factor. If the algorithm does not include size/weight, it will need to be added to this requirement text.

A separate requirement may be needed if red/green color vision deficiency (CVD) is not accounted for within the contrast algorithm.
:::

appliesWhen: • text is presented, including text embedded in an image format.
exceptWhen:
• the text is:
    • also present elsewhere in the page/view which meets the requirement
    • part of an inactive interactive element
    • pure decoration
    • not visible to anyone
    • part of a picture that includes significant other visual content
    • part of a logo or brand name
notes: Transparency can cause testing issues, but should be tested as the rendered color.
editorNotes:
The contrast algorithm used in WCAG 3 is yet to be determined. For this draft, the requirement assumes the algorithm will include a size/weight factor. If the algorithm does not include size/weight, it will need to be added to this requirement text.

A separate requirement may be needed if red/green color vision deficiency (CVD) is not accounted for within the contrast algorithm.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each foreground and background combination of text:

  1. Identify the foreground color.
  2. Identify the background color.
  3. Check the contrast of text meets the [TBD algorithm].

Expected results

  • #3 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Text must maintain strong visual contrast against its background so it can be easily read by everyone, including people with low vision or under bright light.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Faint or low-contrast text forces users to strain their eyes and makes reading impossible for low-vision users.

title: Text Customizations Retained
rawBody:
Content that is exported, saved, or printed retains user-applied text-appearance customizations.

:::applies-when
* the page/view can be exported, saved, or printed.
:::

:::example
Examples of interoperable formats
* PDF
* HTML
* SVG
* OpenDocument
:::

:::example
Examples of non-interoperable formats
* Scriptable Network Graphics
* DOCX, unless you know your audience has the required software (for example, you’re writing internal documents for your company which provides employees with the necessary software)
* Java object code
:::

appliesWhen: • the page/view can be exported, saved, or printed.
examples:
Examples of interoperable formats

  • PDF
  • HTML
  • SVG
  • OpenDocument

Examples of non-interoperable formats

  • Scriptable Network Graphics
  • DOCX, unless you know your audience has the required software (for example, you’re writing internal documents for your company which provides employees with the necessary software)
  • Java object code
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each page/view:

  1. Adjust aspects of the text appearance, such as size, style, and color.
  2. Export, save, and print the content.
  3. Check that the customizations in #1 remain intact in the exported/saved/printed version. If there are multiple export options, check that at least one preserves the customizations.

Expected results

  • #3 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where content can be exported, saved or printed, the user's own text-appearance customisations survive into the exported copy.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Adjustments that vanish on export mean the saved copy is unreadable to the person who saved it - and they usually have no way to reapply them.

title: Text Size Adjustable
rawBody:
Text can be increased in size to at least 200% of the platform’s default body-text size.

:::except-when
* the same text is available elsewhere in the page/view which can be increased to at least 200% of the platform’s default body-text size.
:::

exceptWhen: • the same text is available elsewhere in the page/view which can be increased to at least 200% of the platform’s default body-text size.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each block of text:

  1. Use each platform mechanism for increasing text size.
  2. Check that at least one mechanism can achieve a 200% text-size increase.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Text can be increased to at least 200% of the platform's default body-text size. Text that also appears elsewhere in the view and can be enlarged that far is exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Enlarging text is the most common adaptation there is. Layouts that clip, overlap or scroll sideways at 200% take it away from people with low vision.

title: Text Style Adjustable
rawBody:
The presentation of text style properties can be adjusted, without loss of content or functionality, to meet the @@ [values to be determined] for:
* typeface
* font width
* text decoration
* capitalization
* automatic end-of-line hyphenation

:::note
The requirement is that the text is manipulable and the style attributes can be overridden.
:::

:::except-when
* the text style property is hard-coded, such as raw text that is capitalized or hyphenated.
:::

:::ednote
If you are aware of research in this area, especially involving non-Latin scripts, please email public-agwg-comments@w3.org.
:::

exceptWhen: • the text style property is hard-coded, such as raw text that is capitalized or hyphenated.
notes: The requirement is that the text is manipulable and the style attributes can be overridden.
editorNotes: If you are aware of research in this area, especially involving non-Latin scripts, please email public-agwg-comments@w3.org.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each block of text:

  1. Apply the highest level of change of each attribute specified in the provision.
  2. Check that the text is changed by the override.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Text style properties can be adjusted without losing content or functionality - typeface, font width, text decoration, capitalisation and automatic hyphenation - to values still to be determined. Hard-coded styling is exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Readers with dyslexia often substitute a typeface, and all-caps or hyphenated text is markedly harder to read. Being able to change these is what makes text legible for them.

title: Text style readable (enhanced)
rawBody:
The default/authored presentation of text style properties meets the enhanced @@ [values to be determined] for:
* typeface
* font size
* font width
* text decoration
* letter spacing
* capitalization
* end-of-line hyphenation

:::ednote
If you are aware of research in this area, especially involving non-Latin scripts, please email public-agwg-comments@w3.org.
:::

editorNotes: If you are aware of research in this area, especially involving non-Latin scripts, please email public-agwg-comments@w3.org.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each block of text:

  1. HTML: Check CSS to confirm that relevant style attributes (such as font size and letter spacing) are set within the values specified in the provision.
  2. Non-web apps: Check GUI toolkit settings (or defaults) to confirm that they apply values within the designated range.

Expected results

  • #1 or #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: The authored presentation of text style properties - typeface, font size, font width, text decoration, letter spacing, capitalisation and end-of-line hyphenation - meets enhanced values, still to be determined.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Defaults decide what most readers get. Setting them at the enhanced level removes the need for individual adaptation.

title: Text style readable (minimum)
rawBody:
The default/authored presentation of text style property meets the minimum @@ [values to be determined] for:
* typeface
* font size
* font width
* text decoration
* letter spacing
* capitalization
* end-of-line hyphenation

:::ednote
If you are aware of research in this area, especially involving non-Latin scripts, please email public-agwg-comments@w3.org.
:::

editorNotes: If you are aware of research in this area, especially involving non-Latin scripts, please email public-agwg-comments@w3.org.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each block of text:

  1. Check that the attributes of the block of text are within the attributes specified in the provision.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: The same properties at a minimum level: the authored text style meets baseline values, still to be determined.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: This is the floor below which text is difficult for a large share of readers regardless of any setting they might change.

title: Human Language Detectable
rawBody:
The human language of all content within the view is programmatically determinable.

:::except-when
* A language tag is not available in [[iso-639-2023]], or
* The technology used to create the view does not support indicating languages.
:::

exceptWhen:
• A language tag is not available in [[iso-639-2023]], or
  • The technology used to create the view does not support indicating languages.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For text content:

  1. Establish which language is used.
  2. Check that the content’s language is identified in the HTML code with a lang attribute.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: The human language of everything in the view can be determined programmatically - unless no language tag exists for it in the ISO register, or the technology cannot indicate language at all.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Screen readers choose pronunciation rules from the language tag. Untagged or mistagged text is read in the wrong accent and is often incomprehensible.

title: Numerical Metadata Available
rawBody:
Numerical information includes sufficient context in written text and a programmatic equivalent to avoid confusion when presenting dates, temperatures, time, and Roman numerals.

:::note
Numerical metadata is information that provides context about the numbers presented. This context helps users understand what the numbers represent and how they should be read. Without these cues, numbers can be ambiguous or misleading, making it harder for users to understand the intended meaning—especially across different regions, disciplines, or assistive technologies. 
:::

:::example
* Dates include markers for day and month such as “3 May 2025” instead of the ambiguous "03/05/2025."
* Temperatures specify degrees Celsius or Fahrenheit such as "0° C" or "32° F." 
* Times specify am, pm, or 24-hour clock such as "1 pm" or "13:00."
:::

notes: Numerical metadata is information that provides context about the numbers presented. This context helps users understand what the numbers represent and how they should be read. Without these cues, numbers can be ambiguous or misleading, making it harder for users to understand the intended meaning—especially across different regions, disciplines, or assistive technologies.
examples:
• Dates include markers for day and month such as “3 May 2025” instead of the ambiguous “03/05/2025.”
  • Temperatures specify degrees Celsius or Fahrenheit such as “0° C” or “32° F.”
  • Times specify am, pm, or 24-hour clock such as “1 pm” or “13:00.”
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each date, temperature, time, or Roman numeral presented visually:

  1. Check that it uses an unambiguous format.
  2. Check that it provides an alternative in an unambiguous format within the same page/view.

Expected results

  • #1 or #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Numerical information carries enough context in the written text, plus a programmatic equivalent, to avoid confusion - dates, temperatures, times and Roman numerals in particular.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: "03/04" is two different dates depending on the reader, and a screen reader may voice a Roman numeral as a word. Context is what stops a number being misread.

title: Text Appearance Not Relied On
rawBody:
Meaning conveyed by text style properties is also programmatically determinable.

:::applies-when
* the styling, weight, or other text characteristics convey meaning beyond what the text itself says.
:::

:::except-when
* emphasis is the only additional meaning conveyed.
:::

:::example
* When bold or italics is used to indicate an error, an additional indicator such as an exclamation mark (!) is also provided.
* When larger text is used as a hint in a puzzle, an additional indicator such as an asterisk (*) is also provided.
:::

appliesWhen: • the styling, weight, or other text characteristics convey meaning beyond what the text itself says.
exceptWhen: • emphasis is the only additional meaning conveyed.
examples:
• When bold or italics is used to indicate an error, an additional indicator such as an exclamation mark (!) is also provided.
  • When larger text is used as a hint in a puzzle, an additional indicator such as an asterisk (*) is also provided.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each instance of text styling, weight, size, or other text characteristics that conveys meaning that is not just emphasis:

  1. Check that an additional indicator of that meaning is available.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: An exploratory requirement: where styling, weight or other text characteristics carry meaning beyond the words themselves, that meaning is also available programmatically. Where the only added meaning is emphasis, the requirement does not apply.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Bold, colour and size are invisible to a screen reader unless marked up. Meaning carried only by appearance simply does not reach the user.

title: Text Detectable
rawBody:
All visible text has a programmatically determinable equivalent.

:::except-when
* making visible text programmatically determinable would lead to duplication within the view.
:::

exceptWhen: • making visible text programmatically determinable would lead to duplication within the view.
derived.tests:
Procedure For all visible text:

  1. If the text is embedded in an image, check that the text has a text alternative or can be accurately read using the accessibility support set.
  2. If text content, check that the text is not hidden using code such as the aria-hidden attribute.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: Every piece of text a sighted user can see has an equivalent that software can read - including text inside images and drawn onto a canvas. The exception is where providing it would duplicate text already present in the view.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Text baked into an image or drawn on a canvas cannot be read aloud, enlarged, recoloured or translated. The programmatic equivalent is what restores all of those.

title: Layout Reflow Supported
rawBody:
All content fits within 320 CSS pixels in the default orientation of text without requiring scrolling in more than one direction. Sections of content within the page/view that scroll in a different direction to the page/view fit within 320 CSS pixels of the page-scrolling direction.

:::except-when
* 2D relationships (for example, tables or electronic program guides)
* canvases of presentational content (for example, slides)
* multiple palettes or panels that act on content (for example, Photoshop or an IDE)
:::

:::ednote
All block-level elements fit within a 320px inline-size without requiring scrolling in more than one direction.
:::

exceptWhen:
• 2D relationships (for example, tables or electronic program guides)
  • canvases of presentational content (for example, slides)
  • multiple palettes or panels that act on content (for example, Photoshop or an IDE)
editorNotes: All block-level elements fit within a 320px inline-size without requiring scrolling in more than one direction.
derived.tests:
Procedure

  1. Set the viewport at 320px in the direction of text.
  2. Check that each section of content fits within 320 CSS pixels.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: The page has to work in a 320-CSS-pixel-wide column - the width of a 1280px page at 400% zoom - without forcing the reader to scroll both across and down. Sections that scroll the other way must fit that width too. Tables and program guides, slide-style canvases, and multi-panel tools such as image editors and IDEs are exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: 320 CSS pixels is what a 1280-pixel page looks like at 400% zoom. Content that forces scrolling in both directions at that size makes reading a line a two-handed operation.

title: Orientation supported (enhanced)
rawBody:
Content supports both portrait and landscape orientations.

:::except-when
* Content is aligned with the physical world.
* The orientation is essential.
:::

exceptWhen:
• Content is aligned with the physical world.
  • The orientation is essential.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For platforms which do not have a default orientation:

  1. Open the content.
  2. Check that the orientation can align with both portrait and landscape orientations.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Content works in both portrait and landscape. Content aligned with the physical world, and cases where a particular orientation is essential, are exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A device mounted to a wheelchair or a bed is fixed in one orientation. Content that only works the other way round cannot be used at all.

title: Orientation supported (minimum)
rawBody:
If the platform has a default orientation, content supports that orientation. If the platform does not have a default orientation, content supports both portrait and landscape orientations.

:::except-when
* Content is aligned with the physical world.
* The orientation is essential.
:::

:::note
For extended reality, the platform default orientation aligns with the real world orientation.
:::

:::note
Content does not have to re-layout or change aspect ratio in a different orientation, it just needs to display in the device orientation.
:::

exceptWhen:
• Content is aligned with the physical world.
  • The orientation is essential.
notes: For extended reality, the platform default orientation aligns with the real world orientation.
Content does not have to re-layout or change aspect ratio in a different orientation, it just needs to display in the device orientation.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For platforms which have a default orientation:

  1. Open the content.
  2. Check that the orientation aligns with the platform default.

For platforms which do not have a default orientation:

  1. Open the content.
  2. Check that the orientation can align with both portrait and landscape orientations.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where a platform has a default orientation, content supports it; where the platform has none, content supports both portrait and landscape. The same exemptions apply.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Locking orientation overrides a physical setup the user cannot change, which is why this is a baseline rather than an enhancement.

title: Text Reflow Supported
rawBody:
Blocks of text are legible at 320 CSS pixels in the orientation of text, without the need to scroll in the orientation of text.

:::except-when
* The meaning of text relies on a two-dimensional structure. 
:::

:::example
Two-dimensional structure might be relied upon in preformatted text such as code, poems, maps, or comics.
:::

:::ednote
Other languages may have other rules around line breaking: https://r12a.github.io/scripts/script-features/index.html
:::

exceptWhen: • The meaning of text relies on a two-dimensional structure.
editorNotes: Other languages may have other rules around line breaking: https://r12a.github.io/scripts/script-features/index.html
examples: Two-dimensional structure might be relied upon in preformatted text such as code, poems, maps, or comics.
derived.tests:
HTML paragraph reflow without requiring scrolling in two dimensions

Procedure

For each page/view:

  1. Set the viewport at 320 CSS pixels in the direction of text.
  2. Identify all the blocks of text within the scope.
  3. Check that each block of text does not require scrolling into two dimensions.
  4. Check that the text in each block of text is legible.

Expected results

  • #3 and #4 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: Blocks of text stay legible at 320 CSS pixels in the orientation of the text, without having to scroll in that direction to read a line. Text whose meaning depends on a two-dimensional structure is exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Having to scroll sideways to read every line makes sustained reading impossible, which is the everyday experience of magnification users on unreflowed layouts.

title: Assistive Technology Supported
rawBody: Content can be controlled using assistive and adaptive technology.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each page view:

  1. Check that each control can be operated using assistive technology and that operating the controls achieves the same results with and without assistive technology.
  2. Check that reading or experiencing non-interactive content produces the same results with and without assistive technology.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: Screen readers, switch devices, voice control, magnifiers and other assistive or adaptive technology can operate the content - not merely read it.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: This is the baseline the rest depends on: content that blocks or breaks assistive technology is inaccessible no matter how well it is labelled.

title: Notifications Adjustable
rawBody:
The timing or positioning of notifications can be changed, suppressed, or saved.

:::applies-when
- Notifications or other interruptions are present.
:::

:::except-when
- The notification involves an emergency or is essential.
:::

appliesWhen: • Notifications or other interruptions are present.
exceptWhen: • The notification involves an emergency or is essential.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each notification:

  1. Check that settings allow the timing or location to be changed.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where notifications or other interruptions occur, their timing or position can be changed, suppressed or saved - unless the notification is an emergency or is otherwise essential.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Interruptions break concentration and can steal focus mid-task, which is particularly costly for people with attention-related and cognitive disabilities.

title: User Settings Supported
rawBody:
Content responds to users’ platform and user agent accessibility-related settings. 

:::note
Accessibility-related user settings include font size, icon size, color scheme, magnification, and motion.
:::

notes: Accessibility-related user settings include font size, icon size, color scheme, magnification, and motion.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each setting:

  1. Change an accessibility-related setting in a platform or user agent in the accessibility support set.
  2. Check content to see that the setting has been applied.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Content responds to the accessibility-related settings the user has already set on their platform or browser.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: People configure contrast, motion, text size and colour once, at system level. Content that ignores those settings makes them configure everything again, site by site.

title: Virtual Cursor Supported
rawBody:
Assistive technologies can access content and interactions when using mechanisms that convey alternative points of regard or focus.

:::example
A virtual cursor is an example of a mechanism that conveys alternative points or regard or focus.
:::

examples: A virtual cursor is an example of a mechanism that conveys alternative points or regard or focus.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each setting:

  1. Access content and interactions by using mechanisms that convey alternative points of regard or focus.
  2. Check that content is readable and interactions are operable.

Expected results

  • #2 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Assistive technologies can reach content and interactions when they use a separate point of regard or focus - the virtual cursor a screen reader moves through the page independently of keyboard focus.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Screen reader users read with the virtual cursor. Content that only responds to real keyboard focus is reachable but unreadable.

title: Change Of Content Notified
rawBody:
Meaningful changes in visual content are conveyed programmatically. 

:::applies-when
- The changes appear before the user’s current position in reader order.
- The changes appear earlier in the process.
- Notifications, status messages, or error messages appear.
- The amount of content changes.
- The change affects the content’s meaning. 
- The audience changes.
:::

:::except-when
- changes are continuous, without pause.
:::

:::example
- A new message is added in a conversation above the current location of focus. A message is provided that programmatically conveys that there is new content above.
- Filters are adjusted which changes the number of items shown. As the number of items changes, that is provided programmatically as a status update.
:::

appliesWhen:
• The changes appear before the user’s current position in reader order.
  • The changes appear earlier in the process.
  • Notifications, status messages, or error messages appear.
  • The amount of content changes.
  • The change affects the content’s meaning.
  • The audience changes.
exceptWhen: • changes are continuous, without pause.
examples:
• A new message is added in a conversation above the current location of focus. A message is provided that programmatically conveys that there is new content above.
  • Filters are adjusted which changes the number of items shown. As the number of items changes, that is provided programmatically as a status update.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each meaningful change of visual content:

  1. Check that the change is conveyed programmatically using the assistive technology in the accessibility support set.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: A meaningful visual change has to be announced programmatically, not just shown. The draft lists what counts: changes above the user's place in reading order, changes earlier in a process, notifications and status or error messages, changes in how much content there is, changes that alter meaning, and changes of audience. Continuous change with no pause is exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A change a sighted user sees at a glance is invisible to a screen reader user unless it is announced, so they act on a version of the page that no longer exists.

title: Change Of Focus Notified
rawBody: When the focus changes on-focus or automatically, the user is notified visually and programmatically.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each instance of focus being changed by the content:

  1. Check that the change is conveyed visually and programmatically using the assistive technology in the accessibility support set.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: When focus changes, whether on focus or automatically, the user is notified both visually and programmatically.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Unannounced focus movement is disorienting for sighted keyboard users and can leave screen reader users reading from an entirely different part of the page.

title: Change Of User Agent Notified
rawBody: When content triggers a device change or an automatic user agent change, the user is notified before the change occurs.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each instance where the content triggers a change of device or user agent change:

  1. Check that the change is conveyed before the chance occurs.

Expected results

  • #1 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: When content triggers a device change or an automatic change of user agent, the user is told before it happens.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Being thrown into another app or device mid-task can drop assistive technology settings and abandon work in progress.

title: Background Adjustable
rawBody: Patterns, designs, or images placed behind text are avoided or can be removed by the user.

plainEnglish.summary: An exploratory requirement: patterns, designs and images behind text are avoided, or the user can remove them.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Texture behind text lowers effective contrast unpredictably and makes letter shapes harder to resolve, particularly for people with low vision or dyslexia.

title: Font Size Not Relied On
rawBody: When font size conveys visual meaning (such as headings), the text maintains its meaning and purpose when text is resized.

plainEnglish.summary: An exploratory requirement: where font size carries visual meaning, such as marking headings, that meaning survives when the text is resized.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Hierarchy expressed only by size collapses once a user sets their own text size - and it was never available to screen reader users in the first place.

title: Media Alternatives Controllable
rawBody: Closed captions and audio descriptions can be turned on and off.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each media asset with audio content:

  1. Check that a mechanism is available so that users can turn on and off the closed captions.
  2. Check that a mechanism is available so that users can change the audio track from a non-audio-described one to an audio-described.

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: The viewer, not the page, decides whether closed captions and audio descriptions are playing, and can change that at any point.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Which alternative helps depends on the viewer. Control is what lets people sharing a screen, or with different needs, use the same media.

title: Media Alternatives Searchable
rawBody: Alternatives for media can be searched and queried.

derived.tests:
Procedure

For each instance of media with captions and / or transcripts:

  1. Check that a mechanism to search the captions or transcripts is available.
  2. Check that a mechanism to search and look up terms in transcripts is available. This can be:
    1. copying and pasting content from the transcript into a dictionary; or
    2. allowing a platform or application dictionary to show a definition of the term.
      • Example: VoiceOver on MacOS includes a feature to look up terms for what is under a ‘mouse cursor point’

Expected results

  • #1 and #2 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: Alternatives for media - transcripts and the like - can be searched and queried.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Search is what makes a long transcript usable for finding one fact, rather than a wall of text to read through.

title: Media Chapters Available
rawBody:
Audio or video that lasts five minutes or longer can be navigated by chapters.

:::except-when
- The media is a piece of music that the composer has not divided into movements.
:::

:::ednote
Research is needed to determine the length of time that triggers the chapter requirement and whether this threshold varies for different languages. If you are aware of research in this area, please email public-agwg-comments@w3.org.
:::

:::example
Gustav Mahler's <cite>Symphony Number 5</cite> is approximately 70 minutes long and is divided into five movements. Each movement would be a chapter.
:::

:::example
Iron Maiden's <cite>Rime Of The Ancient Mariner</cite> is approximately 14 minutes long and isn't divided into movements. This meets the exception and would not need to be divided into chapters.
:::

exceptWhen: • The media is a piece of music that the composer has not divided into movements.
editorNotes: Research is needed to determine the length of time that triggers the chapter requirement and whether this threshold varies for different languages. If you are aware of research in this area, please email public-agwg-comments@w3.org.
examples: Gustav Mahler’s Symphony Number 5 is approximately 70 minutes long and is divided into five movements. Each movement would be a chapter.
Iron Maiden’s Rime Of The Ancient Mariner is approximately 14 minutes long and isn’t divided into movements. This meets the exception and would not need to be divided into chapters.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For media that lasts five minutes or more:

  1. Play the media.
  2. Check that the media is divided up using chapters.
  3. Check that the chapter titles have descriptive names which are suitable for their content.

Expected results

  • #2 and #3 are true.

plainEnglish.summary: Audio or video of five minutes or longer can be navigated by chapters, unless it is a piece of music the composer did not divide into movements.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Scrubbing a timeline precisely is difficult with a switch, a head pointer or a tremor. Chapters give structural navigation that does not depend on fine pointer control.

title: Page/view audio adjustable
rawBody:
A mechanism is available to pause, stop, and adjust the volume independently of the overall system volume level, of any automatically playing audio in a page/view.

:::applies-when
- Notifications or other interruptions are present.
:::

:::note
Mechanisms include controls on each instance of content, or a single app-wide control that disables audio, for example: app-wide earcons.
:::

appliesWhen: • Notifications or other interruptions are present.
notes: Mechanisms include controls on each instance of content, or a single app-wide control that disables audio, for example: app-wide earcons.
derived.tests:
Procedure

For each page / view:

  1. Check for audio that starts automatically.
  2. For audio content in a media player, check that the media player has controls that can pause, stop, or adjust the audio volume.
  3. For audio content set at an application level, check that there is a central setting that enables or disables audio across the application.
  4. Check that one of these are present: a. There is a mechanism within the first three elements in the page / view for the user to pause, stop, or adjust the audio volume; b. There are keyboard controls that can pause, stop, or adjust the audio volume.

Expected results

  • #2, #3, or #4 is true.

plainEnglish.summary: Where audio plays automatically, there is a way to pause it, stop it, or adjust its volume separately from the system volume.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Background audio masks a screen reader's speech, making the page unusable until it stops - and the system volume control turns off both at once.
